div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

- The Duke and Duchess of Westminster are enter- taining numerous visitors at Eaton Hall, Cheshire, where they intend to stay until the 20th, when they 00118 to town for the season. The Duke and Duchess will go to Clievden at Whitsuntide. _

_ I bear that the Empress Frederick will probably live in England for at least three months of each year, and that the Queen contemplates giving her Bushey Palk as a residence, if the Due de Nemours can be induced to give up that place, which he has rarely visited of late years.

The Baring collapse is being most severely felt in South Devon. Lord Revelstoke and Mr. Idildmay kept up two of the largest country establishments in the West of England, at Membland and Flete re- spectively, buy now both places are practically closed, and all the gardeners, keepers, and other 'ser- vants and employes have been sent away.

Mrs. Douglas, the Cheshire philanthropist, who was nominated by the Duke of Westminster as poor- law guardian for the parish of the Cheshire union, was, on Saturday, returned unopposed. Mrs. Douglas is the first lady who has ever been chosen for the; Cheshire Board. She has also been nominated for two other parishes in the union.

Mr. Ouless, R.A., has finished the picture of Mr. John Morley, which he has been painting for Lord Rosebery, in whose rooms,it will hang among.such important personages'as Pitt, Washington, and Mr. Gladstone. I hear that the painter found 'bitch difficulty in rendering Mr. Morley's mobile features, but it is generally thought that lid has succeeded.

•' 'Prince Napoleon, who observed on his deathbed that he could not succeed in anything, not even )n. - dying, was not very successful in will-making. That he would disinherit his eldest son Victor was , expected, but he has left nothing either to his wife, who repaid his cruelty with kindness, or to his de- voted daughter. lie has left everything to his son Prince Louis, including the " leadership," which is worthless.

The German Emperor's perpetual motion craze has, I hear, set in again with renewed violence. Alsace, Lorraine, and the Rhenish provinces have all to belaspected within the next month, and in addition to his vi6itB to England, the Austrian manceuvres, and Norway, William 11. has "proposed himself " to the King Regent of Holland, at Amster- dam, and the King of the Belgians at Brussels. Half a dozen other "surprise" excursions at least are under discussion.

, Gamblers, beware! Mr. Vaughan (of Bow-street) ii t ibis eye on you. A gang of small boys were on Monday fined merc:kfully, but the, worthy magistrate intimated that hi future no quarter will be shown to "delinquents of this description, as gambling is too often only the prelude to theft and even more serious crimes." So be careful, your Royal Highness, aid you Sir William, and you, Mrs. Arthur W., and all the rest of you noble lords and ladies, whom Mr. Vaughan was evidently alluding to.

Dr. Tanner is not the man who will trouble much about a khockdown blow, but the loss of his favourite blackthorn will be a sad blow to him. It accompanied him on all his travels, and the "twig," as he termed it, was one of the finest specimens of an Irish blackthorn that the island has produced. He was very proud of it; and it very probable that an unnecessary display of it provoked, as is stated, the assault upon him and the logs of the trusty weapon which will no more bear him company.

The Scotland Yard authorities, it is understood, do not attach any importance to the statement made by a man at Maidstone as to the latest White- chapel murder. The story that the unfortunate woman was an accomplice at a burglary is discre- dited for the reason that her movements have been traced up to within a Very short time before the commission of the crime, and it is known that she was then in such a condition that nobody would think of selecting her as an accessory to a robbery.

Father MacLaughlin,who has just issued a new edition of his work, "is- One Religion as Good as Another ?" is one of the most eloquent preachers in the Catholic Church in England. Although his life has been mainly spent in this country, he is, as his name implies, an Irishman, and was born near the town of Rilrea, in the north of Ireland. The scene of his birth is known as "MacLaughlin's Corner," and the pulpit'orator's 'lame is well and honourably known tnroughout Ireland, and in many parts of England and Scotland.

Last week I censured the Lord Chancellor for having jobbed his private secretary into a registrar- ship of bankrupts. lam assured that this appoint- ment has been generally and warmly denounced by the bar, and with good reason, for this Mr. Hope knows nothing whatever of bankruptcy procedure, and he has never in his life been concerned in a bankruptcy case. Lord Halsbury's latest piece of nepotism is the more reprehensible inasmuch as it is well known that more than one eminent bank- ruptcy lawyer would gladly have accepted the vacant place.

As on Good Friday, those who spent their holiday in London on Easter Monday found it bright and oold, but the cold was not quite so intense, and the brightness proved more lasting. From morning till evening the sun continuously shone, bidden now and again behind a bank of cloud; but there was neither the snow nor the keen, cutting wind which made Friday such an unenjoyable day. Easter Monday is to Londoners the holiday par ercellowe. Li] restraints are thrown off, and people troop away in trains, brakes, and wagonettes to the seaside, or into the country, or up the river.

The laws against the Jews in Russia continue to be enforced without diminution of rigour. Those living within the fifty verst limit continue to be forced to leave, though in a particular case so poor were they that, having no means of support, some were allowed a further respite In St. Petersburg, the Prefect shows as--great activity against them as he shows in all his deeds. In a particular case, a rather well-to-do Jew, a furniture dealer, got three days' notice to quit the city, being forced to get rid of his stock at a ruinous price. And the regulations against foreign Jews coming to Russia to transact business as agents or representatives will he strictly enforced.

Human nature, as people say, is very much the same everywheie. The other day a merchant of Berlin remembered it was his servant's birthday, and calling her to him said she might visit her parents in the village hard by. It was then noon, but she must rettun at eight p.m. as his wife, as she knew, was not. in good health. The girl, in ligh glee, sped off. Eight o'clock—then nine o'clock, came, but without the servant. At about midnight the merchant was aroused by a loud knocking and the flashing of a light freim a lantern across his bedroom window, On going down to ascertain the cause, the owner of the lantern thrust a telegram into his hand. It ran:—" This is fete day in our village. Am enjoying myself much. Cannot come to-night. Return early in the morning !—LorrIE."

The practice of putting satirical things into wills —by way of a sort of Parthian shot at the faults and foibles of mankind—is no new thing, but it has i rarely been exampled n a more conspicuous way than in the "curious Irish will" which Mr. Courtenay Moore, of Michelstown, has brought to light. It was made, it appears, by a medical practitioner in the south of Ireland in 1874, and it opens with a bequest-of an a nnu M ity of OO a year, "an ample provision for an .irreclaimable booby, to my nephew, I. L. C., to be paid him only in Australia or any British Colony, where he may desire it to be remitted to him. 'Should he (continues the docu- ment) return to Ireland, England,or Scotland,l then revoke his annuity, and he has my leave to die in the poorhouse."

Lord Granville was a Whig who progressed with the times. He was an enthusiastic adherent as well as a private friend of Mr. Gladstone's and was one of the very few Whigs who accompanied the Liberal leader in his transition to Home Rule. He was es- teemed an excellent man of business, easygoing, full of tact and delicacy, firm where occasion required it, and singularly " ribh in saving commonsense.' As a publi speaker he was distinguished by a pecu- liarly bri Olitd natural vein of humour. He had not the p Heal gifts wild] are requisite for popular oratory, but:as a debater and leader in the House of Lords he iwis eminently successful ; and he was, without doubt, the best after-dinner sPeaker in England. " I have taken the chair so often at public dinners," he used to say " that my friends have nicknanaed me Are la Chaise." LI
GENERAL Satisfaction commands the vast army of people *bo us* "SUNLIGHT SOAP."—Adrt.
THE LATE MR. BR4DLAUGH M.P. "

Mrs. Besant furnishes the Character Sketch for the March nnzaber of the "Review of Reviews," the subject being "Charles Bradlaugh." As might be expected, it is sympathetically written, and pre- sents a vivid picture of the freethonght leader. We subjoin the two extracts:— T f-va) HOW HE BECAME A FREETHINKER. " But now another great step was to be taken. His political education was bowling along merrily under the impetus Chartist meetings; his theological edu- cation was to receive &stimulus in its turn. Charles Bradlaugh was earnest in his religion as in every- thing else; in him all the motive springs of life quivered with passion, and however sternly domin- ant the intellect, every conviction burned like a fire within him. Ile could never hold a belief half- heartedly, and the germs of that intensity of the man were in "the boy. Chosen to prepare for con- firmation, as one of the most promising of his young flock, by the Rev. John Graham Packer, clergyman of his parish church, St. Peter's, Hackney Road, he must needs study the Thirty-nine Articles and com- pare them with the New Testament. Alas for the boy! he found contradictions that puzzled him, and in no spirit of scepticism, but simply desiring help and explanation, he wrote to Mr. Packer and ex- plained his difficulties. That this boy of fourteen, who was expected to do credit to his spiritual pastor, should try to understand instead of learn- ing, was too much for the reverend gentleman's patience. Ile wrote to the parents, denouncing the lad as an atheist, and suspended him for three months from his office as teacher in the Sunday school. This treatment offered no solution to the perplexities in which young Bradlaugh was in- volved, but it did drive him in the direction of free- thought, for, too proud to attend the church while excluded from the school, he betook hithself to Bonner's Fields, where political and religious dis- cussions were held on Sundays. He soon began to take part in these. defending Christianity against its assailants, but losing, bit by bit, in argument, the faith whiCh Mr. Packer had maintained only by terrorism.. So things went on, and the end of the three months did not see the teacher back in the Sunday school; and months passed over, and the old beliefs crumbled away. A debate on the ." Inspiration of the Bible" in 1849 gave the coup ofs grdes to his boyish faith; he suffertd and struggled and prayed, but all in vain; he clung to his reli- gion, but it melted away beneath his grasp. At last, towards the end of 1849, he made one last attempt. He had been studying Robert Taylor's " Diegesis," and he asked Mr. Packer to help him to find some answer to it. But Mr. Packer still owned no argument but force," and the fact that this per- tinaciously inquiring lad of sixteen had filled up the measure of his sins by becoming a teetotaller rendered desperate the irate cleric. He persuaded his employers to give him three days in which "to change his opinions or lose his situation "—taking the very means to stereotype the boy in his views. Even then, Charles Bradlaugh did net know how to hesitate between personal auvantage and honesty of life. He stood to his opinions and lost his situation, and went out alone into the world, outcast from home, knowing not how to earn his bread, a boy in his sevunteenth year; but in his dauntlessness, his honesty, his determination to be true at any cost, he was even then the Charles Bradlaugh whose watchword was "Thorough" all through his gal- lant life. .Mr. Bradlaugh enlisted in the' 7th Dragoon Guards when he vias 17, and was a soldier for about three years. Mrs. Besant thus describes SOME OF HIS EXPLOITS. "Leaves" was his regimental coubriquet,,for he drank only tea and was always reading books, and 'when they found that being a .teetotaller and a student didinot prevent him from exhibiting excep- tional physical courage, and from often standing between ti-tem and unfair treatment, the name of "Leaves "became one of affection instead of con- tempt. On one or two occasions, however, he nearly came to grief. At Rathmines the clergyman of the parish preached a sermon, which was, he said, above the heads of the soldiers present. This annoyed Private Bradlaugh, and he wrote to the preacher, criticising the sermon and pointing to various blun- ders contained the? ein. On the following Sunday, the regiment marched to church as usual, but "Leaves" and his comrades were prepared for action if any insolence should be shown in the pulpit. A contemptuous sentence began, and in a moment three hundred heavy cavalry sabres smote the floor, unhooked, and allowed to fall in one mighty crash. An enquiry was ordered,and Private Bradlaugh was summoned,but luckily the Duke of Cambridge came to hold a review, and no further action was taken. The other occasion was even more critical. He was orderly-room clerk, and a newly-arrived young officer came into the room where he was sitting at work,and addressed to him some discourteous order.l Private Bradlaugh took no notice. The order was repeated with an oath. Still no movement. Then it came again, with sonie 'foul words added. The young soldier rose, drew himself to his full height, and, walking up to the officer, bade him leave the room or he would throw him out. The officer went but in a few moments the grounding of muskets was heard outside,the door opened, and the Colonel walked in, accompanied by the officer. It was clear that the private soldier had committed an act for which he might be court-martialled, and as he said once, "I felt myself in a tight place." The officer made his accusation. and Private Bradlaugh was bidden to explain. lie asked that the officer should state the exact words in which he had addressed him, and the officer who had, after all, a touch of honour in him, gave the offensive sentence,word for word. Then Private Bradlaugh said, addressing his Colonel, that the officer's memory must surely be at fault in the whole matter,as he could not have used language so unbecoming an officer and a gentleman. The Colonel turned to tne officer with a dry remark: "I think Private Bradlaugh is right ; there must be some mistake," and he left the room. Mrs. Besant concludes with the following lofty tribute :—" To us who loved him `the loss is izre- mediable, and England will seek.long ere she find a sturdier and more. loyal son, • Without faith in God but full of love td man, he led a pure and noble life, and he has won the only immortality his strong soul craved, the memory of honest service, faith- fully wrought, loyally rendered—deathless memory in a world made nobler by his living, richer by his sacrifices, poorer by his death." BILLED AT AN ENTERTAINMENT.

The Manchester coroner held an inquest on Wednes- day touching the death of a youth named Thomas Whalley, who was fatally stabbed the previous night while personating Mercutio in the duel scene of " ttomeo and Juliet "at a school entertainment. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," the coroner characteris- ing the swords used as most dangerous weapons.

div.head: TRAGEDY AT LINCOLN.
div.p: TRAGEDY AT LINCOLN.
MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.

A sho'clitiim—urde-r and attempted suicide were com- mitted in Lincoln on Tuesday night. The victim is a widow named Garner, about 32 years of age, and her murderer and the would-be suicide is a young man about 23 named Alfred Spencer. It appears that Spencer, who is a butcher, lodged with Mrs. Garner, who is the widow of an ostler, and who has five children, at Stanley- Chelmsford-st. After nine months his master dis- charged him for the reason, it is alleged, that he and the widow had become too intimate. Since then the man has had no regular employment, but he continued to live with Mrs. Garner. On Sunday evening he went to her house and again tried to induce her to marry him. She still declined, whereupon he produced a pistol and threa- tened to. shoot her. On Tuesday night, about nine o'clock, Spencer again presented himself at the house, and afterfurther trying to induce the woman to have him, produced the revolver and shot her in the breast. He then placed the weapon to his own mouth and firea, afterwards shooting a third shot in the region of his heart. The occurrence was witnessed by the woman's children, who at once raised an alarm. Medical aid was soon obtained, but little could be done for the unfortu- nate woman, who died about ten o'clock. It was found that the man's injuries were not of so serious a nature. The bullet fired at his heart had failed to take effect through the clahing, but the shot into the mouth had produced a seveie'wourid. He was removed to the County Hospital,.wher'e, he now lies.

div.head: . T.IIE-EX.11611-NER, SA LIBERAL BAZAAIi. AT ST.:
div.p: . T.IIE-EX.11611-NER, SA LIBERAL BAZAAIi. AT ST.:

HELENS. OPENING BY, LORD ABERDEEN. A three-days' bazaar, under the auspices of the St. Helens Liberal Association and the St. Helens Women's Liberal Association, was opened by Lord and-Lady Aberdeen, in the St. Helens Town Hall,on Wednesday afternoon. This is the firsts occasion upon which the, local Liberals have adopted such means to further the cause they have at heart ; and the declared objects they have in view are the pro- vision of funds to continue the work of political I, education by public meetings, lectures, and litera- ture, and to ensure the registration of every one entitled to vote at the coming general election. The response to the appeal for contributions was of a liberal character, and the attendance of the Earl of Aberdeen and of the Countess of Aberdeen at the opening ceremony proved a cheering augury of the ultimate success of the move- ment. Of the St. Helens Liberal Association Alderman Thomas Cook, J.P., is the president, Councillor John Forger chairman of the executive committee, Councillor Martin treasurer, Councillor J. P. Mearns honorary secre- tary, and Mr. Joseph Bain secretary and agent. Mrs. J. P. Mearns is the president of the Women's Association; Mrs. Martin, chairman of the committee ; Mrs. Forster and Miss Dale, treasurers ; Miss MiKinley, secretary ; and Miss G. Whittaker, assistant secretary. Special committees were appointed for the bazaar arrangements and these included Councillors J. B. Leach (chairman), H. Martin (treasurer). Messrs. F. Dromgoole, G. Moon and J. Bain (secretarie.) ; Mrs. Martin, chairman of the ladies' committee ; ire., Forster, treasurer • and Miss M`Kinley, secretary. The erection of the stalls and the decoration of the hall was entrusted to Messrs. Wilkin- son and Co., of Liverpool, and the committee selected designs representative of the village of Hawarden with its quaint old-fashioned cottages, whilst stretched across the platform was a splendid painting of Hawarden Castle, the residence of Mr. Gladstone. There were five stalls in addition to the refreshment and flower departments, and they were distinguished by.appropriate political titles including " Gladstone" stall, the " Nationalist " stall the " Harcourt" stall, the "Morley" stall, and a stall of provisions and groceries. There was in additien a " Rosebery " flower stall. Other attractions included exhibitions and entertainments of a miscellaneous char- acter. The official catalogue of the bazaar was of an elaborate description, and contained excellent photo- graphs of Lord and Lady Aberdeen, Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C., and Mrs. Kennedy, Mr: J. T. Brunner, M.P., and Mrs. Brunner, Alderman T. Cook, J.P., Colonel D. Gamble, C. 8., Mr. A. Sinclair, J.P., Counicllor John Forster, Councillor H. Martin, Councillor J. P. Mearns, and Councillor J. B. Leach. The Earl and Countess Aberdeen journeyed from Lendon, via Crewe and War- rington, and arrived at St. Helens station about one o'clock. The London and North-Western Railway Com- pany had placed a saloon at the disposal of the dis- tinguished guests, and they were' accompanied by their daughter, Lady Marjorie Gordon. They were met at the station by Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C.. and Mrs. Ken- nedy • Alderman Cook and Mrs. Cook, Councillors Fors- ter, Martin, Warns, and Leech, and a number of other gentlemen. The party were afterwards driven in open carriages to the Town Hall, and outside the station and fronting the Town Hall large crowds had assembled, who heartily cheered Lord and Ladv Aberdeen. At the Town Hall the Mayor (Councillor E. Johnsou) welcomed Lord and Lady Aberdeen, after which luncheon was served to about 70 ladies and gentlemen in the new sup- perroom. On-the entrance of Lord and Lady Aberdeen into the hall where the bazaar was held they were warm- ly cheered by the large audience,and Miss Coek,daughter of Alderman Cook, presented a handsome bouquet to the countess. At the opening proceedings Alderman T. Cook presided. and he was supported by Lord and Lady Aberdeen, Lady Marjorie Gordon, Mr. and Mrs. W. R. Kennedy, QC., Mr. J. A. Duncan, M.P., Mrs. Cook, the local Liberal leaders,and a number of promininent politi- cians from Liverpool and the district. The Chairman ex- pressed the pleasure and satisfaction the Liberals of St Helens felt in being honoured hy the presence of their distinguished visitors. Councillor John Forster then gave an address in explanation of the objects of the bazaar, and said they had determined that the repre- sentation of St. Helens shculd be changed, and they had made up their minds that that should be brought about, If possible, by educating the constituency and by the con- tinuous hard work of the Liberal workers. Councillor J. P. Warns next read an address to Lord and Lady Aberdeen by the Executive Committee of the Liberal Association. Lord Aberdeen was received with prolonged applause. He said he had often heard of a Lancashire welcome, and now Lady Aberdeen and himself had experienced what was meant by a Lancashire welcome., They had not only given them a most kind and genial reception, but they had handed to him a more than kindly-worded address, beautifully illuminated, which would form a lasting and most pleasing souvenir, and would certai9ly be a most interesting ' recollection and experience. He thought they were to be congratulated upon their prospects and upon the results of the per- severing work they had bestowed upon the preparations. It was inevitable, at the same time, that that day a feel- ing of sadness should tinge the inaugural proceedings. The Liberal party, nay, the whole country, was distinctly the poorer because of the loss of that most accomplished and eminent man who had passed away from them—the late Lord Granville. He knew all their hearts would go out with feelings of deep sympathy towards his noble widow, who had watched as only a true wife could watch through those many sad weeks of illness. And, again, they could not but think with deep concern and sympathy of their great leader and chief, Mr. Glad- stone--(cheers)—who had lost in Lord Granville the oldest and, he ventured to say, the most trusted and the most intimate of his colleagues and friends, one whose loyalty to Mr. Gladstone could never be surpassed or equalled, one who had showed again and again that he had the power of self-abnegation, the power of ignoring himself, which set an example that every man or woman in the country might do well to follow. Turning to the immediate objects of their gathering, he said he found they were not three "isms," but three " ations"—regis- tration, organisation, and education politically. He understood that for the last three years their association had devoted themselves to studying the exact position of the constituency and paving the way for future suc- cess, and that work of laying a foundation for the coming struggle was one of the utmost importance and had evi- dently been pursued, and would be pursued, with that earnestness and perseverance which alone could guarantee the required results. When they looked at a wider field—the main objects they desired to promote and secure—he could not help being re- minded of the expressions in the address where they spoke of the great cause of Home Rule. It was a great cause, and it was founded upon great princi- ples—upon the principles of justice and conciliation ; it was based upon experience—the experience of all history .that they would never coerce people into exercising goodwill. They might lead and,guide them by conciliation, but force would never be a remedy. He did not desire to enter upon that large theme, but he would like to say in passing that he thought they had fresh proof that the support of Home Rule was more than a mere matter of principle and conviction. And the proof was found in the fact that the recent troublous period through which they had been passing had had no appreciable effect in shaking the alle- giance of the Liberals in regard to that matter. There had been much to deplore, bet he trusted some of the painful phases in regard to the unhappy division amongst the Irish party were passing away. He Sometimes felt an if Mr. Parnell wished to get rid of his old colleagues and friends in a summary sort of fashion.politically speaking, but he thought heewould-find them of very tough mate- rial, and that they would not be easily disposed of. His (Lord Aberdeen's) impression was that events would i shape themselves n the matter, and he trusted speedily. But they must not be impatient. In time the Irish party would once more be in a position to hold their own and to press forward that policy .to which they had been so long devoted, and in regard to which they had -.exercised a great deal ,of patience which he trusted would soon be rewarded. (Applause.) Proceeding to speak col social reform and , social legislation, he remarked that it was coming knore and more to the front, but they,rnust not speak as i they,as Liberals, had anything like a monopoly in that respect. What he said was that everyone who Was prepared to strive for the promotion of social refoi•ms.in Ihe many directions which would occur to all,. was jeining in patriotic work. They were accustomed to associate the picket. of patriotism with the defence of their position and their prestige in the world, and by war if necessary, at all hazards, to maintain their dignity and posit ion. 'That was quite right, but it .was not less patriotic or less noble to fight 'an unflinching war against such internal enemies as vice, crime, and pauperism. It was in those matters that they should join hand in hand and strive until they saw some practical advance and changes. In many respects there was room for reform, and so long as that was the case they should not be idle or flinch from .the.work before them. (Applause.) He concluded by re- marking that he had some regard for their present mem- ber, Mr. Seton-Karr, and he would like to see him tnern- .ber for some other constituency, but he ventured to pre- dict, after what he had seen and heard, that St. lichens would be represented by another member at the next general election. (Applause.) They had a cause in which they believed, and they had a candidate in whom they believed, and he felt sure they would carry him to victory. (Loud cheers.) The Countess of Aberdeen then, in response to an appeal from the chairman that she should speak a few words of encouragement, said she did not think they needed any encouragement,for it was rather she and Lord Aberdeen who sought encouragement, and she was sure they wouldgo away very mubh encouraged. (Cheers.) She should go to other places and encourage the Liberals by telling them of what they had done and were doing at St. Helens. She 4.sked.tp be excused sayiner any more, as she was really afraid to speak before Lord Aberdeen. (Loud laughter.) They need not laugh, for it was per- fectly true. (Renewed laughter.) She hoped they would not press her further, but if on some future occa- sion she needed more encouragement they would perhaps. allow her to come to St. Helens and have them all to her- )

div.head: TUB open.
div.p: TUB open.

self. (Loud applause She had very great pleasure in declaring the bazaar (Cheers.) On the motion of Councillor U. Martin, seconded by Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C., a vote of thanks was tendered to Lord and Lady Aberdeen; and Lord Aberdeen, in res- ponding, moved a similar compliment to the chairman, which was seconded by Mr. J. A. Duncan. M.P., and sup- ported by Councillor J. B. Leach.—This cencluded the proceedings. SPEECH OF MR. BRUNNER, M.P.

The attendance throughout Wednesday was very large, and the total receipts amounted to .£'27l. The bazaar was again opened on Thursday after- noon, when the ceremony was performed by Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. for the Northwich Division, who was accompanied by Mrs. Brunner. Aid erman T. Cook, president of the association occupied the chair. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., who was warmly received, congratulated tnein on the success of the enterprise in which they were engaged and upon having secured the attendance of Lord and Lady Aberdeen on the previous day. The good things of this world, as the ladies would know, came to those who deserved them. It was said •' Faint heart never won fair lady," and certainly it was true in politics that courage begets success. And in Lord and Lady Aberdeen they had representatives of Liberal principles—the best of their kind. (Applause.) His presence in S. Helens that day carried him back a long way. He had old associations of thetown, and it was now 23 years ago since he came to give his first parliament- ary vote, and he remembered very well the cheers that greeted the omnibus in which he drove from Widnes. Widnes, as many of them might not, perhaps, be aware, was at that time a satellite of the great sun of St. Helens, and he might therefore claim to be almost one of themselves. (Laughter and applause.) He remembered very well how, in 1865, he was not a Toter for South-west Lancashire, when there was oppor- tunity of giving a vote on the winning side and of return- ing their great leader to Parliament. He had saved his money, and had not been quite twelve months in the house he occupied. He begged the rate collector not to charge him the full year's poor-rate, and in consequence of that he saved is. 3d. and lost his vote. (Laughter.) Now, that should boa warning to them not to save their money that day, but to spend it freely for the Liberal party. (Applause.) Be briefly referred to the wintry weather that day, and said that inside the hall he found the political atmosphere as balmy as it possibly could be. They were in the full tide of spring, and were looking forward to a glorious summer. The weather they had gone through since 1866 had been one of a gradual bright- ening promise, though they had a capful of wind at Don- caster. They had perhaps half a gale at Bassetlaw ; they had a damp, dull, drizzling, disagreeable, fog at Aston Manor, and they had a regular " blizzard " -last November from the direction of the Divorce Court. But I they as Li barals, were old sailors, and they passed through that sort of thing unscathed. (Applause.) There were two speeches in the morning papers, through which he had read with some interest. The address by Lord Aber- deen had given him unqualified pleasure, and the refer- ences to their old friend Lord Granville were graceful and fitting as they were heartfelt to a degree. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: ......_.4._ LABOUR AND EDUCATION
div.p: ......_.4._ LABOUR AND EDUCATION
BY H. WHITHAM.

Why should the working-man be educated, and what should his education consist of? This is a big question, and I rather doubt my ability to deal with it. Mr. Atkinson, an American political economist says, " Other things being equal, high wages, coupled with low cost of production are the necessary result of the most intelligent application of machinery to the arts, provided the education of the operative keeps pace with the improvement of the machinery." Again, we have it on the authority of Mill that, "it is questionable if all the mechanical inventions yet made have lightened the day's toil of any human being." Individual inventiveness has got ahead of the education of the operative,therefore individuals make fortunes,while the workers' toil is not lightened. I think none of my readers will accuse me of putting forth any new or strange ideas. If there are any such. I ask them s'anply to look around and tell us what they see. Is the world all that is desired ? Is it no question of" Darkest England, and the way out ?" What it is in England, it is here in America. Throughout the continent of Europe it is the same. A timid and half-frightened Emperor is stepping carefully to- wards Socialism. The Russian Emperor is gradually withdrawing himself outside the pale of civilization. America and England are the only nations whose doors are open to the oppressed, and of these two the dcors of America are gradually closing. And what of the doors of England? Every large city has now forming within its boundaries a I foreign colony. I see that in Whitechapel, Lon- don, with a population of 700,000, more than one half are foreigners, and speak a foreign tongue. Surely none will say this is desirable. We are bound to put to ourselves the question, why is it ? here in America we are yearly receiving thousands from Germany and Scandinavia; in fact from all parts of the European continent; and they come well equipped for the struggle. The Germans and Austrians seem well, and better educated than the English. Like the American boy op leaving school, a large majority are fitted to take pesitions either in the workshop or the office. Do these men come because they love America rather than their Father- land? Certainly not. They come because they hope to find the conditions of life more favourable, be- cause they are sick of the horrible grind, in fact because the . education they have received has taught them what the pleasures of life are, and, that there is something in the world besides work, work, work. Let no one overlook the fact, that in every civilized nation there are thousands upon thousands who, anxious to work, can not by any means find employment. I have myself seen, nay have with pleasure found a home for, a fellow- countryman, who has tramped this city all over seeking work, and who as .11 last resort offered his labour for food and a bed—and was oven then un- successful. The world's

WORK MUST BE MORE EQUALLY DIVIDED. In this nineteenth century, among any people who have begun to utilize the forces and methods of modern production, there is no necessity for want. There is no good reason why even the poor- est should not have all the comforts, all the luxur- ies, all the opportunities for culture, all the grati- fications of refined taste that only the richest now enjoy. There is no reason why anyone should be compelled to long and monotonous labour. Did invention and discovery stop to-day, the forces of production are ample for this. There can be no doubt as to the long hours men have to work. Quite recently, in the debate on the hours of railway ser- vants, in the British House of Commons, Mr. Chan- ning denounced the conduct of the North British directors as deplorable and discreditable,' and nut a word was said in their defence in the course of the night. On twelve English and Welsh lines, he said, 33,179 out of 55,278 men worked over twelve hours a day during September. 1889. There were 69,825 cases of duty for upwards of fifteen hours, and 7,341 for upwards, of eighteen hours. The minor railways were even worse. The North British, in Scotland, in September, 1887, employed 554 engine drivers over eighteen hours a day, and in September, 1889, the number had increased to 927, while be- tween March, 1888, and March, 1890, the number rose from 514 to 1,016. The working man should be educated to put a stop to this. It works well for neither individual nor, nation. .11e should be taught that—

To live is to labour, and vest, To swim, and to ride, and to run, To delight whom ctelightestus best, To rejoice in the wind and th,e sun,. To lean all the lessons of nature That body and soul may be one.. I have no desire to pose as a croaker, nor yet am I at all pessimistic. I. have before me Utterances of the highest and most respected of the Church dignataries who, venturing to look ahead, h ave dared to give expression to their opinions; and one and all are agreed that the future welfare of the civilized world depends largely upon the intelli- gence of the masses. SOCIALISM l UPON,. US. Whether it is to be on,the whole lines of selfishnessr so well desCribed by Lord Woliley with reference. to the white traders in Africaor not remains to be i4en. The noble lord.-sais-: It is useless to appeal to their humanity or feeling. The average trader does not care whether the vile stuff he sells claims more victims than war or pestilence, or whether the arms he barters broil and ivory causes large districts to be laid waste by the slave-dealer. If he only-grows rich he cares nothing for all the suffering he may infliet. The mouth of this same trader is often filled with moral platitudes when speaking on European African topics." These traders' have all, no douht, been well educated so far as " the three R's "go, but it is certainly not the education we want now. I propose in mV next to make a few remarks further on this subject, with reference to the child's school or Kindergarten.

div.head: solks DAY, APRIL 4, 1.891. PERCIVALO., GORDON; THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT.
div.p: solks DAY, APRIL 4, 1.891. PERCIVALO., GORDON; THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT.
BY SYLVANUS Core
CHAPTER V.
*A
A FRIEND IN DISTRESS-PERCIVAL ON THE TRAIL.

When the bandit chief had signified his desire to converse with the colonel upon a matter of business both Crawford and Wilson had politely withdrawn; so now Maxwell sat alone while Don Lopez was absent; and he was wrought to a pitch of deepest indignation. The family seat of the Archers was only across the border between Devon and Dorset, and not more than a score of miles from his own favourite hunting lodge; and in the chase, and at social gatherings, he had met both Richard and Roland Archer many times. He had known them during the life of their father, when they were but youths ; and he had held social intercourse with the elder brother since he had come to the title. Richard he knew to be an honourable, true-hearted man, brave and loyal; but Roland he had never liked; nor had he been liked generally. He was selfish and unprincipled, professing to be of a religions bent, while at heart, and in truth, he was a whited sepulchre. xwell was busily engaged in overhauling his rernemisrance of the two brothers, when a curtain that hung at the entrance to his apartment was pulled aside, and Don Lopez entered, followed ny a roan and a little girl. The man was young—not over thirty—tall, and strong, and handsome. In height he was over six feet, but the perfect symmetry of form and pro- portion, with the beautiful contour of the whole man, served to deceive one unless be stood close bcsido or before him. At a little distance, with no one near him to afford contrast, he did not appear so tall as he really was. His abundaut hair was of a rich auburn colour, gracefully curling about his shapely head ; his eyes were of a deep, dark blue, and his handsome, manly face the mirror of all honour and truth. The child had her fsther's beautiful eyes; the same curling, golden hair, and, as the brigand had intimated, she was beautiful in every way. Dimples were in her cheeks and in her chin' and when she smiled the whole face was lighted up with a radiance that was seraphic. Archer came in like one doubting. As he after- wards explained, "he dared not believe in such a piece of heaven-sent good fortune." But a single look into the brave, battle-worn face banished the last shadow of doubt. The brigand saw that the recognition between the two men was mutual, and without waiting for more he quietly slipped away, letting the arras fall behind him. With both hands outstretched, and big tears starting down his cheeks, the baronet hastened forward with tottering step, and embraced the new-found friend as he might have embraced a new life; for, really, the promise of redemption had come to him with the sight of this true man. " Maxwell 0, thank God I—lt is Harry Maxwell 1" holding him at arm's length, while he scanned the well,reinembered features. "0, this is a blessing indeed !" Maxwell returned the embrace with a love and goodwill not to be doubted. " My dear Archer, you must have suffered." " The brigand told you how I was situated?" " Yes, I understand the whole." "Then, dear Colonel, look at this," and he lifted the child in his arms. " Look at her. Is she not a cherub? And think of the awful doom that has hung over her 0, I have suffered 1" Maxwell offered to take the child, and she sat upon his knee right lovingly. She saw in him a friend, and she was old enough to fully realise the value of friendship in such au hour. "0, good sir I—good Lord Clavburn 1 you will help nly dear papa if you can. He has been very unhappy; and I have tried to make him smile as he used to do, but I cannot. But dear, good sir, you must not think my papa is afraid. 0, no 1 It is because of my naughty—" " Carrie !" "1 must tell him papa. He ought to know what Uncle Roland has done. "Alas 1" groaned Sir Richard, as he took his little daughter upon his own knee, and ten- derly kissed her, "I fear she. shadows forth the truth." " Donot distress yourself, Sir Richard," reterned the colonel, with sympathetic tenderness. "Our captor has told me sufficient to enlighten me upon the whole matter. I know your brother of old, and you will parden me if I confess to you that I am not surprised at his cold-blooded treachery." "I do not think I can say quite so much," responded the baronet, with a mournful shake of the head. "I knew that Roland was not like others, and that his tongue was not entirely unused to falsehood; but that he could thus coolly and wickedly consign me to a horrible and untimely death—depriving this cherub of a father, in her tender age, and in this far distant—" "Papa 1 papa 1" broke in the child, "why don't you speak the whole truth? My naughty uncle knows that they will kill me, too—as I should want them to do if they killed you. I don't think they would make me suffer." Archer drew the child more closely to his bosom while both the men wiped away the tears they could not keep back. "Enough of that," said Maxwell, when he could command his speech. "Only, you may tell me, if you will, how you wrote to your brother. What means had he for raising the money ?" "I have written three times; and we know that one of the letters, at least, came to his hand; and, if one did so, so must have done the others. I sent him a cheque on my banker for considerably more than the amount required. 0, there can have been no miscarriage—nu mistake. Roland wants my shoes 1" "So I do most sincerely believe," Maxwell re- plied. "But rest you easy. We will pay a visit to your dear brother when he least expects it. Be sure you shall be set free with me." Before Archer could collect himself for speech, little Caroline sprang forward and threw her arms around the colonel's neck, and kissed him ' • and for a long time he held her there, pressed lovingly against his throbbing heart. The sweet cherub imaged to him the home of his childhood in the far-away land, and his great heart went out te her with its full strength of fatherly affection. "There, there, no more of that.," he cried, inter- rupting Sir Richard in a lame attempt to return thanks that could satisfy himself. "I can under- stand your feelings. And do you not forget that I am to enjoy as much in this deed as you are. And now, dear fellow, tell me how you came here. How did the brigands come to pick you up?" "I left England chiefly for my wife's health," the baronet commenced, "our physicians having declared that only a visit to the continent and a passing of the winter in a more genial clime could save her. We settled down for the winter in Naples, but my wife contined to fail there, and the wise ones said she must be taken away from the coast. We planned to go to Spoleto; but we took Rome in our way, and in that city she was taken down, entirely unable to proceed further. And there, early in February, she died. , I re- mained in Rome with my child and her nurse until April, when I took passage in an English brig, which would laud me on the southern coast of . Spain, at Malaga. "We reached Malaga safely, and thence I pro- posed to make my way to Madrid. Early in May we reached Talavera, ; but, as the French' under Victor, were marching in that direction, we did not tarry there. On the second day from that, while making our way along the Northern bank of the Tagus, with two hired guides in company, we were stopped by the brigands. One of the guides cried aloud the name of Don Lopez, whereupon both of them ran away, leaving us to our fate. "And that is all. Of course, I offered no battle against such a force. The brigand chief had gained full information of my name, my rank and my cir- _ _ _ _ _
c-umstances. At fira I wenderecl_ how he 'Could

have done it; but I have solved the mystery, at ,least to my own satisfaction. My two innocent appearing guides were devoted to him. He brought me to this place; named fifty thousand Engli,,th crowns as the ransom of myself and child and nurse. That was at the beginning of the second week in May ; so we have been here almost tin•ce months. The brigands have been kind to us; ann, as you will readily believe, Don Lopez, actuated by his own interest, has done all in his power to assure the transmission of my letters and the retuin of money." - Having asked a few questions, Maxwell told how 110 been entrapped, after which the conversa- tion turned upon other subjects, and so they talked until almost midnight, the child asleep all • this time in the colonel's' arms. Then me of the brigand sentinels came and conducted the baros..ep. apd his daughter to their own dormitory. On the following morning Don Lopez appeared, sfrci acaed, Maxwell what he thought of Sir llade caw. The answer was brief, and to the

^g My dear sir, will you be kind enough to hold Sir Richard Archer as you hold ? Treat him kindly, as he assured me you have done, and await my ability to help him ; for this assurance I give you. I shall not leave you without taking him with me, provided he shall be alive and able to travel." "That is all sufficient, my lord, and you may depend upon it that I will keep the faith." with a polite bow he departed. That morning, at the breakfast table, the ecn- versation of the hussars turned upon the subject of the boy Percival. The brigand had offered to st-,‘.'e his lordship's meals at a ellars.te board, but he would not have it so. Ai ke bad said once before : "We are brothers in ..niefeaune, and we will be l)rothers indeed." _ _

Wilson was sure he had seen the boy crawling away upon his hands and knees, and it was plainly lo be seen that he attributed his conduct to fear. Not so Tom Crawford, however. He could not put away the impression that the little hero would yet show his hand. The oolonel, who had listened for a time to the conversation without offering a word, now said :

"The boy has not forsaken us, and if you wish to know how strong in that direction my faith is, I will tell you." He cast a quick glance around, to be sure no eavesdropper was near, and then went on. "I have resolved to put off writing any letter for money until our boy hero has had a fair opportunity to show his hand. We must not for- get the giant difficulties in this way, nor can we guess at the plan he will adopt. All is,—l am content to wait a reasonable time. The mixing of Sir Richard Archer's business with my own affords me an excellent excuse for my delay in writing." "Bless you, my lord," cried Tom, in the fullness of his heart. "You know the boy, and you do him only justice. Let us wait." Three days passed after this, and Sir Richard was permitted to enjoy the pleasure of the com- panionship of his countrymen as he pleased. The hussars fell in love with little Caroline, and more than once Tom Crawford was heard to say to him- self, what a handsome pair this bright-eyed girl and his Percival would make. What a pity that the boy could not be with them. On the evening of the fourth day, when Don Lopez had come in from a minor expedition, he sought his lordship, and was anxious to know when he would write his letter.
"I have waited," said Maxwell, "in the hope, or, at least, in the strong desire that we might bear from Sir Richard's brother."
" Humph " exclaimed the brigand, "you do not expect to hear from that man! I -tell you lie thinks full sure that the baronetcy is his own, and I am told the estate is valuable." .
"Many an English peer is not so wealthy. However, you may let me have materials for writing, and I will go at the letter on the morrow." _

"Why not this evening?" "I must confer with Sir Richard first, and I would like to have him by me when I write." "Very well. I will send him to you at once, if that will please you." "I wish you would." "And mark you," the robber said, stopping and turning near the entrance, "you do not wish to write more thhn is necessary, so be careful that you convey no intelligence to which I could object. Do not mention these particular mountains, and you had better not speak of the cavern. Let your friends in England simply know that you are in Spain, that Don Lopez de Miranda holds you in keeping, and that the nearest point for the deposit of letters to his addrese is at Truxillo. That is all I have to suggest." And so saying he lifted the arras and passed out, and shortly thereafter Sir Richard Archer came in. To his friend Maxwell made known the way and manner in which the business stood between him- self and the brigand; and having made this clear, ho said : _ _

"I must take the pen to-morrow; but I can write one letter at least that shall be condemned, and that, too, without any appemance of inten- tional wrong on my part. I tell you, Sir Richard, my hope of help from that noble boy of ours does not fail. At all events, do you hold yourselves in readiness, and be ready for movement at a moment's notice."

"Really, my lord, your faith in the infant surprises me. If I mistake not, he is no older than my little Carrie." "Only one month older; but he comes of heroic blood. His father was one of the bravest, and one of the most intelligent, and one of the very best men in our army. .His father's father was Captain Archibald Gorden, younger son of Sir Timothy Gordon, of Gordoncroft ; and his father's mother was Mary Pattern, daughter of George Patten, of Devonshire. So, you see, he conies of the best of stock. Yes, I have faith in him. Of his own brave thought and purpose, entirely unaided, he saved the lives of more than a thou- sand men at sea; and he will not fail us if he lives, and has his strength. You will be on the lookout ?" Aud the baronet promised that he would be ready when called upon ; and shortly thereafter he took his kayo, leaving Maxwell to study over the fram- ing of his letter. * •

Colonel Max well had not mistaken the character nor the purpose of Percival Gordon ; for be it known that the boy's name had been already changed on the rolls and roster of the regiment. The little fellow was wonderfully precocious. lie had heard much of the noted brigand of the San Benito, and ha 4 studied his methods; and from the moment he had seen the skulkers in the village of St. Martin he had been strongly impressed with the thought that the ambulance, being far behind the rear-guard of the army, might be attacked.

So, when the first note of alarm had come, he was as certain of the situation, and set his wits au work to plan how he might best assist his colonel and his companions. It flashed through his mind that so important a man as Lord Clayburn would be holden for a heavy ransom, and, of course, the three sergeants would be held with him ; for it was not the enstotn of the brigands to butcher any one who might pay even the smallest ransom.

He did not believe that the brigands knew o his presence. He had suspected them from the first, and had kept himself in hiding almost, entitely. Should he make his escape from the vehicle the robbers would not miss him. While he was wondering how he could escape, the rear part of the ambulance was driven far Into the thick tangle of the wildwood, and he seized the opportunity. Quickly and noiselessly opening the door, he slipped out, sinking at once upon his bands and knees, and plunged into the thicket, graf,ping firmly the large pistol, and stopping not until he had g,ined a point beyond the boands of the brigands' vision, and yet by slight movements to and fro, he was able to keep a strict watch uron the enemy.

And so he watched until the brigands had secured their prisoners, and set forth on their departUre, when he prepared to follow. But the guard which the chief bad left behind to pull the ambulance out of the way troubled him materially. However, he watched his opportunity, and Pre:3ently the burly ruffians made a movement that favoured him. • Ttiey all entered the carriage to see what they could bring to light worth appropriating, and while they were thus engaged the boy crept from hiding.place, and soon gained the road at a point where the robber guard could not discover•

And he was not a moment too soon; for as ho rounded an abrupt turn shortly after emerging into the path, he saw the last of the brigands'disappear- ing beyond a hedge by the wayside, and on coining up to the spot he could not, for the life of him, see where the passage had been made; but he had seen where the rascals had surely disappeared, and reason told him there must be an opening in the dense wall of wildwood somewhere; so he investigated, and very soon had the satis- faction of having discovered eue;e-...0" contrived curtain of interlaced vine and snrub. With some difficulty, for the tangled MANS was heavy to lift, he made his way through, and found a wed-defined path beyond, and in the distance he saw the rear files of the brigand troop. For a time hi S course was simple. He had only to .keep the troop in sight nod avoid di-lcovery, which he miklav%.,done easily enough had not uli tilleltpecteaTobOtiele presented itself. At three several stations on the way guards u ere posted, ireni the manner of whose challengirg our hero judged that they were a fixture—tleat sEntiuels were kept there night and day, to prevent surprise of the brigands in taleir mountain retreat, wherever it might be. But fortunately he was ab,e to pass tle2se.guards without betraying himself, which he did by. climbing to the • overhanging crags, thus niaizinglis way high above the watchmen a heads. And .I,his very need was, in the end, to favour him exceedingly. Upon coming .in sight, of the third sentinel, whose pest the boy jteied to be fully half way up the meuutain.side,_he de' ested,a

convenient shelf far above the path. which he reached by way of a broad fissure filled with s growth of moss and shrubbery. l'AUpon arriving at the summit of the shelf, he saw the head of the brigand troop filing to the left, his station being on the right of the path as he ascended. The brigands were turning to the left, and entering upon a broad table of rock shaped like an amphitheatre, the points of the arch pointing towards his ownposition, while on the far side arose a perpendicular wall, its towering summit crownea with fir. And presently he saw something that interested him deeply. '.%idway in this high wall was a vertical rent or fissure, wide at the bottom, and closing in a point about two-thirds of the way up. And this rent he found to be the entrance to a cavern, within which the whole party disappeared without leaving their saddles. So here was the brigands' rendezvous. He stood for a little time, and finding that none of the gang seemed disposed to reappear, he thought he would sit down and rest. "'Close at hand he saw a bed of golden moss, whereon he found a spot that could not be seen from the amphitheatre opposite, it being shielded not only by a large boulder, but also by a thick curtain of waxberry bushes. And here he• sat down—sat for a season, and then suffc3red hie head to sink. He had endured a great deal; he had slept but little since the retreat of the army had begun ; and very soon after his head had found the soft pillow sleep overcame him and he slept soundly. i _ .
(To be continued.)

div.head: FATAL RESULT OF IMMERSION.
div.p: FATAL RESULT OF IMMERSION.
EXCITING SCENE AT ARPLEY.

There was an exciting scene at Warrington late on the evening of Good Friday, when an elderly widow named Mannion,was rescued from drowning in the river, near lArpley. Soon after half-past ten o'clock, Police-sergeant Rowbotham was at Bridge- foot, when he heard a shout that sounded to come from the riverside. He went in that direction, and, getting close to the edge of the river, he saw woman about three yards from the side, up to her armpits in water. He asked her if she could get to the side, and she replied that she could not stir. The sergeant, encouraging her to hold out a few minutes longer, proceeded to get assistance, and was joined by Mr. Walter Sampson, of 24, River- view, Wilderspool-road, who at once pulled off his clothes. The officer then fastened a rope round him, and Sampson entered the water and seized the woman, just as she was falling down from exhaus- tion and cold. With the added assistance of Ed. Jordan, a signalman, and Thomas Toft, a platelayer, the poor woman, who was 78 years of age, was re- moved to her home in Bakslhouse-yard, Latch- ford. She never recovered from the exhaustion and shock, and died on Monday morning. INQUEsT. On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquest at the Norton Arms Hotel, on the deceased.—Bridget Mannion, the deceased's daughter said the deceased's name was Honor Man- nion, and she was the wife of John Mannion, bricklayer's labourer, of Bakehouse Yard. Mrs. Mannion left her home alone on Good Friday night to visit in Dolman's-lane, her son, whose child had died. Witness never saw her mother alive again until 2 o'clock the next morning.—Catherine Knock - ton, a married daughter of the deceased, gave corro- borative evidence, and deposed to Dr. Kisby neixag sent to come to her mother and pronouncing her case hopeless. He came again on Sunday, but said there was no chance of recovery. She died at about a quarter to 2 o'clock on Monday morning. The deceased was very short-sighted.—Police-Sergeant Rowbottom detailed the circumstances connected with the woman's rescue, as given above. The tide, the witness said, was running out not in, or she would have been drowned. She was taken home. He could hardly say whether she was sober or not. His idea was that she had missed her way, and having lost her shawl by the river side,went to recover it, and was blown into the river, the night being very stormy and dark. When rescued she could not give any account of herself. She kept cry- ing out about her shawl.---,The Foreman expressed ' the opinion that the deceased was blown into' the river, and thought a woman of her age ought to have been accompanied by some one on such a night. The jury returned tie verdict that the deceased died in consequence of shock to the system caused by her immersion.
