EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS.

ST. ANNE'S. The annual vestry meetinz in connection with this Parish was held at St. Ann's Church, on Tuesday morn- ing, the Vicar the Rev. J. G. Richards in the chair. The Vicar nominated Mr. Edward Gibson as his church- warden for the ensuing year. On the pro position of Mr. Robert Knight, seconded by Mr. Dagnall, Mr. James Baird was appointed people's warden there being no other nomination. Messrs. R. Knight, Hughes, Aldred, and Fryer, were appointed sidesmen,and the lay representatives chosen were :—Messrs. James Baird and R. Knight. The Vicir having thanked Mr. J. Baird, his retiring warden, for his services during the past year the meeting closed. ST. PAUL'S, WARRINGTON. The annual vestry meetingwas held on Monday morn- ing, the chair being occupied by the Vicar (the Rev.H.V. Pigot). There were also present—Mr. Thomas Sutton (vicar's warden), Mr. Daniel Jones (people's warden), Dr. Adams, and Messrs. D. W. Finney, Joseph Lawless, John Hough, J. Lawton,John Hayes, George Bebbington,sen., George Rebbington, jun., William Bebbington, and W.D. Jeans (vestry clerk). Mr. Jones made a statement with reference to the accounts,and observed that every penny owing had been paid. The receipts for the year amounted to £431 2s. nd., and the expenditure to £428 7s. 2d., leaving a balance in hand in favour of the wardens of £2 1.55. The subscriptions to the organ fund amounted to £175 Bs. 4d. ; the sale of work (surplus) realized £80; the Sunday evening collections, £94 3s. 110.; the con- gregational tea party, £24 id. ; and the organ open- ing services £2). Os. Bd. The Vicar appointed Alderman tltton as his warden for the ensuing year, and Mr. D. Jones was re-appointed people's warden. Mr. Sutton appointed Mr. Ashurst as his sidesman, and Mr. Jones selected Mr. Thomas Morris. The other sidesmen ap- pointed were Dr. Adams, and Messrs. James Smethurst, Joseph Lawless, John Hayes. W.Chantry, and A. Jolley. Messrs. D. W. Finney and William Richardson were ap- pointed to represent the vestry at the Church conferences to be held during the year.

_ HOLY TRINITY, WARRINGTON. The vestry meeting of this church was held on Thursday evening, there being a small attendance. The Vicar the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton,presided.—Mr. M'Gregor read the statement of accounts as follows :—lncome, £302 ss. sd. -expenses, £298 13s. 9Jcl. ; cash in hand, £3 us. Md. ; outstanding liabilities, £l5: leaving a deficiency of £ll Bs. W.—The accounts were unanimously passed.—Mr. Di' Gregor again accepted the office of vicar's warden, as Also did Mr. Fairclough that of people's warden. The following sidesmen were appointed :—Messrs. Hatton, Halton, Gasket!, Bowson, Harding, Booth, and Hoult. Lay representatives :—Messrs. Sharpe and Dobson. Mr. G. F. F. White was re-appointed vestry clerk.

THE PARISH CHURCH. Tho vestry meeting in connection with the Warring- ton Parish Church was held in the National Schools on Thursday evening. The Rector (the Rev. F. Vi. Willis) presided, and there was a large attendance of parishio- ners. After the notice convening the meeting had been read by Mr. White (deputy vestry clerk), Captain Buck- ton asked if the notice had been signed by the church- wardens in addition to the Rector.—Mr. White: It has not.—Captain Buckton : Then it is not a legal notice. —Mr. White: It is not necessary for the chureliwardens to sign it.—Mr. A. Woods said it had been ruled the other day that it was not necessary for the churchwar- dens to sign the notice.—The matter then dropped.— Mr. A. Woods (people's warden), in submitting the accounts said that at the commencement of the year there was owing to the churchwardens £1 19s. 3d., and there were outstanding accounts amounting to £42 9s. 3d. In the income this year there had been an increase of £194 Os. Bd. over that of last year. The offertory had Produced £5BO us. 4d., as against £443 55., being an in- crease last year in the offertory of £147 6s. 4d. It would be interesting to know that the number of coins re- ceived had been 55,225. In gold and notes 50, amounting to £B2 ; 53 half-sovereigns, amounting to £26 10s. ; three five shilling and four shilling pieces, amounting to 14s. ; 177 half-crowns, amounting to £22 23. 6d; 259 two shilling pieces, amounting to £25 18s. ; 1,329 shill- ings, amounting to £66 Os.; 3,305 sixpences, amounting to £B2 12s. 61. ; 6,016 threepences, amounting to £75 4s. ; 28,766 pennies, amounting to £l2O 13s. 10c1. ; and 15,067 half-pennies amounting to 27 Os. 4d. The increase was very largely due to the establishment of several afternoon offertories, There was also an increase in the early services, and a slight amount of extra generosity at the morning ser- vices. Having given some information as to the rein- vestment in consols of certain funds, he said the total outstanding debt at the present time was £143 18s. 2d., towards which there was a balance of £2B Bs. id, leav- ing a nett deficiency of £ll5 10s. ld.—Mr. Coates moved, Mr. Dewhurst seconded, the adoption of the accounts, the last-named gentleman referring to the improve- 1 ments which had been made during the past year at the church.—The accounts were adopted. The retiring wardens having been accorded a vote of thanks, the Rector re-appointed Mr. N. B. Percival as Rector's , warden. Mr. Robinson moved and Mr. J. Walton I seconded the re - election of Mr. A. Woods ' as people's warden, and this proposal was agreed to unanimously. Mr. Percival then nominated Mr. T. Robinson as his sidesman,and Mr. Woods nominated Mr. W. Gill. The following sidesmen were also elected, viz: —Messrs. Dewhurst, Fairelough, Walton, Davies,. Scot- gen, Moores, Coates, and Gaskell. Alderman Wright was elected sidesman for Crossley-st. Missicn ; and Mr. Downs for Bank-st. Mission. Mr. J. Buckton and Mr. R. T F airclough were re-elected lay representatives.—On the motion of Mr. Woods, Mr. H. B. White was re-elected vestry clerk. Messrs. F. Taylor and J. E. Wright were re-eleeted anditors.—Mr. Woods, in proposing that a voluntary church rate of 3d. in the £ be again levied, mentioned that the rate last year realised £2l 12s. 3d.— Mr. S. Davies seconded, and the proposal was agreed to. Votes of thanks to the ladies who decorated the church, and to the Rector for presiding, closed the meeting.
ST. BARNAB AS'S VESTRY.
LIVELY PROCEEDINGS,

The vestry meeting in connection with St. Barnabas's Church, Warrington, was held on Wednesday morning. There seemed to be a considerable amount of interest taken in the meeting, and although it was held at 10 o'clock in the morning—a rather inconvenient time for Many people—there was a large attendance. The Vicar, the Rev. G. Allton, presided, and amongst those present were Messrs. W. H. J. Jenkins (solicitor), R. Proud, R. T. Smith, G. Plumpton, S. Jones, Looker, &c. THM CMURCII IN NEED OF REPAIRS.—THE NOTICE OF MEETING.

The notice convening the meeting having been read, the Chairman said the first matter he had to bring before the meeting was the question of the repairs of the church. —A parishioner, interposing, referred to the notice con- vening the meeting, and said that he had not seen the name of Mr. Smith, one of the churchwardens, on the . notice.—The Chairman said it was not necessary that Mr. Smith should sign it.—The Parishioner said that, seeing Mr. Smith was the people's warden and elected by the people, it was rather strange his name was not on the notice. He did not say it • Was illegal, but he thought it peculiar. Perhaps Mr. Smith would say whether he had been asked to sign it or not —The Chairman remarked that the business before them was the repairs of the church.—Mr. Smith did not know what objections Mr. Allton had, but hitherto he had been there to sign the notice as one of the church- Wardens.—The Chairman : We are discussing the repairs of the church at the present time. The church had been , built something like eleven years in October, and they Were in need of many repairs. There were wanted a new heating apparatus, renovated windows, a screen to keep out the cold, and a great many other repairs. As it was Possible for the authorities to orderthe repairs to be done, he supposed it was also possible for them to say how they were to he paid for, whether the parish should be rated to provide for the repairs or otherwise. The Church belonged to the 'Ecclesiastical Commissioners, to whom he he supposed they would have to apply if the repairs could not be done in proper order in their own parish. —k Parishioner You are not bound to pay the rate.—The Chairman: No Person can vote in a vestry unless he pays the rate.—Mr. : If he pays the poor-rate he is entitled.—The Chairman: Yes. May I ask what you propose in re- gard to the repairs of the church P—After a short silence, the Chairman said : May I ask if anybody had anything i to suggest es to how to get out of the difficulty ?—A Parishioner suggested that it would be advisable to send the hat round when there was such, a good muster. • 4Laughter.)—Mr. Throssell asked if all the income for 'church expenses had been aJeounted for.--The Chair- inan We are not discussing that question at present: 'we are discussing the repairs of the church.—Mr. Thros- 'Sell said he wanted to see if there was not some fund thatthey could devote to the purpose.—The Chairman said Mr. Looker had a small fund left from their tea Party.—Mr. Thrown : It would net be sufficient for the purpose P—The Chairman: Oh, no ; not a quarter. --Mr. Looker said the amount was about £l6 1.03.—At this point, Mr. Wollacott, the schoolmaster, said that there were certain persons in the room who had no right to, attend. These were Mr. Proud's sons and Mr. Gor- uoc.—A Voice: And Mr. Allton's son.—The Chairman said some of them would be entitled to vote.— Mr. Woollacott : I do not think they ought to be in the meeting. He asked the Chairman to call Upon all those who had no right to vote to leave the t°oro.—Mr. Jenkins said it was purely a matter of taste, not of law. (Hear, hear.)—A Voice: Call a police- „lliac • (righter. )----The Chairman said he must ask them be orderly in the vestr‘v.—Mr. Woollacott : They do not tttend church at all.—Mr. Plumpton :It is not a ques- ion of attending church at all.—Mr. Woollacott : I do speak of parishioners and ratepayers.—Mr. Jenkins ~.ought it would be io bad taste to turn people out if eY behave: themselves. (Hear, hear.)--me. Woolla- tet :It is difficult to tell who are voters.—Mr. Jenkins: w can easily remedy that.—The Chairman: Are you !filling to subscribe or to pay .0 rate ?—A Parishioner: It not compalsory.—The Chairman t Those who do not PaoY their rates or give their mone)y have no power to ov te at any vestry.—Mr. Plumpton : I think if we pay or poor-rate we are entitled to vote.—Mr. It: Proud :

Perhaps the Chairman will explain what he is doing. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman: It is sot my business to go into matters of that kind. I should like to know what you have done, but we are not here to discuss mat- ters of that kind.—Mr. Jenkins thought that something might be done by voluntary effort.—No progress having been made with regard to church repairs, the Chairman referred to the desirability of providing a salary for the organist.—Mr. Proud thought that ought to be part of the churdh expenses, and he asked if there had been no collections.—The Chairman said there had not for that purpose ; there had been a collection for the choir, the proceeds of which had been handed over to the treasurer.

• APPOINTMENT OF A VESTRY CLERK. The Chairman suggested the desirability of appointing a vestry clerk, and Mr. Woollacott moved that Mr. Jenkins be appointed.—Mr. Jenkins explained that he had come there, at Mr. Alton's request, in a purely friendly way and not in any spirit of antagonism to any ratepayer. He should be glad to remove any difficulty, and he thought the time had some when they should all put an end to those troubles. It would be with that hope that he would consent to act.—Mr. Hope seconded the proposal to appoint Mr. Jenkins.—A Voice: Is Mr. Hope a parishioner ?—Mr. Woollacott : Yes, he is. —A Parishioner suggested that Mr. Woollacott was entitled to the position of vestry clerk. (Laughter.)—Mr. Jen- kins was then appointed vestry clerk, no hands being held up against the resolution.—Mr. Jenkins said that, having regard to the finances of the church, he would not trouble them to name a salary; they would talk about that when it was worth talking about. (Hear, hear, and applause.)
ELECTION OF CHURCHWARDENS.

The Chairman said the next business was the election of churchwardens. He might say that he had written to the solicitor of the diocese and he had been informed that they were not a parish even, but simply the district chapelry of St. Barnabas. When they had arrived at the dignity of a parish, they would come under a new act, but at present their churchwardens must be mem- bers of the Church of England and fit and proper persons residing in the parish. The fit and proper persons might be two women.—Mr. Lloyd: The bible does not say that women are to hold office.—The Chairman : I do not want them here, I can assure you. (Laughter.) He only placed the thing before them as it stood. He wished to be perfectly fair and legal. and as they had had two churchwardens in the past, with their co-operation they would have two again. During the last year they had much to be thankful for as well as much to regret, and he hoped that whoever was now put in office would work with the con- gregation. The congregation had resolved that in future it would support no an in that church whe did not work with them, and also that they would never attend a vestry meeting till such time as the vestry can be quiet and conducted in an orderly and proper manner. All the heads of the congregation had come to him and given him to understand that they would not be over- ridden by men who neither support the church nor the parish; they would manage their own affairs, and what- ever churchwarden had their funds they were determined that. he should come before them at a meeting of the congregation and show how the funds had been spent. He only said that so that they might be understood. He wanted to begin the year without unpleasantness of any kind, and he wanted to work with the men in office. There was no one who had ever been to his house could say ' that he had been rudely or improperly treated ,and, there- fore, if they wanted him let them come to him.—There was at this point some interruption, and Mr. Woollacott said it was due to Mr. Proud's son, who should be called to order.—The Chairman said. every man present, whether he was a dissenter or whatever else he might be, knew what religion meant and what it ought to be, and therefore there was no one present who had got a right feeling would wish• to upset a church or congregation (hear, hear)—any more than he should by going to a chapel. He knew Mr. Plutnpton and Mr. Jones to be good, respectable, honest men, and he was pleased to see them there as honest men who came in a right spirit,and not to cause the enemy to blaspheme and to disgrace God's house and their most holy religion. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman concluded by nominating Mr. Jno.Looker as vicar's warden for the coming year.—On the motion of Mr. Lloyd, seconded by Mr. H. Jackson, Mr. R. T. Smith was re-elected people's warden.—The Chairman referred to the duties of a churchwarden, who was, he said, the guardian of the parish. It was his especial duty to see that peace was well kept in every meeting of the congregation. If a churchwarden failed to fulfil the duties of the office he could be presented and removed from office.
APPOINTMENT OF SIDESMEN.

The Chairman and Mr. Looker appointed Mr. Trevett as Vicar's sidesman.—lt was suggested that Mr. Thro3- sell should be re-elected a sidesman.—The Chairman said, Mr. Throssell had been sidesman for two years, but had never qualified for the office. If he was re-elected, he would have to be sworn in the service of the church otherwise he (the chairman) should present him to the bishop and chancellor of the diocese, and have his name removed.—Mr. Plumpton : Will it not be better to wait until that happens.—The Chairman: He has not attended for two years.—Mr. Plumpton : He is well known as a churchman, and perhaps he has had his reasons for not attending. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman : I have heard he was a Roman Catholic.—Mr. Plumpton : I have heard that about our Chairman. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) —The Chairman: People do get erroneous ideas.—Mr. Throssell was then elected sidesman, on the motion of Mr. J. Battersby, soconded by Mr. S. Mason.

div.head: LAY REPRESENTATIVE.
div.p: THE LAY REPRESENTATIVE.

. - The Chairman moved, and Mr. Smith seconded, that Mr. J. Battersby be elected lay representative. Mr. Woollacott moved, and Mr. Looker seconded, that Mr. W. Smith be appointed. On being put to the vote, Mr. Battersby was elected by a large majority.

THE REPAIRS AGAIN. The Chairman said that before they left it would be advisable to again discuss the question of the repairs of the Church. He would ask if any gentleman present would volunteer to contribute or to help them to get the church repaired.—Mr. Smith : Is it not the usual thing to call over the accounts for the current year ?—The Chairman: Let us do this first please.—Mr. Battersby : What method do you suggest, Mr. Chairman ?—The Chairman said it seemed te him that, if in the coming year the churchwardens worked amicably and properly with the congregation, there would not be much diffi- culty. He did not want any rate to be put upon the parish, and he wanted to be fair and square in these matters. He might say that the congrc gation were very strongly against bringing the accounts before any meet- ing but one of the congregation.—Mr. Smith said the •Chairman had a good deal to say about the churchward- ens working amicably together, and he should like to ask Mr. Looker if they had not worked amicably to- gether. He wanted to know if .Mr. Looker had anything to complain of.—Mr. Looker said he had no one to complain of.—A question was asked if any one was present to represent the congregation, and to this the chairman replied that the congregation was not repre- sented.—A voice: It does net say much for the congre- gation. (Hear hear, and laughter.)—The Chairman, again referring to the question of repairs, said it was a matter to be left in the hands of himself, the church- wardens, and the congregation. If necessity required,he should call a special meeting of the ratepayers of the parish and place the matter before them, and then they would have to take action to do something towards re- paring the church. He-then thanked those present for their attendance, and declared the meeting closed.--Mr. Jenkins said he would like to read over the minutes of the meeting he had taken, and this he clid.—Mr. Smith : And what about the accounts.—The Chairman : Our meeting is now over; the members of the congregation will remain to discuss the accounts with the church- wardens. Nearly all of those present then left the vestry and the meeting terminated. ST. JAMES'S, LATCHFORD. _ _

- -- - The Vicar of the parish (the Rev. F. Slater) presided at the annual vestry meeting, which was held on Easter Monday. There were also present—Mr. C. S. Burgess (vicar's warden), Mr. J. W. Tauranac (people's warden), Councillor Hutchinson, and Messrs. Shaw, Astlev, Mill- wood, Dobson and Duckworth. Mr. Burgess presented an abstract of accounts of the wardens, from which it appeared that the income amounted to £204 9s. Thd., and the expenditure to £205 7s. id., leaving a balance due to the wardens of 17s. 54d. The general offertory ' realised £B3 ZS. W., and the special offertories £55 6s. 110. The offertories for church expenses realised £2O 15s. Did.; the tea party £2O 45., and (part) pro- ceeds of the sale of work £25. The offertories for the year, Mi. Burgess said, were more than they were last year, although they had had a short ecclesiastical year. He thought they might congratulate- themselves as churchwardens, and the members of the congregations, upon the satisfactory condition of the finances of the church. With reference to a report made the other day, that the three hours' devotional services were a compara- tively new institution in Warrington, he wished to remark that they had been held in St. Anne's Church for nearly twenty years,and at St. James's for over ten years. On the motion of Mr. Hutchinson, seconded by Mr. Mill- wood, the accounts were passed. The Vicar again ap- pointed Mr. Bingess as his warden, and Mr. Tauranac was re-elected people's warden. Mr. Burgess observed that the Vicar and Mrs. Slater were going away for four or five weeks on a holiday to the Pyrenees. He hoped it would be a pleasant holiday to them, and that they would , return with renewed health and vigour to carry on the good work they were doing in the parish. (Hear, hear.) They would carry with them the best wishes of all the members of the congregation. (Heat, hear.) The Vicar said he was much obliged to Mr. Burgess for his good wishes, but it would be a great grief to him to leave the church so long. Messrs. Hollowell, Venn, Cotton, and Shaw were appointed sidesmen, and Messrs. Burgess and H. N. Houghton lay representatives. This was all the business.

div.head: ST. THOMAS'S.
div.p: ST. THOMAS'S.

The annual vestry meeting in connection with St. Thomas's, Stockton Heath,Warrington, was held on Tues- day morning, the Rev. T. Rolfe, the curate, being in the chair, in conStquence of continued indisposition ot the Vicar (the Rev. •T. S. Tofts). Mr. R. Davies intimated that he had meived a letter from the vicar re-appoint- ing him his warden for the ensuing year. Mr. E. W. Woods was re-appointed people's warden ; and Messrs. L. Wright, James Tinsley, Charles Seward, V. B. Davies, R. W. Francomb, and Arthur Davies, were appointed
I
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1891.

sidesmen. Mr. E. W. Woods submitted the year's accounts, which showed a balance Of £ll 12s. due to the wardens, and outstanding liabilities which brought the balance up to £l7 es. 9d. The general offertory had amounted during the year to £l5B. It was decided to hold a special service in order to make up the deficit. WALTON. The annual vestry meeting was held at St. John's Walton, on Monday morning when there were present— the Vicar (the Rev. L. J. T. Darwell), in the chair. and Messrs. T. S. Burgess, Muskett, John Weir, and T. Lane. The Vicar said tke past year had passed off very satis- factorily, and he thought the old churchwardens, Sir Gilbert Greenall and Mr. John Weir, should remain in offiee. (Hear, hear.) It was agreed to keep the old war- dens in office for another year. The Vicar read a letter from the Ecclesiastical Buildings Fire Office, Limited, with reference to the insurance of the church. If it was agreeable to Sir Gilbert Greenall, who paid the insurance money, he thought it would be advisable to transfer the insurance of tho church to the Ecclesiastical Buildings Fire Company, as the profits derived by that company, were distributed solely for Church purposes. It was re- solved to ask Sir Gilbert's consent. The Vicar produced the accounts, which showed that the income for the year was £157 7s. 54d.,that amount including gifts from Sir Gilbert of £5O for organist,£s6 10s. for general expenses, and £9 ss. 11d, for parish room. The church collections amounted to £25 4s. ed. Mr. John Weir said that many of the parishioners were not satisfied with the time for the forenoon service. The Vicar said that before the al- teration was made to eleven o'clock he consulted the farmers, and he found it suited them best. He should certainly change the hour if it was desired. Mr. Burgess suggested that from November to January the service should be held at eleven o'clock, and during the remain- ing months at 10.30. This course was decided upon,and the meeting terminated. GRAPPENHALL.

The Easter vestry meeting was held at the Church on Tuesday morning, the Rector (the Rev. Canon Greenall), in the chair. The Rector nominated as his warden Mr. Allan Lister Kaye, and Mr. Thomas Wm. Jones sidesman. The parish appointed Mr. Leigh Leyland warden, and Mr. William Peacock as their sidesman. Messrs. Lister Kaye and Leyland were appointed representatives to the Ruri-decanal and Diocesan Cohferences. The church accounts for the year were produced and passed, there being a satisfactory balance in the hands of the church- wardens. The Rector represented the statement of accounts with reference to the restoration of the church bells, which he explained was entirely free from debt, the expense having been cleared by the sale of work held last year, which realized £270 13s. 6d. The balance of £44 had been devoted to three objects, viz., providing new surplices, the sick fund, and for assistant clergy. The Rector said that in addition to the restoration of the bells, oak fronts had been erected in the front seats of the church. The chancel screen (the faculty for which had been granted), which was being erected as a memorial to the late Mr. John Tinsley, was not yet com- pleted, though the full amount of its cost, about £l6O, had been subscribed for and £lOO already paid on account. _

After the meeting, Mrs. Greenall and Mr. Jones distri- buted about £7 worth of calico to the deserving poor in Christ Church, Latchford, and the Grappenhall parishes. Over 100 persons benefit by this annual charity.

• , , and jiassed. Mr. Swinton was nominated by the Rector as his warden, and Mr. Worsley was re-appointed people's warden. The Rector stated that shortly after entering into residence he commenced to hold an early celebra- tion of the Holy Communion in the church, and as the winter approached it became necessary to light the chancel. One of the churchwardens had ascertained that the Society of Friends at Warrington had in their possession an antique chandelier of brass which formerly hung in the meeting house at Warrington, and he had applied to the society to be allowed to purchase it; as it was exactly what was wanted, for its antique appearance would harmonize with the chancel. When that fact was represented to the Society of Friends, they informed the Rector and wardens that as arrangements were being made for greater facilities for religious worship, they would take no money for the chandelier, but would pre- sent it to the Church. The chandelier was regilded, and was a great ornament to the building. It was decided that the vestry record, its hearty thanks to the Society of Friends at Warrington for their handsome gift; and that a copy of the resolution be forwarded to them. The Rector referred to the retirement of Mr. Joseph Kerfoot, who has held the post of organist at Winwick Church for 52 years. On the motion of Mr. Worsley, it was decided That this vestry expresses its regret at Mr. Kerfoot's retirement, and wishes him continued health and happiness." It was also decided to make Mr. Ker- foot a suitable present in commemoration of his long connection with the parish. It will be remembered that some time ago a handsome gold watch and address were presented to him, and the present gift is merely intended asa farewell acknowledgment. The usual vote of thanks brought the meeting to a close

ANNI THIATION OF A BRITISH FORCE -iN MANIPI7R. THE BRITISH COMMISSIONER AND SEVEN OFFICERS MISSING. TWO DAYS' DESPERATE FIGHTING. CALCUTTA, MONDAY.—Yesterday two Goorkhas be- longingto the Assam Frontier Police, reached Kohima, the station nearest to the Assam-Manipur boundary, and brotaht the disastrous intelligence that a British force has been cut to pieces by some of the savage tribes of Manipur, and the British Commissioner of Assam and seven officers were missing. Some while ago the Rajah of Manipur, at whose capi- tal resides a British Political Agent, was deposed by the chief of one of the warrior tribes which infest the coun- try. The Rajah made an appeal to the Government of India, and Mr. J. W. Quinton, C. 5.1., Chief Commissioner for Assam, whose headquarters are at Shillong, started for Manipur with a considerable escort, consisting of detatchments of the 42nd and 44th Goorkha Light Infantry. Having adyanc,ed across the border and reached the seat of disturbance, Mr. Quinton snmmoned a durbar of the chiefs for the purpose of obtaining the arrest of the rebellious chief who had overthrown the Rajah. On the same night the camp ef the Commissioner, which was at some point south of Kohima, and between that station and Manipur was attacied by tribesmen. For two whole days the assault was withstood and the foe driven back, but at length the ammunition of the gallant Goorkhs, who had fought splendidly under the direction of their British officersovas exhausted, and Mr. Quinton then gave the order for a sauve gut peut. The refugees report that fully 450 to 470 Goorkhas were killed. With regard to the officers, the accounts differ slightly. One says that one British officer is known to have been killed, but does not specify his name. The same report states that Mr. Quinton and his staff were seized, and that their fate is unknown. Another account says that Colonel Skene, commanding the 42nd Goorkha Light Infantry; Lieutenants G. H. But- cher, E. J. Lugard, and J. B. Chatterton, of the same regiment; Captain T. S. Boileau, second in command of the 44th Goorkha Light Infantry; Lieutenant L. W. Brackenbury, of the same regiment; and Mr. Calvert, and finally, Mr. Quinton, are missing. There seems to be little doubt that the attack on the British camp by the Manipuris, who are as netorious for their treachery awl cunning as they are famous for their bravery and indifference to danger, was deliberately Planned. They had for one thing cut the telegraph wires in order to prevent Mr. Quinton's force from communi- cating with Assam. As soon as the news of the slaughter reached Simla, the Viceroy, summoned the Council to meet there in haste. Two native regiments quartered in Assam were at once despatched to the Manipur frontier, and the 3rd Bengal Infantry start in the morning. It is believed that Mr. Quinton was not accompanied on the fatal ex- pedition by his son and daughter. CALcurrA, Moxpty.—Mr. Quinton and his escort reached Manipur on the twenty-second inst., and was well received. The following troops have been ordered to proceed to Kohima forthwith : 13th Bengal Infantry ; Ist and 2nd Ghoorkhas ; Bth Bengal Mountain Battery; 36th Bengal Infantry ; Sikhs ; 3rd Bengal Infantry. The Viceroy has abandoned his tour, and will go direct to Simla to-morrow. THE FATE OF THE CIVIL AND MILITARY OFFICERS.

FOUR REGIMENTS ORDERED TO THE SCENE OF THE MASSACRE. SIMLA, TUESDAY, 7 P.M.—The Rajah of Manipur, Mr. Quinton, Chief Commissioner of Assam, Colonel Skene, and Mr. Grimwood, Political Agent at Manipur, are held as prison ers by the revolted tribes. Mrs. Grimwood, Captain Boileau, and Lieutenants Gurdon and Wood, Assistant Commisioners, have escaped in the direction of Silchar, and it is hoped that they will have met with the rescuing detachment. Surgeon Calvert is wounded. Nothing is yet known regarding the fate of the remain- ing officers. Four regiments are now on the way to Manipur. CALCUTTA, TUESDAY.—Mr. Quinton and his escort reached the town of Manipur on the 22nd inst., and were well received. He ordered a durbar to be held,with the intention of securing the arrest of the commander of the Manipur troops, who was regarded as the cause of ' the troubles. The attack on the British force was made on the following night, namely the 23rd inst.,.and che fighting continued through the night and the whole of the next day, until the Goorkhas's ammunition, was exhausted.

div.head: PADGATE CHURCH.
div.p: PADGATE CHURCH.

This vestry meeting was held on Monday forenoon, when there were present the Rev. J. J. Langham, vicar, Messrs. Wm. Royston (warden), Thomas Yates, Thomas Houghton, William Houghton, James Houghton, Joseph Houghton, John Houghton, George Mather and George Howard. The warden's accounts were submitted, audited, and unanimously adopted. They showed a balance in hand of £l3 15s. 6d., but Mr. Royston pointed out that the outstanding liabilities for the year were £l2 15s. The total amount of collections and communi- cants' alms was £III 9s. Bd. The Vicar reappointed Mr. Wm. Royston as his warden, Mr. John William Fowles was elected people's warden; and Messrs. William Houghton, George Mather, W. H. J. Jenkins, and Thos. Yates were appointed sidesmen. The allotment ward- en's account was audited and adopted. It showed a balance in hand of £4 3s. 10d. and a balance in the bank of £35 4s. Bd.—The Vicar read a correspondence which had passed between him and the rector of War- rington and the Board of Agriculture, regarding the cus- tody of of the award of the Enclosures Commissioners with reference to the allotments at Woolton. At last year's vestry meeting the Vicar was authorised to write the rector of Warrington, requesting the documents to be transferred to him. The rector replied that he and his wardens would be quite willing to-do so on receiving sanction from the Board of •Agriculture. The Vicar wrote to the Board of Agriculture accordingly, and pointed out that Padgate was now a separate parish, and that it was inconvenient for the parishioners to have to go to Warrington whenever they wished to see the award. The Board of Agriculture replied on the 20th September, 1890, to the effect that when sealed docu- ments had been deposited with churchwardens, the Board, in pursuance of the,General Enclosures Act, 1845, had no further jurisdiction to order their transference to any person or body of persons. The matter was left in the hands of the Vicar to take further steps in the matter if he thought necessary. After comments on the very satisfactory nature of the year's accoun s, the meeting was brought to a conclusion by a vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: MR. MORLEY ON THE CORK TRIALS.
div.p: MR. MORLEY ON THE CORK TRIALS.

In a letter to the Times, Mr. John Morley writes : Nobody whose mind is not poisoned by faction will agree with you that the failure of the Crown to secure a con- viction at Cork is of no material consequence. The judge told the jury that Colonel Caddell and the police witnesses were on their trial no less than the de- fendants, and that if they believed the case for the Crown they should find the defendants guilty. The jury there- upon disagreed as to two, and acquitted three of the de- fendants, including Keating, whose case I had always described as the most wanton, unprovoked, and outrage- ous of all. Therefore the verdict, which you think of no material consequence, showed that in three instances the jury disbelieved the ease for the Crown, and con- demned Colonel Caddell and the police witnesses, and in no instance acquitted them. This is quite material enough for me.

The failure of the Crown was due to no want of pre- caution. They changed the venue. They had special jurors, they directed no fewer than twenty-four of these special jurors to stand by, until they supposed they had got twelve men to their mind. The presiding judge al- most went out of his way to testify to the high charac- ter and reputation of the special juries of the city of Cork, and declared that he had never seen a case more carefully and conscientously considered. The result of this careful and conscientious consideration is that the jury in no case agree to find the official story to be true, and in three cases unanimously find it to be false. Does this shed no light on the Irish Minister's unfaltering as- sumption during the whole of the last four years, that every word from a constable or a resident magistrate must be gospel, and any contradiction from a mere mem- ber of Parliament must be an exaggeration or a lie? The Irish Government should stick to their two resident magistrates in a snug Coercion Court, and give careful and conscientious juries a wide berth.

THE EASTER HOLIDAYS AT WARRINGTON.

The Easter holidays were not this year favoured with mild open weather, but nevertheless the people of Warrington largely availed themselves of the holiday to make excursions to various towns which:are usually resorted to on these occasions. in the town the main attraction was the football con- test between the Warrington players and a team from Hartlepool, which included Alderson, the well- known international. The local team upheld their reputation by a rather decided victory. Eastertide is generally looked upon as the opening of the c 3 cling season, and the number of wheelmen who passed over the bridge in the course of Monday was a striking proof of the popularity of the "flying wheel."

div.head: CAIRO-ST. TEACHERS' TEA.
div.p: CAIRO-ST. TEACHERS' TEA.

On Monday evening the annual tea or the teachers of Cairo-st. Sunday School was held in the.schoolroom. The tea was not largely attended, but at a dance which sub- sequently took place there was a more numerous com- pany. Mr. John Chalmers acted as M.C., and Mr. T. R. Ford as pianist. Dancing was continued till about 11 o'clock.
ALL SAINTS' MISSION. CONGREGATIONAL GATHERING.

The annual congregational tea party in connection with All Saints' Mission, Bewsey-st., was held, in the Mission Room, on Tuesday evening. A large number sat down to tea. The tables were presided over by Mesdames Pigot, Chorley, Griffiths, Fryer, and Worley; Miss Bur- rows, Miss Woodward, Miss E. Woodward, Miss Hether- ington, and Miss Schultze. After ' tea a c•ncert was given, the•vicar, the Rev. H. V. Pigot, presiding. The mission choir gave a couple of glees, "Up, quit thy bower," and " I love the merry springtime." Miss Pic- ton sang " Daddy," and "The lost chord " ; Mr. Parkin- son gave "Anchored," Mr. Sherlock "The yaChtsmair" and "True till death." Miss Cosgrove obtained encores for "To happier hours," and another song. Master and Miss BoAhroyd were twice encored for some capitally played pianoforte and violin duets. Miss Oxley sang "Widow Malone" and another song, and had an encore for the first. Mr. Fryer was most vociferously encored for a comic song entitled "Little Scrub." The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCHES.
div.p: THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCHES.

On Sunday the festival of Easter was celebrated in the. usual manner at St. Mary's Church, Buttermarket2stj All signs of mourning had disappeared, 3,nd the banners' were arranged in the chancel and side chapels. The High Altar was elaborately adorned with flowers and plants. At eleven o'clock solemn high mass commenced,. Father Sumner. 0.5.8., rector of St.:Mary's, officiating.. The sermon was preached by Father Flanigan, 0.5.8,, who wished the congregation, upon behalf of the priests of St. Mary's,a very happy Easter. The music of H.aydn's Grand Mass No. 4 was rendered by the choir in an OR- 'dent manner. Mr. Richard Eccles conducted and Mr. Thomas Mather was at the organ. In the evening at half-past sir, English Vespers were sung, and Father Perkins preached. After the sermon the . High Altar was lighted for the Benediction Service.—The Easter services at St. Alban's were of a -very impressive character. On Sunday morning solemn high mass was celebrated at eleven o'clock, Father Dolan being cele- brant. A full orchestral band, under the leadership of Herr Praeger, asssisted the choir. Mr. E. Whitehead conducted, and Mr. J. B. Caldwell was at the orno, n. The music of Haydn's No. 16 Mass was given with much precision, and was a great treat to all present. Father Feeny, 0.5.8., rector of St. Alban's preached to a large congregation at the evening service, the orchestra again assisting during the solemn Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament. The music in the evening was very well ren- dered, and praise is due to both choir and orchestra for their services. The altars were decorated with beautiful flowers arranged with great taste.

------- of a battle-piece by him, in oil; and there ought to be no difficulty in obtaining a "black and white" by Sheffield. There are several works of this class in the town which are too large for a private collection. They arc suitable only for an art gallery, and those who own them would bo easy to deal with—for such a purpose. It should not be forgotten in this connection that the Turner collec- tion of drawings is still on view,as a loan for twelve months from the trustees of the National Gallery. We have previously had occasion to comment on their unique qualities; and would add that all who have a taste for art and have not yet seen the drawings have a treat in store. With regard to the Museum, which is one of the best in the country, having regard to the size of the town, :it is cstimated that it now contains "a total of about 42,000 specimena the various collections, the property of the Corporation." During the year the Warrington Field Club have added as many as 400 specimens of insects and plants —a contribu- tion of no small moment. The club does not matte much stir, but it does good work; its members , are workers rather than talkers. The Museum ' and Library Committee have shown a considerable desire of lato to popularise the institution; they are on the right track as the report shows, and nothing, in our opinion, will hasten their progress so much as carrying out their proposal to make the Library free.

The Late THE death of Lord GRANVILLE is Lord a great loss to the country; and Granville. to the Liberal party the loss is irreparable. For forty-five years a member of the House of Lords and for thirty years of that period the Liberal leader in the Upper House, it is not too much to say that no one better understood the peers than the late earl. It was said of PEEL, before Mr. GLADSTONE loomed so large, that he was the greatest member of the House of Commons in his day, by which it was meant that he knew the tone and temper of this branch of the Legislature better than any other man; and, speaking of Lord GRavviLis in a similar way, we should say he was the greatest member in his day in the House of Lords. His tact, geniality and courtesy were un- ivalled in that assembly; and these were qualities of tho highest order in a loader who was doomed from the circumstances of the case to be constantly n a minority. No person who ever heard him address an assembly could fail to be charmed with' his grace and courtlinesa of manner, which carried with it, however, no suggestion of weak- ness. On the contrary, the hand was iron though the glove was silk, as many a foreign statesman has found when trying a policy of "bluff" in the brusque Bismarck style. Lord GRairviLLs Was Foreign Secretary as far back as 1851 when, With Lord Joint RUSSELL as Prime Minister, he Was the successor of Lord PIL3LER4TON. He occu- pied the same important post in the Administra- tion of Mr. GLADSTONE, after the death of Lord CLARENDON in 1870; and was again Foreign Secre- tary under MT. GLADSTONE from 1880 to 1885. It cannot be said that he never made a mistake in his dealings with Foreign Powers; but it is certain that, on the whole, he succeeded admirably under circumstances the most trying. His despatches are masterpieces of clear statement and sound reason- ing, while their courtesy is of a kind which could not fail to ensure them due consideration. If Mr. GLADSTONE had not been head and shoulders above every other statesman in the country, the late Earl would long ere this have become Prime Minister. The opportunity of forming a Government was given him in 1859 ; but he did not succeed with such veterans to deal with as Lord PA.LMERSTON and Lord tJoint Russinx. In 1880 he was again sent for, after h QUEEN had consulted Lord HARTINGTON ; but he recognised, as Lord 11.4.axixgroic recognised. that the demand of the country was that Mr. GLADSTONE should have charge of the helm of State It thus happened that Lord GRANviLLs died at seventy-five without having attained the highest honour that the country could confer; but there was never at any time a trace of jealousy or disappointment. His Liberalism was too robust, and his character too noble, to suffer from such failing. He stood by JOHN BRIGHT half a century ago when it was the fashion to denounce the tri- bune of the people as a reckless demagogue; and how loyal and helpful he was to Mr. GLAD- STONE, Mr. GLADSTONE alone can say. He was indeed a true man; iv birth and breeding and natural disposition what Chaucer describes as "a -verY perfect gentle knight."

"At Macclesfield Police Court, on Tuesday, John T. Corbishley, labourer, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment for an aggravated assault on the police. Ho thereupon uttered an oath, and threw his hat at tho magistrate, hitting; him in the face." There are various ways of mak- ing a protest; it may be written, or it may be spoken; but when a" hat" is thrown in a magis- trate's face should it not be said that it is a pro- test which is " felt ?"

-- The influenza epidemic has become a veritable death-plague at Chicago. Victims are perishing at the rate of 300 per day. People were disposed to make light of la grippe when it was first heard ; but even in this country there is sad evidence that it is not to be trifled with. There is a gap in many a family as the result of last year's ravages. It is to he hoped that, after travelling round the globe, the malady will vanish as suddenly as it appeared.

John " Warring.o.:. " again! This time he is committed to the assizes for stealing a spade at Poulton. Why, oh why, did the workhouse authorities give that nameless child the name of the town? Couldn't the lad be re-named, say, John Devilshoof ?

Tho Clitheroe abduction case is like John War- rington—it will be heard of again ; there is to be an appeal to the House of Lords. There is a good deal of feeling at Clitheroe against the woman who marries a man, and then declines to live with him because she has changed her mind. If she is to be at liberty to take such a course, the husband ought to be entitled to a divorce. What the law has given with one hand it has taken away with the other; and, as the children say : Taking back and giving, Old Nick's living.

7- ' Separation orders will be unnecessary, if, under the new ruling, a wife can leave her husband when she likes. In the West London Police Court, on Tuesday, the presiding magistrate, in reference to a case before him, said "A wife was under no legal obligation to live with her husband. It was now no longer necessary for a wife to apply to the courts for a separation, as she had the power of separating herself. That was the law which had lately been declared, and it could not be too widely known amongst the poorer classes." It is becoming every day more evident that the judges' meddle is a muddle. There will soon be a very pretty kettle of fish.

It is estimated that over twelve million Germans insurance system. now under the operation of the state system. One half o 2 the premium is paid by the workmen and the other half by the employers. The payments vary from about twopence per week,on a small salary, to 3id. on salaries of £lOO a year. This is certainly an easy way of providing for old age. The experiment will be watched; it may be found desirable to adopt a similar scheme for this country. Provision for the night which cometh when no man can work is not so common as it should be.

The Conservative is getting tired of speaking of the Liberal Unionist as a man after his own heart. "It was thought some time ago that Mr. Victor Cavendish, grandson to the Duke of Devonshire, would be induced to contest Barrow in the Union- ist interest at the next election, and his consent had been all but given. A hitch, however, has occurred, owing to the Conservatives stipulating that he should come forward merely as the Union- ist candidate, and not as a Liberal Unionist." It is "all off." In future, the notice to candidates will read thus :—"No Liberal Unionist need apply."

The Brewer gets long profits, and the Brewery man long hours; that is one way of dividing the fruits of industry. In a case heard in London, in which a drayman was charged with drunkenness, it was stated that the man "had been at work since five o'clock in the morning, and it was mid- night when he fell helplessly off his dray and was apprehended. Fatigue and want of meals—for which it was represented that he had had no time —had in the clerk's opinion as much to do with the man's condition as intoxicating liquor." The man was fined, though he was more sinned against than sinning. But what of the brewer? Does he not deserve to be punished?

Township and vestry meetings have for the most part been as dull as ditchwater. ThPre are no great grievances, and the official mind is at rest. The redoubtable Robert turned up as usual at Frodsliam, and as usual he had no supporters. The Rev. G. Allton had a lively time of it at St. Barnabas meeting. He will not forget saying, when Mr. Throssell was proposed as sidesman, that he had "heard he was a Roman Catholic," for Mr. Plumpton irstantly rejoined—" I have heard that about our chairman." The retort courteous was very muck enjoyed, and caused the reverend chairman to remark that people did get erroneous ideas, whereupon everybody could or should have said "Amen."

JAPANESE FANCY FAIR IN LIVERPOOL. On Tuesday next, as will be seen from our adver- tising columns, the Mayor of Liverpool will formally open one of the most attractive, if not absolutely unique, exhibitions which the people of that city have had an opportunity of seeing for a very long time. Mr. Bowes, the honorary Japanese Consul for Liverpool, has given his beautiful and commo- dious residence, know as Streat lam Tower's Prince's Road, for the purpose of holding in it a Japanese fancy fair. It is said that Streatlam Towers contains within its walls the finest collection of Japanese art in the world. There is no doubt, therefore, that dur- ing the week in which it will remain open the fancy fair will attract an enormous number of people to its halls. The money raised at the " fair " will be devoted to benevolent purposes. Ample arrangements have been made for the supply of music and miscellaneous entertainments, so that there will be no lack of attractions. ASTER SHOW OF NOVELTISS.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey- Warrington.—Advt. NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING. On Monday afternoon, a little girl named Laith- waite, residing with her parents in Williamson- squats, Earlestown, had a narrow escape from drowning in the canal near Sankey locks. It appears a number of children were playing on the swing bridge which crosses the canal, wheu the girl Laithwaite accidentally fell in, while the bridge was turned. Two young ladies from Collins Green, who were passing at the time saw the danger the girl was in, and they set to work to effect her rescue, which they accomplished, but only just in time, as the unfortunate girl had already sunk twice. When taken from the water the girl was completely exhausted. She was at once taken to Mrs. Powelis, who resides near the locks, and restoratives were administered until she recovered sufficiently to be removed home. The courageous and prompt action of the young ladies deserves great praise, as had they not acted promptly, the girl would certainly have been drowned. CURIOUS BREACH OF AN AGREEMENT. At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Mr. Samuel Thompson, plasterer, sued Mr. Peter Hanratty, of Oxford-st., for .£3 damages caused to plaintiff through alleged breach of covenant not to carry on the trade of a plasterer in St. Helens, such covenant being contained in a deed of dissolution of partnership dated 9th July, 1890. Mr. Thomas appeared for plaintiff, and Hr. Mearns defended. There was an injunction to restrain the defendant from carrying on or assisting in carrying on directly or indirectly the business of a slater, plasterer, and tiler, within a distance of ten miles for ten years from the 9th July, 1890. The two parties had been in partnership at St. Helens until July last, when throtwli some difference between them they agreed to part, the defendant signing the said covenant. The plaintiff stated that defendant was working as a master plasterer, and he had lost .£3 through Ilan- ratty tendering against him. His Honour made a perpetual injunction, damages is. There are draughts and draughts; nd, if the contest had been one of draughts of ale, warrington would have been to the fore with quite a host of well-trained competitors.

The people of Penketh are acting wisely in looking to their common rights for recreation puyposes. It is satisfactory to see that the Hon. Michael Hughes, as lord of the manor, is accommo- dating. Let them make the best bargain they ean, and as soon as they can. As the village grows, the Recreation Ground will become invaluable.

"To be in complete touch with his men" is all very well, in the ordin- 4rY way of things, but not when it means" sitting on theni."

DBA.TH OF 1 NORTON GAMEICEBPER. On Tuesday the funeral of Mr. George Har- greaves, of Stockham, keeper for Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., of Norton Priory, took place at llal- ton Cemetery. The deceased, after 30 years' ser- vice, retired in consequence of failing health, and Sir Richard Brooke sent him to Southport there to recruit his health ; but ak, there was no improvement in his condition, he was pensioned off, but did not live long to enjoy it. The Rev. G. D. Wray read the funeral service, and, as a mark of respect, the Vicar, Mr. Churchwarden Wright, and Mr. Richard Nixon, of Stockholm, headed the procession. The hearse and mourning coaches were supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros., of Runcorn. A WIDNES MAGISTRATE REFUSES A COMMITMENT. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, School Attendance Officer Grant, on behalf of the School Board applied for a commitment order against Alice Brown, of Warrington-road, who, a week ago, was fined ss. for not sending her child regularly to school. The officer stated that Mrs. Brown had no goods and therefore a distress warrant would be useless. The Chairman (Mr. A. Fletcher) : What will be the effect of it ?—Mr. Lewin : She will have togo to gaol.—The Chairman : I have never signed one of these things and I never will do. I do not believe in sending a woman to gaol for that.—Mr. Lewin advised the officer to make his application at the next sitting of the Petty Sessions. EASTER SHoW OF IcOvELTIES.—J.&. W. DUTTON'S Sankuy- at.. Warrington.—Advt. CHESHIRE LIBERAL FEDERAL COUNCIL. The Cheshire Liberal Federal Council met at Crewe on Saturday last. Mr. J. T. Brunner. M.P., presided, and gave an excellent address on the pre- sent position of politics inside the House of Com- mons and in the constituencies. There was a uood attendance the Liberal associations of all the Par- liamentary divisions in the county being represen- ted. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., was re-elected presi- dent of the Council, and Mr. W. S. B. NPLaren, M.P., chairman. Mr. James Tomkinson was again elected treasurer, and Mr. T. W. Killik honorary secretary of the Council. The reports of the state of • the Liberal party in the various parts of the county were satiafactory- and encouraging, and very hopeful views were expressed as to the results of the ap- proaching elections. DEATH OF ,THE OLDEST INHABITANT AT liALTON. On Wednesday the remains of Mrs. Elizabeth Bar- row, the oldest member of the Halton Female Friendly Society, were interred at Ilalton Cemetery. The Rev. J. Judson, Wesleyan minister, officiated. The deceased entered at the commencement of the society 72 years ago, and had attained the extraor- dinary age of 94. Out of respect for the deceased, a most unique procession took place, consisting of Mr. John Henry Gamon (trustee), Mr. T. Wright (secretary), and a considerable number of old members dressed in black, wearing the regalia of the club, consisting of white shawl with blue bor- der. Mr. Charles Reynolds. J.P. the other trustee, regretted his inability to be present, owing to prior engagements. The old lady was very highly res- pected in the parish. EtsTva Snow OF NOVELTIES.—J. & W. When they considered the benefits derived already from the supply of 'elementary education ; and how that education had become absolutely essential to those who were making their way in the world ; and when they saw that probably in the next few years science would become more and more the question of the day. It would be suicidal if the Board did not take every available step to give the youths of the towns the benefit of a scientific and technical education.—Mr.Pritchard,replying to Mr. Meadowcroft, said the School Board had done what they possibly could by establishing evening classes for teaching elementary schools, and there was a drawing class under way.
