div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday morning. Mr. S. Taylcr presided, and there were present Messrs. J. W. Lightburn, W. Fisher, J. Pritchard, F. Wiswall, J. Meadowcroft, H. Abel,. Imison,W. Hankinson,E. W. Humphreys, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Mars:iall (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor).

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer (Dr. MacDougall) reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 45, of which two were inquest cases, and of the remaining 43 nine were due to whooping cough, four co senile decay, three to phthisis, three to mesenteric disease, two to diseases of the liver, two to convulsions, an one each to inflammation of the heart, apoplexy, epilepsy, inflammation of the lining menabraae of the brain, albumimaris, continued fever, debility, dropsy, cramp, diabetes, and heart:disease. The ab e 45 deaths showed an average death-rate of 30 per 1,000 of the estimated population and exclusive of the inquest cases of 29.5.—1 n reply to Mr. Hutnphreys, the surveyor said in the corresponding month last year the number of deaths was 38.—Mr..Meadowcroft said the rate seemed unusually high.—Dr. MacDougall said there was a wave of whooping cough passing over the district, and the ex- ceptionally severe weather had increased the death-rate, as bronchitis was a " weather disease." There was no epidemic disease in the town. He did not think there was one case of fever.
NRW BUILDINGS.

The Highway and Buildings Committee approved of the following plans: Mersey Mission to seamen for the erection of an Institute in Station-road, (subject to the outhouse in Pig-lane being kept in line with the fence leading from the Co-operative Stores) ; Mr. Thomas Reynolds for the erection of 10 cottages in a new street off Norman-road (subject to a passage drain being connected with the main ~ewer) ; Messrs. John Wilson and others for the erection of four houses in Orrcd-st. The minutes were passed. FINANCE.—THE YEAR'S ESTIMATES.

The Finance Committee reported that during the past month the treasurer had received the following sums : General district rate £572 6s. sd. ; market rents and tells £3l Os. 3d. ; slaughter-houses, &c £3 17s. Od. ; overseers of thelpolr—ren , £l7 10s. Od.; Library rent £36 Os. Od. ; nightsoil sales £25 Os. 2d. ; Cheshire County Council— Sanitary inspector's,salary £62 10s. Od. ; canal boats fees £33s. 6. ; total £751 7s. 4d. Accounts amounting to £lO9 lls. 2d. on general fund, £7O MI loan account, and £8 18s. 10d. on Library fund. The Committee made the following recommendations :—That the estimates of the money required for the year ending March 25th, 1892, be approved. Estimated expenditure, £6,148 Os. Od. ; esti- mated income £655 Os. Oil.; amount required. £5,493.— That a general district rate at the rate of 2s. 3d. in the L for OK, year ending 25th March, 1892, be made; and that is. Id. be collected in the first six months, and is. lid, in the second six months.--With respect to the assessment and levying of the general district rate for the year ending 25th of March, 1892, it is recommended that the owner instead of the occupier, be rated, under the provision of Section 211 of the Public Health Act, 1875, where the rateatle value of any premises liable to assessment does not exceed the sum of Ten Pounds, and that he be assessed on a reduced estimate of three- fourths of the net annual value of such property.— Mr. Imison moved that the Board go into Committee to consider these minutes.—Mr. Fisher seconded—Mr. Meadowcroft asked for the reason of this curs, be- cause the nainutes of the Finance Committee were ex- tremely important.—Mr. Imison explained that there was a';,,ery " thin" attendance of the Committee at the time the minutes were passed, and the estimates were among the most important parts of the Commissioners' business, and he thought the members would like a fuller explanation than could be given in open meeting. Per- sonally he was indifferent whether the Board went into Committee or not.—The Chairman said there would be more free discussion in Committee. After further discus- sion,it was decided to go intoComimittee, Messrs. Hump- hreys, Hankinson, and Meadowcroft, voting against. TECHNICAL EDUCATION. Afters long discussion in Committee, the Board meet- ing was resumed, and on the motion of Mr. Humphreys, seconded by Mr. Wiswall, it was resolved that the following motion take precedence of the Finance Com- mittee :—" The Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, being the Local authority under the 'Technical Instruc- tion Act, 1889, do supply out of the General District Rate an amount not exceeding id. in the £, for the year ending 25th March, 1892 for the purpose of supplying or of aiding the supply of technical instruction in their district."—Mr. Pritchard thereupon moved the resolution, and pointed out that the County Council had decided that, any Urban Sanitary Authority adopting the Technical Instruction Act ; and levying a rate for technical instruction purposes,the County Council would be prepared on receiving the amount allocated to them under the Local Taxation Act 1890, to make a grant at least equivalent to the ratc so levied, not exceeding id. in the L. If this resolution were not passed that morning. the Commissioner would be jeo- pardising the £2OO which the County Council would be prepared to hand over to them. They could not say definitely that the money would be spent this year, be- cause some time must elapse before a scheme could be carried out ,but if they passed the resolution they would be entitled to the grant from the County Council. A scheme had been drawn up and submitted to the County Council ; the Board had asked for an annual grant in :Lid of the maintenance of a technical school ; and for a building grant. In addition, as they were aware, the Member of Parliament for the Division had offered to subscribe an amount equal to any amount that might be raised locally by subscription up to the extent of £5OO. Seeing they had so many friends favourable to technical instruction, he felt that the Board would not be consulting the interests of the ratepayers if they did not pass the resolution,and put them in a position to re- ceive the grant from the County Council.—Mr. Wiswall seconded the motion. He had received such benefits from popular and technical education himself and had seen such benefits derived, that if lie did not support that move—lent he should deserve whipping. There were managers ot schools on that Board, and he hoped tbey would welcome an effort of this kind, bemuse it would be one of the best t hings for them that could be Imagined. —Mr, Meadowcroft said he did not wish to lie considered opposed to terthnical education,but in his opinion the question was premature. Some consideration ought to be given to the supply and requirements of intermediate education, or education for the middle classes. They were increasing the taxation and neglecting the roads and streets of the town, many of which required immediate attention. The estimates of the various Committees were equal to a rate of 2s. 54. in the R. lie urged that the resolu- , Lion be not pressed.—Mr. Lightburn said practically they had

div.head: EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS.
div.p: EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS.
HOLY 'TRINITY RUNCORN.

The annual meeting of the parishioners of Holy Trin- ity Church, Runcorn, was held on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of the Rev. A. H. Sanderson the curate. There were present Messrs. W. Fisher, T. H. Annett, T. Salkeld, W. Hankinson, J. Buckley, Jobn , Meadowcroft, W. E. Lee, C. Timmins, A. G. Brigley, and W. J. Cunningham. Mr. Fisher,the vicar's warden. read the statement of accounts which showed that the col- lections for church expenses had a mounted to £59 Os. id. and for special6hjects £2l Be. lid. There was a balance in hand of 10s. 24d. but it was probable when all the accounts were paid that there would be a deficit.—On the proposition of Mr. Salkeld, seconded by Mr. Nankin- son, the accounts were passed.—The Vicar (Dr. Preston) who is travelling in the Holy Land, had sent a letter, in which he said there had been unity and harmony in Trinity Church during the past year and he hoped the j like would continue in the year to come. He heartily , thanked Mr. Fisher and the other officials for their kind- ness and for the judicious help they had rendered. He expressed regret that Mr. Fisher declined to serve again as warden and appointed Mr. Brigley in his place.--On the proposal of Mr. Fisher, seconded by Mr. Salkeld, Mr. Meadowcroft whose services were spoken of in terms of high praise was re-elected people's warden.—The following were elected sidesmen :—Messrs. C. Timmins, J. H. Salkeld, H. A. Hankinson, N. Large, W. E. Lea, and J. Savage; and these with the wardens were to form the Church Council.—Mr. Brigley and Mr. W. Plankinson were appointed the representatives of the church at the rural-decanal conferences.—On the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. Fisher, the choir were thanked for their excellent services; and Messrs. Timmins were thanked for having repaired the heating apparatus of the church free of charge. On the proposition of Mr. Cunningham seconded by Mr. Fisher. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings.

div.head: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.

The annual vestry was held on Tuesday night in the National Schools. The vicar, the Rev. G. H. Garrett M.A., presided, and there was a good attendance.—Mr. Dwerryhouse suemitted the accounts of St. Mary's Church, which showed an income for the year of £BO ss. 6id., and an expenditure of £79 2s. 3d., leaving a balance of El. 3s. 30.—Mr. Neil presented the accounts of St. Paul's Church : The income had been £BB3e. 10d., and the expenditure £56 33. 5., leaving a balance of five pence. The accounts were passed—The Vicar then made a speech, in which he referred to the ethication of the Young both, secularly and spiritually. In the past the Church of England had made provision for this by build- ing excellent day and Sunday schools in the town, and he expressed the hope that by the combined efforts of the clergy and laity, this good work would he long continued and still more glorious results be achieved. He hoped that in the near future St. Paul's Parochial Room would be constructed, And said it was intended to be used as a Sunday School. He thanked Mr. Neil, his warden ant the other officials for their valuable help in the past. He regretted that Mr. Neil wished to retire, and he appointed Mr. D. J. Brookes in his place.—On the notion of Mr. W. Treacy, seconded by Mr. Neil, Mr. Dwrrryhouse was re-appointed people's warden.—Messrs. Fl. N. ‘Vharton and F. Neil were appointed the lay repre- sentatives to the ruri-deCatial conferences.—The Vestry elected the followinz sidesmen :—St. Mary's Messrs. W. Treacy, T. Bruce, W. Hunt, A. Borthwick, P. Tomlinson, and J. L. Briscoe. St. Paul's: Messrs. J. Beach, J. Bar- clay, J. Burrows, T. Atherton, William Palin, and A. Case. —The Vicar appointed the following sidesmen :—St. Mars's: Messrs. L. Kilcross, J. Farrant, F. Beattie, T. Davies, C. Stead and J. Ward. St. Paul's: Messrs. J. Arnell, W. Lowe, S. Upward, J. Hodgson, R. Faulkner, and R. Carlisle.—Messrs. W. Treacy and J. Farrant, were re-elected auditors and Mr. G. R. Joynson was re- appointed vestry clerk. After a discussion respecting the way in which the books were iilused in the churches, and the necessity for more kneeling accomodation, the meeting concluded.

div.head: FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH.
ALLEGED POPISH PRACTICES.

The annual meeting of the vestry of Frodsham Parish Church washeld in the Kiag,%ley Chapel of Overton Church, on Monday. Ile Rev. H. B. Blogg, the vicar, presided and there was a large attendance. Amongst those present were the Rev. S. C. Barnby, Rev. R. D. Ringrose, Messrs. R. Foulks, H. E. Heywood, T. Lewis, C. Reynolds, J.P., Dr. Robinson. H. Tiley, S. Sharp, J. Pollard, senior, H. Watson, J. Austin, R. Holland, A. E. Pollard, W. Gaskell, T. Riley, G. Ashton, T. Ainsworth, G. Maddock, A. Lieaker, T. D. Timmins, F. Jolley, H. G. Linaker, R. Bate, G. Gleave, C. E. Linaker, J. Edwards, Sze.
THR ACCOUNTS.

Mr. C. E. Linaker (vicar's warden. ) presented the state- ment of accounts which showed that the offertories at the Parish Church amounted to £164 3s. lid.; proceeds of cantata £43 16s. id. ; Iron Church offertories £lB 18s. 7d.; special collection for Charities £73 55. Os. ; Harrison's Charity £2 18s. 4d. ; total £3lO 3s. Od. Ths expenditure included payment of balance from last account £2 18s. Od. Sexton £4O; maintenance of divine worship £62 us. 6d.; allowance paid vicar for distribution, and Iron Church expenses £49 15s. 20. There was a balance in hand of £29 Os. ld.—The account wm•regarded as very satisfac- tory and on the motion of Mr. Heywood seconded by Mr. R. Holland, the statement was adopted.
HARRISON'S CHARITY. This charity of £2 18s. 4d. had been distributed by the Vicar to poor widows. Each widow had received 55., the charity having been added to by a contribution from the alms.
ORGAN TRUST FUND. • This fund amounted to £69 19s. 5d., and after paying I Mr. Riley £2O as organist and ether expenses, there was a balance of £43 18s. sd. carried forward.
THE, SUNDAY SCHOOL'S : HITRAORDINARY LEAFLET.

Miss Crosfield had sent an. account of the Church-st., school, and Miss Wright an account of the Overton school.—Mr. Foulkes drew attention to a leaflet circu- lated by one of the teachers of the Sunday school amongst the young women,, and he wished to know whether this lady was a fit and proper person to be a Sunday school teacher. The•leaflet was entitled "Sins against the ten commandments," and it stated it was a in against the first "to prefer my own opinion to the teaching of the church," against the second "to receive the holy communion not discerning the Lord's body and blood—failed to receive it fasting when my health permitted, omitted to use conftsion' when I knew I needed it; gone to a place of worship not belong- ing to the church, neglected to say grace before and after meals, said my prayers not kneeling down." What asked Mr. Foulkes became of the Scotch people who said their prayers standing up, and of the many clergy who said prayers standin up.—The leaflet also said it was a sin against the third commandment to have wilfully kept back something in confession; slurred over a sin to avoid the full shame of it. A sin against the fourth commandment to neglect the holy days and fast days of the church, broken holy days by excess of eat- ing, excess of merrymaking; failed to practice self denial on fast days. "What rot" exclaimed Mr. Foulkes.— Mr. C. E. Linaker : Are you prepared to move a resolu- tion.—Mr. Foulkes: I lay it before the vestry meeting.— Mr. Heywood: Cut it short.—Mr. Foulkes: I have done. He added that many sentences in the leaflet were taken from Canon Carter's, the famous ritualist's "Treasury of Devotion." He proposed that the Vicar deal with the question.—The Vicar said he was ignorant of any such tract being distributed; this was the first he had heard of it, and if it were true that such a tract had been distributed amongst the young people, there were one or two points which were very reprehensible, and he should make it his duty to inquire into the matter.

THE PASSING BELL. The Vicar said he was constantly receiving complaints of the annoyance caused by the ringing of the passing bell on the day previous to the funeral, and he moved tha it be discontinued.—Mr. Foulkes seconded.—Dr. Robinson said he did not think the vicar was in order in bringing the matter forward without notice. He argued that it was an old custom to ring the passing bell, and there was a scale of fees approved by the Chancellor.— Mr. C. E. Linaker said although he did not agree with the ringing of the passing bell, yet Dr. Robinson's objec- tion was valid.—Mr. Reynolds concurred, and the vicar did not press the matter.
ATTEMPT TO PLAY TUNES. On the suggestion of the Vicar, Mr, A. Linaker pro-

div.head: TOTES OF. TIIANAS.
div.p: TOTES OF. TIIANAS.

Votes of thanks were. Ceralered to the choir for their services, and to ladies for gifts of flowers, Mr. Fox pro- testing that flowers were not out of place in a church. A vote of condolence was passed, on the motion of the Vicar, with reference to the death of Mr. Linaker, and carried unanimously.

ALLEGED 3.IALPRACTICES IN THE CIIURCII, Mr. Foulkes now entered his protest against the pro- cessions in the church, ridiculing the fact of a congrega- tiAn of 200 doing homage to a set of lads and men. He also protested against the adoption of the eastward posi- tion. He thought it would be better if the clergy did not give Bible lessens in the day schools, and objected to their comments upon the reading, and to the doctrine of Apostolic succession being taught in the "Parish Magazine." Then what right, asked he, had the curate, ths. Rev. Mr. Barmby, to go into a Nonconformist family and tell them a Nonconformist minister could do no good, because the Bishop had not laid his hands upon him? Several hymns in the Hymns Ancient and Modern were discribed as rank popery.—Mr. Edwards proposed that Mr. Foulkes be not heard.—Mr. Watson seconded.—Mr. Foulkes proposed that the processions in church and the eastward position be discontinued, and that a more sound doctrinal hymn book be obtained. There was no seconder to this proposition, and the meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the Chairmin.

ELSBY. The annual vestry meeting was held in the Infant , Schoolroom on Monday evening. The Vicar presided,and , the accounts showed a balance of between £2 and £3 in hand. Messrs. Baird and Crosslani Taylor were re- elected wardens, and Messrs. James Reynolds, Garner, James Taylor, and Whiteley were elected sidesmen. Votes of thanks were accorded to Mr. Hill, the voluntary organist, and the choir, and a small pecuniary acknow- ledgment was made to Mr. Hill. ST. MARY'S, HALTON. The annual vestry meeting of the parishioners of St. Mary's Cburch was held on Tuesday night, in the Parochial Schools, the Vicar (the Rev. G. D. Wray) pre- siding. The accounts presented by the wardens were very satisfactory, the income for the year with the bal- ance from last year amounting to £17925. 90., and the expenditure £153 Os. 80., leaving a balance in hand of £26 2s. id. The accounts having been passed, the Vicar re-appointed Mr. Thomas Wright as his warden, and Mr. Joseph Stokes was unanimously re-appointed people's warden. Messrs. J. M. Baguley, J. Ackerley, William Nixon, E. Buckley, J. H. Horton, and J. Rutter, were elected sidesmon. Votes ot thanks were given by the Vicar to the wardens for their services, also to Mr. J. W. Haddock, lay reader, and to the choirmaster and choir. The charity accounts for 1890 were then presented, from which it appears that the total income from St. Thos's. charity was £24 10s. 11d., and the distribution £2l 65., leaving a balance of £3 4s. 114. The Stockhana charity with a balance in hand amounts to £B5 19s. 54. ; dis- tribution, £1 Is. ; leaving a balance of £B4 18s. 54. The Vicar's and wardens' coal charity showed receipts £4 9s. 5d.; expenditure, £3 is. ; leaving a balance of £1 Ts. Bd.

div.head: DEATH OF MU. S. T. ALLEN OF WIDNES.
div.p: DEATH OF MU. S. T. ALLEN OF WIDNES.

r The inhabitants of Widnes were plunged into mourning, on Saturflay evening last, by the sudden death of Mr. J. T. Allen, the clerk to the Widnes Local Board. Although the public offices were closed for the Easter holidays on Saturday, Mr. Allen came down to business as usual in the morn- ing, and attended to his correspondence. About half-past nine he called in the Free Library and complained to Miss Proctor of feeling unwell. He afterwards called at Parr's Bank and Hutchinson's estate office in Ditton-road, and was on his way to the public offices when he was seized with severe pains at the region of the heart, and he was at once driven to Dr. O'Keeffe's surgery in one of Mr. Lee's cabs. He was evidently in terrible agony, his face was deathly pale, his lips livid, and his hands as cold as ice. Dr. O'Keeffe did all in his power to alleviate his sufferings, hut in view of his critical condition he called in Dr. MacLennan to his assis- tance,and by their united efforts the pain was consi- derably eased. In the meantime, Mrs. Allen had been acquainted with her husband's condition, and she quickly came to Whines, accompanied by her family. Acting on the advice of the medical kentle- men Mrs. Allen called in Dr. Carter of Liverpool, to net in consultation. The physician arrived at half- past two, and after having made a careful examina- tion he held out no hopes of Mr. Allen's recovery. Gradually the patient became worse, and about nine o'clock he passed away in the presence of his wife and family and the medical gentlemen. Ile was conscious to the end. The disease, which had un- fortunately so fatal a result, was angina pectoris by which Mr. Allen had been twice previously attacked. Mr. Lea, undertaker, prepared a shell in which the deceased rentleman was conveyed to his home at Heugh Green, early on Sunday morning. When it became known that Mr. Allen was lying dangerously ill at Dr. O'Keeffe's house, there were in- quiries made by all classes of the community and with the exception of Mr. Gossage and Mr. Carey, who were absent from the district, the whole of the members ot the Local Board called and made anxious inquiries. His death caused widespread grief and sorrow throug,houtthe town and the suddenness of the sad „event added to the keen- ness of the blow.

_ Mr. Allen, who had attained the age of 49 years, had been clerk to the Local Board for 12 years. Previously he had been engaged in the accountant's department of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., chemical manufacturers. He went to the works as a junior clerk, in the cashier's department, under Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., for the Nerthwich Division, who was then the manager of the works. By his ability as a financier and his steady per- severance, Mr. Allen became chief of the accountants department, which position he filled up to the time of succeeding Mr. Beasley as clerk to the Local Board. At that time the financial affairs of the Local Board were in a most involved condition, but Mr. Allen reduced choas to order and placed the acountant department of the town's affairs on a sound and con- venient basis. He made himself thoroughly conversant with the acts relating to local authorities, and by his careful, cautions, and able management he, during his clerkship, saved the Board some thousands of pounds which had formerly been spent in law. No ques- tion was too difficult and no labour too hard for him to undertake, and it is generally believed that he died a martyr to duty. His labour in connection with the re- cent application for a charter of incorporation had been very great, and when hi a office was closed he had spent many scores of hours at home with his books and papers.

THE FUNERAL. The respect and esteem in which Mr. Allen was h eld was shown at the funeral which took place at Hale wood , Church, on Friday at 5 p.m. Gentlemen and tradesmen I from all parts of the district assembled to take part in the last sad rites and the sight was a most solemn and impressive one. The funeral cortege left Hough Green about four o'clock, and following the hearse were five mourning coaches. The occupants of the coaches were first: Three sons of the deceaged and Mr. T. Allen and H. K. Douglas ; second: Mr. Young. Mr. P. Rurphey, Mr. H. R. and Mr. R. Allen and Mr. Mybrea (Douglas) ; third : Revs. C. W. Wool! and G. A. Le I3ert, Dr. O'Keeffe and Mr. B. Brown ; fourth : Mr. G. H. Danby (clerk to the School Beard) and Captain Lewis ; fifth : Mr. J.Mid- wood and Mr. S. Sadler. The private carriages of Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., Mr. 11 Wade Deacon, J.P., and Dr. Cooper were in the procession, and the last-named car- riage was occupied by Dr. fludsen and Dr. Hutchinson. The funeral con/ye was met at the graveyard by a large number of friends and public men, amongst them being Mr. F. H.Gossage,J.P.,Chairman of the Local Board,Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, J.P., Chairman of the School Board, Major Wareing, Chairman of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians, Mr. James Handley, J.P., Mr. J. Squarey,barrister- at-taw, Major Brunner, Major Cross, Rev.C. J. Robinson, Rev,G. H. St. Patrick Garrett, Dr. Hurter, Dr. McDon- nell, Mr. W.Christy (secretary of the Widnes Ratepaypts' Association), Mr. H. S. Timmis ' • the following members of the Local Board :—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. F. Heyes, J. Houghton, E. Carey, W. J. Hargreaves, D. Wright, F. C. Liddell, John Taylor, S. Sadler, J. Midwood, R. Cook, G. I. Neil, S. Hoyle (chief clerk), J. S. Sinclair (surveyor), and I. Carr (engineer), and J. H. Wilson, J. Heyes, W. Lowe, C. Whit field, I. Sankey, ,t. Ground, T. Hughes, J. Y. Dale, and G. Hackney, (Officialsof the Board) ; Miss Proctor, (librarian) ; Miss Walker. (assistant librarian) ; Superintendent Noblett, Inspector Keighley. Messrs. C. H. Lewin (deputy magis- trates clerk) ; F. Neil, (overseer) ; J. Goff, (assistant overseer) ; G. E. Sayce, C. Hemingway, J. Beech, R. Booth, H. Singleton* D. Hurst, W. Farrant,F. H. rank- hurst, J. Morrison, V. C. Driffield, J. C. Routledge, J. Buckley, J. Hough, W. Hunter, J. R. Lea, J. S. Snoddy, T. Handley, 'l'. J. Peters, A. E. Calvert, F. J. pole, Oppenheim (Oppenheim and Malkin, St.. Helens) ;John Heyes, J. Cooke, Booth, (Ditton) ; Sergeant Clarkson, W. Pritchard, W. Trea,cy, J. Treacy, G. Stead, E. V. Bibby, (Garston) ; F. Knight, J. Hurst, S. Evans, J. Dixon, J.Chaoman, S. Owens, J. Crawshaw, J. Davies, John Matthews, R. Harriman, N. Parkes, Thorpe. J. ' Kershaw, R. Fogg, S. Robinson, S. Kidd, and ex-Inspec- tor O'Donnell. The funeral service in the church and at the graveside was conducted by the Rev. C. W. Wooll, Vicar of Hough Green,aml the Rev. G. A. Le Bert, Vicar of St. Ambrose, Widnes. The deceased gentletnan tiad expressed a desire that there should not be any flowers, but a number of friends who were not a.•;quainted with this wish had sent beautiful floral tributes. PUBLIC SYMPATHY. From numerous persons and all sources,Mrs. Allen has received expressions of regret and condolence in her

great sorrow, showing hu her that her late sband was universally esteemed. The local representatives of the press have forwarded the following resolution 1--Wo, the representatives of the newspaper press in Widnes District desire to record our appreciation of the ability and talent displayed by the late Mr. Allen in his fuLfittnent of his important duties as clerk to the Widnes Local Board, of his geniality of character and kindness of heart and to acknowledge the readinesswith which he always' as far as lay in his power, aided us in placing the rate-' rxiyers in possession of the fullest information on public affairs. We also desire to express our deep sympathy With you in your great bereavement."

THE LOCAL BOARD. A special meeting of the Local Board was held on Thursday under the presidency of Mr. F. H. Gossage.- There were present Messrs. E. Carey, B. Brown, J. Mid 'wood, D. Wright, R. Cook, H. S. Tiramis, G. I. Neil, W• J. Hargreaves, J. Taylor, J. Houghton, S. Sadler, r, Heyes, and Dr. O'Keeffe. H. S. Oppenheim (law adviser) and S. Hoyle (assistant clerk), and J. S. Sinclair (sur- veyor.) The Chairman explained that it had been neces- sary to call the meeting owing to the great loss the Board had sustained by the death of Mr. Allen. the clerk. Ar- rangements would have to be made for the conduct of business until such time as the result of the Board's application for a charterof incorporation was ascertained He expressed his sorrow at Mr. Allen's death, and said the loss to his family and friends was a great one, and certainly Widnes had lost one of the best servants it ever had. (Hear, hear. 1 He proposed the following resolu- tion :—" That the metuliers of the Board desire to record their high appreciation of the ability, self-sacrificing zeal, and success with which Mr. J. T. Allen has served the ratepayers of Widnes during the 12 years that he has been clerk and accountant to the Widnes Local Board. They desire also to express their great sorrow at his death, and their heartfelt sympathy with his family:— Mr. Midwood seconded, and remarked that he was cu.- tai with regard to finance that no man could ever work better than Mr. Allen had done. He was untiring and indefatigable, and he frequently took his books borne at night. With regard to Incorporation he had worked very hard, and he was of opinion that it was the manner in which he had worked on that question which had brought about his death. His demise was a great loss to the ratepayers of Widnes, and he did not believe that they could replace him.—Mr. Brown said,personally, Mr. Allen had been a friend to him for many years. He was a reasonable, consistent man, and his willingness to serve anyone, in times of necessity, was a marked feature in his character. He was a man the longer they knew hint the more they loved him.—Mr. Carey also supported the resolution, and echoed Mr. Brown's remarks, and spoke of Mr. Allen's ability, tact, and zeal, in the public service. The resolution was carried unanimously.—Mr. Oppen- helm read the following letter :—" 50, Palace Chambers, Westminster, S.W., 7th April, 1891. Dear sir,—l am very sorry to hear of Mr. Allen's death, which I am sure will be a grert loss to the town of Widnes, as well as to his own personal friends. 1 was struck both with his ability and with his kindness of disposition. When I left him, last Wednesday at the foot of the Bridge, the chair- man who accompanied me on to the Bridge, remarked that the town and Local Board were very fortunate in having so excellent a clerk. lam much obliged to yon Bin letting me know of the sad occurrence.—lieve me, yours, faithfully. —T. H. W. PELHAM. H. S. Oppentiem, hsq..st. Helens."—The Board then went into committee to discuss the mode of carrying on the business tem- porarily until it was ascertained what reply would be given to the petition for a charter of incorporation. After a long discussion the matter was referred to the Finance Committee to work out the details. eseesee......

- - - RUNCORN WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION. The inauguara.l meeting of this association will be held in Bethesda Lecture Hall,on Friday evening,the 10th inst., when the principal speaker will be the lion. Lady Sebright. Mr. W. Parish, J.P.,has consented to preside, and the event will be one of great interest in temperance circles. PRESENTATION TO A FOROEMAN COOPER. On Thursday, the coopers at the British Alkali Works presented Mr. William Newton, of Peelhouse-lane, who has just retired after having been foreman there nearly fifteen years, with a beautiful tea and coffee service and a handsome silver mounted walking stick, suitably in- scribed which they had purchased at a cost of ten guineas. APPOIN'TMEXT OF OVERSEERS AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Tuesday the 4sts of per- sons nominated to serve as overseers were presented and the Magistrates (Mr. Brundrit and Major Hazlohurst) appointed the following—Acton Grange : Robert Bate, and Thomas Challoner ; Aston by Sutton : George Percival and William Wilkinson; Clifton : Joseph Stokes, and Samuel Rowlands; Halton: Thomas Wright, and Hugh Rowe; Norton: Thomas Percival, and Clement Baguley ; Runcorn : Edward Imison, and Samuel Tay- lor; Sutton : William Lowe, and John E. Bate ; Stock- ham: J. W. Baguley, and James Clarke; Weoton : Edward Aaron, and Thomas Ford.—Mr. James Collier was re-appointcd assistant overseer for Weston.

div.head: RUNCORN RIFLE CY:CR.-GOLD MEDAL COMPETITIOK.
div.p: RUNCORN RIFLE CY:CR.-GOLD MEDAL COMPETITIOK.

The first of a series of eight competitions for 1891 took place on Saturday, under circumstances very unfavour- able for good shooting, the wind blowing very strong from the right front. The following are the totals made by those present : Points. Sergeant W. H. Harvey 79 Sergeant D. Itclwards 76 Sergeant J. A. Itashton 74 Corporal W. Cooper 7l Corporal G. R. Joynson 7l Pi irate Joinson 69 Sergeant J. W. Woodland 6B RUNCORN DISTRICT NURSV FUND.

On Thursday evening, the " Negro Nomads" amateur troupe of minstrels gave an entertainment in Runcorn Public Hall to a large audience. Mr. Lightburn opened the proceedings by stating that the proceeds would be handed over to the district nurse fund for the purpose of augmenting the fund already in the hands of the trea- surer which it was intended to invest, and so endow and give a permanent form to a very excellent institution. The first part of the programme consisted of songs and choruses and the usual conundrums and jokes. In the second part "Professor Snowball, F.R.0.G.5." (Mr. Halliday) gave a capital stump speech, and the banjo eccentricities and the selections of the banjo and Mando- line band were much enjoyed.

WIDNES CYCLE CLUE. The members inaugurated the season on Wed- nesday evening, by a smoking concert at the Gros- venor Hotel. Mr. W. G. Bucknall presided, and the large number present spent an enjoyable time. Songs and musical selections were given.

SHIP CANAL MISSION RUNCORN. During the Easter holidays a reading room has been opened in connection with this mission. On Mcnday a meat tea was provided and partaken of by 130 persons. Afterwards a public meeting was held under the presidency of the Hon. and Rev. R. Grimston. Addresses were delivered by Messrs. R. Wilson, W. Shaw, J. B. Dennis, J. Watson, (former missionary) and Mr. J. Mufdin. SCALDED TO DEATH BY A CrP OF COFFEE. On Tuesday, Mr. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at Widnes Folice Station. touching the death of Charlotte Powell, aged two years and seven months, the daughter of John Powell, of 124, Lugsdale-road. On the 24th ult. the father was having his supper at the kitchen table, with the deceased standing between his knees. The girl was playing with a doll made up of cloth, and with this she upset a cup of hot coffee, a quantity of which , , fell upon her breast, and scalded her. The usual re- medies were applied, and Dr. McLennan called, but the child, who had been delicate from birth, died early on the morning of the 27t1s ult. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. on, YES I' Cough Mixture, Chiretta Balsam. Relief in three minutes. Cures Bronchitis. Hope. late Methuen, Deansgate, Manchester. and all Dealers.—Advt. FIRE ON THE SHIP CANAL AT RUNCORN. Early on Wednesday morning several barrels of crude oil, which were placed near a lucigen light. at the Old Quay Docks,caught fire and were quickly in flames. The workmen took prompt measures to extinguish the fire and they succeeded admirably. , The damage is roughly estimated at .£5O. PRHMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire. —GARL itin„Warrington. I —Advt.

At the St. Helens Town Hall. on Monday, Bridget Kildare, a notorious local character, wag charged with drunkenness.—Chief Constable Wood stated that the prisoner had been 189 times previously con- victed.—She pleaded guilty, and was lined ss. and costs. or 14 days' imprisonment. BASTER SHOW OF NOVELTIES.—J. & W. Durrom's Sankey- et., Warrington.—Advt. GOOD TEMPLAR CONFERENCE. The Grand Lodge of Good Templars contirued its sittings on Wednesday, at Great Yarmouth, when papers were road and discussed on temperance education in lodges. A scheme for the visitation of lodges was agreed to. At the evening sitting a largo number of the Grand Lodge members were initiated into the Juvenile Order, taking the four- fold pledges against drink, tobacco, gambling, and profane swearing. EASTHR SHOW OF NOVELTIF-4.- J. & W. DurTos's, Sankey- et., Warrington.— Advt. SUICIDE AT ASHTON.

On Tuesday evening, Ellen Stockley, an elderly woman, residing in Liverpool-road, Ashton, commit- ted suicide by taking poison. She had complained of feeling unwell, and was sitting in front of the kitchen fire, when her son not iced that she held in her hand a bottle labelled "Carbolic acid." He asked her if she had been drinking the poison, and as she made no reply, he sent for a doctor. She died a short time afterwards. BAssmErrEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Adrt. THREATENING TO MURDER HIS WIFE. On Monday morning, Alfred Lord, a collier, residing at the Barracks, Lanehead, Lowton, was charged before Mr. Walter Tunnicliffe (chairman), and Messrs. J. Green, and W. H. Arnott, at the Leigh Police Court with threatening to murder his wife, Martha Ann Lord, on the afternoon of March 28th. ! —Mr. Superintendent Higginbotham said that the prisoner had been married about 18 months. During the whole of their married life they had lived un- happily together, and on Saturday afternoon he jumped up and ran to the back of the kitchen door, where a coat was hanging. He took a revolver from the coat and pointed it at her,and she screamed out " Murder.' She ran into another room, and whilst there he put the revolver back into the coat pocket. Soon after he put his jacket on and told his wife that he was going to give himself up, and that she would not again see him for years. He met a constable and gave himFelf up, and the constable brought him to the station. He was examined by Dr. King, who declared that the prisoner was suffering from some mental delusion. Prisoner's wife said she had led a very unhappy life, and was really afiaid of her husband, who was of a jealous disposition.—The magistrates remanded prisoner for a week. div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday week. Mr. W. J. Wareing presided, and there were alse present Rev. S. A. K. Silvester, Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. Johnson, Leatherlaarrow, Middlehurst, Ranson, Davies,E. Birchall, James Burchall,J. Buckley, Longton, Kenwright, Joseph Burchall, and S. H. Hartley (clerk.)

RELI-EF. —The Workhouse Master reported that there were 570 inmates of the house this week, 566 last week, and 586 in the corresponding week last year. THE LIVERPOOL INFIRMART.—A letter was received from the Local Government Board intimating that they con- sented to the payment of a sum of £2l per annum to the funds of the Royal Infirmary at Liverpool. THF ALTERATION OF RELIIIF DISTRICTS.—The Local Government Board wrote consenting to the proposed alterations in the general relief districts of the Union, and requesting to be furnished with particulars of the I appointment of Messrs. Flampson and Wood as relieving officers for the Widnes and Ditton districts respectively. The Clerk stated that he had forwarded the information ' asked:for. RELIEVING OFFICERS AND THEIR WAGES.—MT. C. M. Stuart, relieving officer for the Windle district, wrote applying for an increase of salary. He stated that he had completed ten years' service, and it was upwards of seven years since he was granted the last increase. During that period the duties had largely increased, and he thought he was fairly entitled to an increase. He did not know of any resolution of the Board fixing a maxim- um salary.—Mr. Middlehurst moved that the communi- cation be referred to the finance committee, and the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester seconded.—The Rev. Dean Fine- gan suggested that the matter might be settled by the board that afternoon. • It seemed to be merely a questios whether or not the Board had ever fixed a maximum salary, and Mr. Stuart's application seemed to be on be- half of all the relieving officers in the Union.—Mr. Leatherbarrow said it had always peen the custom to refer all finance matters to the committee first.—The motion was then passed. A MESSENGER FOR Sr. HELENS—In accordance with notice given at the last meeting, Mr. Middlehurst moved that James Littler, formerly an inmate of the Work- house, be appointed messenger and assistant at the relief offices in St. Helens at a salary of 13s. per week.—Mr. Ranson seconded, and the motion was carried. This was all the business.

div.head: SHOCKING ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT
div.p: SHOCKING ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT
F RODSFIAM.

A serious wounding case has been reported to the police. It appears that on Wednesday night, about seven o'clock, a Mrs. Latitam, wife of a labourer, living on the quay at Frodsham Bridge, was passing the house of a neighbour named Mercer, who also lives on the Quay. Mrs. Mercer, who is the wife of a labourer, em- ployed at Weston Soapery, was standing at her door at the time, and she said to Mrs. Latham, " What have you been saying about me ?" Mrs. Latham denied that she even mentioned her name, whereupon, it is alleged Mrs. Mercer struck the woman on the head with a poker, remarking," I will let you see." The injured woman fell to the ground, and as she was rising Mrs. Mercer, it is said, struck the woman another blow on the head with the same instrument. Mrs. Latham became unconscious, in which condition she remained until some neighbours who happened to come at the time, picked her up, and conveyed her to an adjoining house. Mrs. Latham's brother lost no time in communicating with the police, and Dr. Weaver was called in to attend' the ,injured woman' who recovered consciousness in aboutour after the assault. Mrs. Mercer will be brought before the magistrates on the charge of unlawfully woundiw.

ERRING FEMALES AT WARDINGTON.—A YOUNG MAN WANTED TO EMIGRATB ? At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, Annie Cunningham, who, it was said, had Coma all the way from Colwyn Bay, was charged with indecent beha- viour in Winmarleigh-st. She was discharged on pro- mising to leave the town. Annie Daley, for sleeping in ' an outbuilding, at Arpley, was sent to goal for 14 days. —Bodielia. Knockton, made her 48th appearance on a warrant for not having appealed to answer a charge of drunkenness on the 21st March. The Bench expressed considerable perplexity as to what they should do with this prisoner, as she had, just prior to the above-named offence, served three months in goal. Alderman Sutton thought it was a—pity-there was not some kind of asylum to send people of this sort to, and the Mayor. suggesz,ed I that some young man ought to fall in love with Bodelia and take her out to Australia, where she might turn • over a new leaf. As Bodelia expressed much penitence and a firm determination to do better in future tile • Bench decided as a kind of experiment, to let her off this time.

A POLICEMAN FELLED WITH A. BOTTLE. At the Borough Court on Monday, a young fellow named John Bowen, of Warieurton-st.,was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on Saturday night, and Henry Bowen, a brother, was charged with having violently assaulted P.C. C3rcoran. It seemed from the evidence that P.C. Corcoran and another officer were on duty at the Empire Theatre on Saturday night, when Corcoran's attention was drawn to the fact that John Bowen, who sat over the entrance to the Theatre, was spitting on people as they entered. The officer at first cautioned Bowen, then shifted him to another part of the building, and at length had to eject him into the street. Henry Bowen was standing in the street when his brother was ejected with a large bottle partly filled with beer in his possession. This bottle he threw at Corcoran with considerable force, and it hit the officer on the head, breaking his helmet and felling him to the ground. Corcoran was stunned with the blow, and fell twice or thrice in attempting to rise, and had to be assisted to the surgery of Dr. Starkey Smith. Both prisoners pleaded guilty, and John Bowen was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days, while Henry was sent to gaol for two months' hard labour. THE AXE-WOUNDING CASE.—SETTLED BY COMPENSATION.

At the Borough PO-lice Court, on Thursday morning, the case in which Wm. Sheldon, aged 16, was charged with striking Thomas Rathhone, aged 20, on the head with an axe and severely wounding him, on the 2nd of March, was again brought up. Mr. Whittle represented the prosecutor, and Mr. A. Brown the defendant. Mr. ] Whittle said he did not propose to offer any evidence, as , after enquiry into the case he found that the prosecutor , himself was not,p,ltogether free from blame; in fact he thought it was six of one and half-a-dozen of the other, up to a certain point. Although nothing could justify the use of the axe by be delendant, at the same time there was a great aeargraravation, and he thought the case would be properly met by thd payment of £lO compensation.—Mr. Browne said he and Mr. Whittle had had a consultation, and it did appear that there was no absolute preponderance of evidence for the defendant, and that the latter was to blame up to a cer- thin point. The prosecutor had been following and an- noying the defendant time after time, and the two lads were fighting on the date in question, when the defend- ant in a moment of excitement picked up an axe, which unfortunately was in the way. Therefore he (Mr. Browne), was advised by his client to offer to the pro- secutor £lO compensation, £5 to be paid down, and the father to be surety for the balance being paid in nine weeks. Sheldon and Rathbone both, in reply to Alderman Sutton, said they consented to the case being settled in the manner stated ; and the defendant was discharged. ScPPOSED ATTEMPT TO COMMIT SUICIDE. Fanny Fern, a widow, 29 years of age, was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Saturday morn- ing, before Alderman Burgess, with attempting to com- mit suicide by taking a quantity of laudanum. From a statement madeby the Chief Constable, it appearEd that on Thursday night, the prisoner who had been drinking during the afternoon picked up a small bottle from the mantleshelf of the house in which she lived, in Ship- yard, and said, "I will go and poison myself." The . prisoner then left the house and shortly after was seen by her landlady, Mrs. Garrity, coming out of Mr. Hales's chemist's shop in Bridge-st. Remembering that the pri- soner had threatened to destroy herself, Mrs. Garrity ran into the shop, and asked the assistant "What have you supplied that woman with ? " and his reply was " pennyworth of laudanum." Mrs. Garrity told the assist- ant that the prisoner had threatened to destroy herself. Hearing that, the assistant rushed out of the shop, and followed the prisoner into a public-house, when he saw her in the act of drinking the laudanum. He knocked the bottle out of her hand, and the remainder of the laudanum was spilled on thefloor. The prisoner who bad already drunk a quantity of it, was removed 4) the Infirmary, where the stomach pump was used. She was subsequently taken to the Police Station, and locked up on the charge Of attempting to commit i sui- cide. The prisoner said she: ad no intention to take away he f life. She drank the udanum to cure a cold la from which She was suffering. n answer to his Worship, the assistant to Mr. Hales said,half,,the quantity of the, laudaniim might have killed . her, or she might have drunk therwhole of it and still have lived. A great deal depended von the constitutiomof a person. His Worship said the prisoner had acted yen, foolishly. He was not sure whether she intenAed to take away her life. He would, therefore, give Tier the benefit of the doubt and simply bind her over to keep the pea for six months in one surety of £5. MINOR CASES.

DRUNK.—Henry Evans, charged with being drunk in Scotland-road, last night, was dismissed. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Cope, drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road soon after midnight this morning, was fined ss. including costs. CHARGE OF WIFE ASSAIJLT.—John Knight was charged with assaulting his wife Margaret on the 31st ult. The crust of a potatoe pie made by the complainant was not brown, and he consequently blackened her eye as she stated, though she did not wish to press the case. The defendant was bound over in his own recognisances of £5 to keep the peace for six months and to pay 10s. ed. costs ; in default 14 days. FZlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall. DRUNK AND DISORDSRLY.—Thomas Dolan, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on Thursday night, was fined ss.—James Disdale and Joseph Anderson were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st , on Thursday night, and Anderson was also charged with assaulting P.C. Cooper. Disdale wasfined ss. and costs, and Anderson was sent to prison for a month's hard labour. DEO:WK.—Peter Fahey, from Manchester, was charged with being drunk in Bridge-st., this morning.—A police officer said that he heard this morning a sound of shout- ing coming from the direction of the river, and on going to the riverside found the defendant in the water up to his arms, and crying for help. With assistance witness got him out. He was nearly perished with cold, and was drunk, and they brought him to the station for safety.—The prisoner was discharged on promising not to come there again. A WOMEN'S QUARREL.—Elizabeth Ditchfield was charged with assaulting Sarah Caldwell, widow, of 599, Knutsford-road, Latchford, next door to the defendant's, on the 24th ult. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecu- tion and Kilshaw for the defence.—Mr. Browne desired that the case might be adjourned, as he understood that the defendant was in Alderman Harrison's employ. Alder- man Harrison indignantly denied this, but said that years ago she was occasionally employed by him as a washerwoman. Mrs. Caldwell and Mrs. Ditchfield had called upon him about the case, but he had told them both, as he always did under such circumstances, that he would not listen to anything they had to say except' in court. Mrs. Caldwell now stated that she was wash- ing in her yard on March 24th when the defendant threw some suds into the yard, and when this was com- plained of threw a bucket of water over her.—Henry Cooper deposed to die latter circumstance occurring.— The defendant denied the assault, and said she merely poured some water down the slopstone, and it went into the complainant's yard. The complainant asked her what she did it for, and used bad language to her, and accused her of murdering her husband, her mother, and her only daughter.—Tne complainant denied this.— Aldermat. Harrison said from what he had heard of Mrs. Caldwell and Mrs. Ditchfield he would not like to live within half a mile of them, and if there had been a cross- summons both would have been bound over as they were one as bad as the other, but as it was, Mrs. Ditchteld would be bound over in one surety of £5 to keep the 'peace for six months. A Row AMONG WOMEN AT LATCHFORD.—The following adjourned cases were now due for hearing.:-.---Sarah O'Donnell, a married weman, and Catherine O'Donnell, her daughter, were charged with assaulting Minnie Bray, a married woman ; Minnie Bray with assaulting the O'Donnell's and Charlotte Elizabeth Johnson, and also with threatening Caroline Davies ; Patrick Glynn, with assaulting the O'Donnell's and Catherine O'Donnell and Minnie Bray with fighting in Foundry-st., Town's End. The O'Donnell's lived in Foundry-st., Bray in Lyon-st., and Glynne in Erwood-at., and the date of the alleged offences was March 7th. It was now intimated ti at Mrs. O'Donnell was dead, and that all the cases would be withdrawn except those in which Bray was charged with assaulting Johnson and with threatening; Davies. Mr. Browne appeared in these for Bray. It ap- peared that Bray went to Johnson's house, dragged her out and kicked her, as' Johnson declared,without provo- cation, hut it seemed that Johnson had previously cut Bray's clothes line, and threatened her about a teapot of hers which Bray had. The threatening language of Bray was used on the 6th of March, when Davies and five other women .went to Bray's with their sleeves rolled up. This charge was dismissed, and for the assault Bray was bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months; and ordered to pay the costs.

He was fined 2s. 6d. and rosts.—Richard Massey was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Liverpool-road, Sankey Bridges. He was fined ss. and costa. TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET.—Peter Thompson was charged by the L. and N-W. Railway Co., with travel- ling without a ticket between Newton and Wigan, on the 9th of February. It was stated for the prosecution by Mr. Preston, solicitor. of Liverpool, that the defendant was a frequent traveller on the line. He left Newton by the 5 45 a.m. train on the 9th of February, and was followed by a detective to Wigan. He left the train there , and went out by what was calledi the fish-house gate, not ' the proper exit door for passengers, but used for boxes. He was seen to take a hamper out with him; then he came back onto the platform,and in fifteen minutes went out at the same door. On being followed and asked for his ticket, he made various excuses for not having one, stating that he was accustomed to take fish through the fish house door, and that he always paid his fare at Wigan, also that he had not had time to get a ticket at Newton. The defendant, who did not appear, was fined 120 s. and costs; in default, fourteen days' imprison- ment.

forwards had the better of a series of scrimmages, and alihohgh Frank Turner got clear,another disappointment was in store when the final pass went forward. .Barnes

and Evans, both of whom hid been comparatively idle, now showed up, and a fine run by the latter saw the visitors again defending. The oval was worked nearer to the line,, and from a scrimmage, James Bate tricked his , opponents in fine style and scored, Evans making a good, though unsuccess- ful attempt at the place. Ashton tackled Al-

derson finely soon after the restart, and although the visitors once mere assumed the aggressive no addition was made up to the call of half time, the score then reading as Warrington 0-1-2, Hartlepool 1-0-2. Frank Turaer restarted; and off-side play ruled the opening/ ime at centre. J. T. Bate kicked finely, and the homesters, improving in their combination as the game wore on, gradually drove the Durham men back on their lines. Barnes, after an unsuccessful effort, gut in his kick to Macpherson, and Daniels promptly, floored his man. The fast pace at which the game had been carried on now began to have a marked effect on the visitors, and whereas their forwards had the better of the Warring- tonians during the first half, they now compared but poorly. Donohue kicked a trifle too hard •to Hodgson, and prompt relief was forthcoming, but another burst by the homesters was luckily saved by Loughborough. Evans made a fine effort to get in from a pass by James Bate, being knocked into touch a yard from the line. Kassall got the ball out of danger, and Barnes failing to take advantage of a pass from James Bate, the Rovers once more breathed freely. J. T, Bate again dodged well and was all but in, and again the visitors were afforded relief by the wild passing of the Warrington back. Amends were made a moment later. for, Bate punting' well, the movement was taken up by Randles,who passed '6 Frank Turner, and the ball was taken over, Ashton claiming the try. Barnes gave his side the lead by placing a goal. 'I his proved to be the turning point of the game, and, although Alderson almost dropped a goal, the result of a penalty kick, the Rovers rarely reached the quarter flag. The visitors were completely played out in . the last ten minutes, and a couple of finec runs by Randles were followed by some grand passing, in which Evans was the final recipient, and a strong run landed him a scorer near the corner flag. Hodgson spoiled some pass- ing amongst the home backs near the call of time, -and Alderson made an effort, but Ashton pulled bi m up before he travelled many yards. Fair Turner got in a kick when in difficulties, and play was on the Rovers' line when the whistle sounded 'No side," the final score reading as Warrington 1-2-2; Hartlepool Rovers, 1-0-2. Hartlepool Rovers team: Loughborofigh, back; Hodg- son, Alderson, and Macpherson, three-quarters; Scott and Kassall, half back ; Yiend, Hill, Hall, Coates, Pease, Lohden, Cook, Burt, and Morgan. Referee, Mr. Naylor, Wigan. WARRINGTON V. ROOIDALE ST. CLEMENTS.

Warrington experienced an unexpected reverse on Saturday, when Rochdale St. Clement's defeated them by a dropped goal and a minor to six minors. -That this defeat will come as a surprise to many is only natural, but the elements en Saturday were of such a -character that those who had forecast the result of many matches were on the wrong side when their calculations came to be reckoned up. The Rochdale men, it will be remem. bered, gave our local team a good game on their first meeting, on December 26th, and although the victory was in favour of the Warringtonians by a goal and four tries, the homesters on the present occasion were confi.- • dent of reversing matters. Barnes and Jolley were absent from the visitors' ranks, a trial being given to Potts, a junior player, who haa lately been officiating with the " A " team. , A strong ,wind, blew from goal to goal, and the game was divided into quarters, of fifteen minutes' duration. Frank Turner kicked off, and the kick being charged the first operator again took up the movement. and Warrington were almost in in the first minute. Over- eagerness neutralized the chance, and although Rigg and Barton got the oval away, Daniels got his kick in when in difficulties, and the Saints again defended. Aided by the elements and a free kick, the Warrington quarters were visited, and James Bate spoiled a movement. Some loose play followed, and W. Rigg tried a shot e goal,with a futile effect.- The drop-out saw the oval hovering at neutral quarters, and a spell of monotonous play was re- lieved when the Bates passed finely, and Evans with a. strong run once more placed the homesters on the defen- sive. Rigg saved his charge in fine style, Ashton making his mark. The kick gained but little ground, and Roch- dale again attacked. The brothers Turner and Bandies were prominentlin relief, and a passing movement be- tween the Bates.'Evans, and Potts saw the latter running and kicking with excellent judgment, staving off the de- termined attack of the Rochdale men. By 'degrees the oval was worked to the line, and Fair Turner, Donohue, Povey, and Ashton were especially prominent at this juncture. Eventually the oval was forced over, and Rigg saved. Fair Turner met. the drop-out, and Warrington claimed a major point, but a scrimmage was ordered on the the, and although a couple of passing bouts were witnessed between the two Bates, Evans, and Daniels, nothing tangible resulted, and ends were changed with a minor each. Aided by the wind, it was generally sur- mised that the Warringtonians would have matters as they pleased, but the prophets had estimated without calculating the qualities of the Rochdale men, for on the restart they played with surprising energy. Play was confined to the visitors' quarters for a considerable period, until Thornily on a couple of occasions came finely through the thick, and took the game to the home quarters. Frank Turner had a couple of shots at goal from beyond the half-way, the first falling short by a yard, whilst the other grazed the post on the outside. The latter was indeed a case of hard lines, and the same remark applies to a; brilliant run by Potts, who ran above half the length of the field, and found his pass knocked on a yard from the line. Daniels and Evans each put in strong runs, and Thompson got the oval away in fine style, but Roscoe?, with a huge pant, again gave his side the advantage of attacking. Daniels saved daringly, and J. T. Bate made his mark, but nothing came of the place, and half time was called with the score as Warrington 0-0-2; Rtlchdale 0-0-1. On resuming, each side at the- onset strove for the supremacy, and the first to show up was James Bate, a fine run being spoiled by an erratic pass to Daniels. A free kick to Rochdale was well met by Boscow, and although Berry and Ashton got clear from a tine-out, the home forwards cleared a scrimmage in fine style, and play was taken under the Warrington posts. Daniels and Donohue soon had the oval back at neutral quarters, and wild passing by the Warrington backs was saved by J. 'l' Bate. A shot at goal by Rigg, the result of a penalty kick, ended in failure, and Pratt endeavoured to get in near the corner, but the defence was not to be tampered with. Daniels and Evans saved well, and Boscow f.v.ot the oval away splendidly on one occasion, but-the climax was reached a moment later, when a return fell into the hands of Hyde on the touch line, and a fine drop lowered the Warrington goal. This was the only point scored during this quarter, but direct on the restart for the last portion, the Warrin:gtonians at once forced the game at the Rochdale 25. Fair Turner became prominent with a huge kick, and Evans was col- lared on the line a moment later. Minors were rapidly conceded to the Warriegtonians, and passing displays by them ought to have been productive of tries if only care had been exercised in the final essay. Povey and Evans were instrumental in relief when the Saints attacked on one occasion. Another brilliant run by Evans was spoiled by a forward pass, and then as a final effort some fine passine between Bandies, James Bate, and Daniels, but the ball was finally knocked on, and the gairie ter- minated in a victory for the Rochdale men, as stated above. Teams :--Warrington: Boscow, back; Daniels, Evans, and Potts, three-quarters; James Bate and J. T. Bate, half backs; H. Ashton, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, Dil- lon, Bandies, Povey, Thorniley, Berry, and Donohue, Rochdale St. Clement's :L. Rigg, back; Thompson, W. Him and Hyde, three-quarters; White and Barton, half backs; Waugh, Hill, Nix, Pratt, Ashton, Rideough, Holt, Farrar, and Tweedle.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office.'Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY RUNCORN V. ST. HELENS RECREATION (A TEANS).—This match was played at St. Helens on Saturday. The Recs. were short of a good many players, and had to find sub- stitutes. A good game ended—Runcorn Al try 3 minors, Recreation A 1 minor.

FRODSIIAM V. MR. GILL'S WIDNES TBA3L—Frodsham has of late played with much ability, and on Saturday met Mr. Gill's team, and a very even game was the result. After some somewhat exciting play Goodall secured a try; but the place at goal failed. Briggs scored a try, but nothing resulted from it. In the second half Frodsham added four minors, whilst their opponents put on three points. Result: Frodsham, one try, four minors; Mr. Gill's team, one try,, three minors. WIDNES v. OLDHAM (" A " Teems).—Played at Widnes on Saturday in boisterous weather. Morris obtained possession, and passed to Rushton. That player put in a splendid run, and grounded the ball behind the posts. Burgess failed to improve. Bennett shortly afterwards scored for Oldham. No goal resulted. Play then settled in midfield. Widnes made some good attempts to make headway, but were handicapped by the wind. Morris broke up a spirited attack by the visitors, and placed Widnes on. the attack. Towards the interval Oldham made great efforts to score, but the home defence was too good. Score :—Widnes 1 goal, 2 tries, 3 minors. Oldham 1 try 3 minors.

div.head: RUNCORN v. STOCKPORT.
div.p: RUNCORN v. STOCKPORT.

Runcorn met Stockport at the former place on Easter Monday, and being a holiday match there was a good attendance, the game being one of considerable interest. The form of Saturday was again shown by Runcorn, who played a champion game. The passing of the locals was too much for the visitors, and occasionally gave them much inconvenience as well as disheartening them, when they thought there was a chance of scoring, Stock- port played a manly game, and endeavoured to the utmost extent to avert a defeat, but were unsuccessful. W. Hughes, Broady, and C. Hughes scored for Runcorn. The first-named scored two tries, and the goal was kicked by Crompton. The visitors were thoroughly de- feated, nevertheless the game was one which reflected considerable credit on both sides.

div.head: WIDNES v. TOTTINGTON.
div.p: WIDNES v. TOTTINGTON.

• The return -fixture between these two clubs was played at Widnes, on Monday afternoon, before a fair number of spectators. Widnes attacked, and from a throw-in in the visitors quarter, the ball was dribbled to the line, where Whelan scored a try. Barber, from a difficult place, made a good attempt at goal. From the kick-off Drummond got away, and after some dodgy play, was only brought down just in time to prevent a further point being scored. Play became even for some time until Widnes again got the ball on the loose, they having on two oocasions hard lines in not scoring. The score at half-timo was—Widnes, one try and two minors; Tot- tington, one minor. On changing ends, Tottington from r. place-kick attempted a goal, a minor only resulting. Some very exciting play followed, in which neither side had the advantage,until just before the close of the game, when Widnes made a rush for the line, but lost the ball when about to score. Widnes continued the pressure, but could not get through, and the game ended in a win for Widnes by one try and two minors to two minors. Widnes were short of Konyon, Brennan, and Johnson.

div.head: WIDNES V. OLDHAM.
div.p: WIDNES V. OLDHAM.

The return fi sture between these two clubs was played at Oldham on Saturday, before about 7,000 spectators. Both clubs were well represented. Oldham kicked off against the wind, and were soon placed on the defensive. A pass from Evans not being taken, the ball was car- ried over the home line in some scrambling play, and eventually made dead. Widnes kept up the advantage gained, and two minors quickly followed to their credit. From a scrimmage near the touch line in the home quarter, Drummond got possession, and kicked a mag- nificent goal. A few minutes later Barber dropped a splendid goal from the 25 line. Thissuccess encouraged the visitors, who completely routed the home forwards, and kept them contintally on the defensive. Five minors were added to the Widnes score. At half time the score was—Widnes two goals and seven minors to Oldham one minor. Oldham now had the advantage of the.wind, Nolan put in a good run, but he was brought down by Hartles. Drummond relieved, and Brennan also sup- plemented his efforts. Pennington in returning kicked the ball dead. Peters got away, but he was tackled by McCutcheon, and Gwynn getting possession dropped a goal for Oldham. Gwynn again got away and looked like scoring, but Hartles and Brennan brought him down. Widnes defended their line with marked ability, and no further point was scored up to the close of the game, when the score was Widnes two goals and seven minors to Oldham one goal and two minors. RUNCORN v. ST. HELENS RECREATION.

These teams met on the Irwell-lane ground-, Runcorn, on Saturday, when there were quite 4,000 spectators drawn together. The teams were not representative,both having important absentees. Seddon kicked off for the visitors; but the ball was returned by Pendlebury. For , a time the play was of a give-and-take character, until pressure was brought to bear on the visitors by Cromp- ton and May. Later on Crompton darted through the visitors' lines; but was brought up in time by Briers. Abrams put in some dribbling play; and a check was put on progress for a time. Ellison, of the "Rees," madel an nnsuccessful attempt to break away, but Crompton I was toe much on the alert for him. Houghton obtained a free kick, and Ellison obtained possession, and madean effort to get away with the ball. Play was confined to the centre ; but the Runcornians dribbled in such a style that Seddon was cotnpelled to touch down. Runcorn at this juncture gave clear evidence of having the best of the game. Then followed some really fine passing, the principal performers being Crompton, Hughes, and May. The latter did gm' service in bringing Pilkington up. Crompton, from a line out, obtained a try; but un- fortunately Houghton's attempt was a failure. The first part of the game closed with the score as follows : Runcorn, one try three minors; Recs. nil. In the second half the play was of the same character, Runcorn adding another try, whilst the visitors succeeded by long kicks in obtaining four minors, which was the extent of their score.
