div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

FOOTBALL—RUGBY. Hartlepool Rovers, the crack Durham team, have not been very successful in their contests with Lancashire teams this Eastertide. On Saturday they were beaten by Swinton by one goal, two tries, and five minors, to one try and ,two minors, and on Monday, Warrington again bowled them over to the tune of one goal, two tries, and two minor; to one goal and two minors. The Durham team are a strong lot individually, and they include in their rank a considerable number who have won county honours, as well as Alderson and "read, two well-known internationals. As a team, however, they did not seem so practised and well-trained as the War- ringtonians, though it is but fair to say that at times they displayed tome very pretty passing and dribbling. The goal dropped by Alderson at the very beginning of the game was a fine performance, and an inkling of what he is capable of doing when he has in front of him a stronger set of forwards and half-backs.

If the International Board can, during the summer months arrive at a satisfactory solution of the scoring difficulty they will do well. There is great diversity of opinion as to the value of the various kinds of goals,and the question of minor points is sap worth considering. Except in cup competitions minors are of no real import- ance, and merely tend to show which side did the most pressing; but as they are the result of good play thereis some reason in the claim that they should be taken int* account in the absence of tries orgoals. Pethaps all these matters will be set in order before September next comes round. ,

The clubs competing for the Yorkshire Cup have now been reduced to four--Huddersfield, Wakefield Trinity,. Pontefract, and Castleford. The triumph of the last- named over Halifax, who,it will be remembered ,knocked' out Bradford, came as a great surprise. Halifax could' not penetrate the Castleford defence One of the winners' forwards was ordered off the ground for violent -conduct. Huddersfield only disposed of Hunslet by means of a, dropped goal.

"The Pall Mall Gazette" asks—ls football dangerous ? and gives a list of the accidents, fatal and other, that have been reported from football fields from September 20 of last year to March 21 of the current 'year, supply- ing in each case the date of the accident and brief par- ticulars. It would appear that the number of fatal acci- dents reported does not at all exhaust the actual list, as on several occasions the report says "not expected to re.- cover." or words to that effect, and the ultimate outcome of the accident is not given. But in the casualties tabu- lated, there are in a space of six months, not less than twenty-one deaths resulting either immediately or shortly after from casualities on the football field, while the number of accidents, many of a very serious charac- ter, is very considerable. In many instances, it is-said, there have been three or four Men temporarily disabled int the same day, and occasionally in the same match.

div.head: ASSOCIAZION.
div.p: ASSOCIAZION.

• The "Manchester Guardian" says, "The Committee of the Football Association Council who selected the team to represent England against Scotland onSaturday (to-day) cannot be complimented on the success of their, efforts. No follower of the Association code can be per- suaded that a team that does not include a single mem- ber of the winners of the F.A. cup is thoroughly repre- sentative of the strength of England. To pass over players of the abilities of Southworth and Barton, to say nothing of Townley and Lofthouse, who did so finely in the finall tie at the Oval, seems extraordinary. No wonder that there is a great outcry at Blackburn, more especially as the game is to come off on the Rovers' ground at Ewood Park. Everton have no fewer than four men in the team, and the North End two, and one of the latter has taken little part in first-class football this season. Marsden of Darwen, ought to have been found a place before Howarth, of Preston, as he has been in great form all the season."

Bolton Wanderers were for the second time successful over. the Blackburn Rovers on Saturday, and are now placed fifth in the League table. They were foitunate to meet their rivals without Southworth and Townley, and vanqUished them by two goals to nil. It is worthy of mention that the Rovers lost all their last four fixtures, Southworth being absent in every instance. In this respect they have been very unlucky. They cannot show such a good League record as twelve months ago, but the reason is easily found. The Wanderers, on the other' hand, have done better, and are higher up the list than in either of the two.previous years. This is largely due to their superior defence, Gardiner, Paton, Jones. and Somerville having all done uncommonly well. The re- turn between Accrington and West Bromwich Albion a week hence will bring the League season to a close.
DEATH OF EARL GRANVILLE.

We regret to announce that Earl Granville died on Tuesday afternoon. His lordship, who was born in 1815, was in his seventy-sixth year. He had been in ill- health for some months, the primary cause of his indis- position being a chill which developed complications. Towards the end of February he, however, grew better, and hopes were entertained tbfat he would be able to spend the recess out of town. On the evening of the 13th March, however, reports gained currency in the Houses of Parliament that the indisposition had taken a serious turn and that considerable anxiety was felt. The* bulletins which were issued somewhat allayed this alarm, but nevertheless the reports seems to have had substan- tial foundation, inasmuch as his medical attendant deemed it necessary to. suinmon further professional aid. Sir Andrew Clark and Sir James Paget were the physi- cians consulted by Dr. Reginald Harrison, his lordship's medical attendant. From the time of this consultation, his lordship appeared to be making sa,tisfactary pro- gress towards recovery, although he never once left his bed.. Favourable' bulletins continu...cl to be issued daily by Dr. Reginald Harrison from 14, South Audley-st., the town residence, where his lordship was lying ill, until Monday evening, when the bulletin issued stated that his lordship was in a very prostrate state. From. this time the distinguished patient never rallied, and after an anxious night the following bulletin was issued at ten o'clock on Tuesday morning Lord Granville's condi- tion has not improved during the night. He continues very weak." Throughout the day a change for the worse was manifest, and at five minutes to five. o'clock his lord- ship passed away. Lady Granville, who had assiduously nursed the late earl throughout his long illness, and all his immediate relations were around him, including Lord Leveson and the younger members of his family. Ifi describing his lordship's last illness to a representative of the Press, Dr. Harrison stated that the earl had been sub- ject to gout for many years, but his death was not attributable to that more than any other cause. Constant and anxious inquiries were made during the illness by all those with whom the earl had been officially and intimately associated. The Minister in attendance upon the Queen was informed daily by Lady Granville as to the noble lord's condition. The Princaof VVale4 made personal inquiries, and Mr. Gladstone telegraphed from St. Leonard& Lord Rosebery, who in the last Liberal Administration succeeded to Earl Granville's posi- tion for many years as Minister for Foreign Affairs.made constant inquiries since his return from abroad, and an hour before the earl's death telegraphed from the Durdans at Epsom to south Audley-st., for the latest information. Among other political colleagues who had been• constant in their calls and inquiries were Earl Spencer, Sir Wtn.., Harcourt, Lord Kimberley, Mr. Campbell-Bannerman,: Sir Geor,geTrevelyan, &a. Lord Granville's death vacates the important appointment of Lord Warden of the Cith quo Ports, carrying with it the beattiful residence of Weimer Castle. near Dover. _ _

News of the sad event was at once telegraphed to. tho Queen at Grasse, and a special messenger was sent to Marlborough House to acquaint the Prince of Wiles,who had arrived there a few hours previously from. Sand- ringham. His Royal Highness at once drove to South Audley-st., and paid a visit of condolence. LORD GRANVILLE'S CAREER.

Earl Granville' K.G., was the eldest son of the first Earl, and was born in 1815. He was educated at Eton and Oxford (graduating 1834). He entered the public service as attache to the British Embassy at Paris, of which his father, first Earl Granville, was the head. Elected to Parliament for MOrpeth (1836), and after- wards for Lichfield. Appointed (1840) Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. He attached himself from the beginning with great zeal to the Liberal party. In 1846 he succeeded to the peerage. He was appointed Vice-President of the Board of Trade in 1848', and he succeeded Lord Palmerston as Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs (1851), but retired with the. 'Russell- Ministry in 1852. During this last year he took an active part in connection with the Hy le Park Exhibition, as vice-president of the Royal Commission, which led to his being nominated chairman of the exhibition of 1862. He held successively the offices of Master of the Buck- hounds, Paymaster-General of the Forces, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, Treasurer of the Navy, and President of the Council, and became Ministerial leader of the House of Lords in 1855. In 1856 he was des- patched to St. Petersburg to represent the British Crown at the coronation of the Czar Alexander. When Lord Palmerston formed a Ministry in 1859 Lard Granville was appointed President of the Council, and in 1865 he was nominated Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports. In 1868 he became Secretary for the Colonies in Mr. Glad- stone's first Administration, and finally succeeded Lord Clarendon as Secretary for Foreign Affairs, holding this office until the retirement of the Liberal Ministry in 1874. Upon the fall of Lord Beaconsfield's Government in 1880, and Mr. Glaalstone's accession again to office, Lord Granville resumed office a second time as Secretary for Foreign Affairs, retaining this post until Lord Salis- bury came into power, 188 S. In the last Gladstone Ad- ministration he held office as Secretary of State for the Colonies (Feb., 1886.) Lord Granvilie has been one of Mr. Gladstone's most powerful supporters since the split in the Liberal party on the Irish question. His Lardshi p was Chancellor of the University of London. He was entertained at the Liverpool Reform Club, October, 1888. FUNERAL
Lord Granvillo's; body will be removed from London to Stine, at eight o'clock to-day (Saturday) morning,and the funeral ceremony will be performed h. Qty.) church on the same day.
31ARRIAGE OF lkilS.s GLADYS KNOWLES.

At Brighton on Tuesday, before the registrar, Miss Gladys Knowles, who receltly recovered £6.500 dam- ages from Mr. Leslie Dunce', was married to Mr. Prager a London dentist. Several, relatives of the bride were present at the ceremony, after which Mr. and Mrs. Prager left for the continent, to spend the honeymoon.
THE CONTEST AT SLIGO.

The two parties at Sligo had a busy day on Saturday. Mr. Parnell left the town early in the morning, and, gatheringa large Mowing in a district friendly to him, re-entered Shgo in triumph. He had a mixed reception from the populace, and on arriving at the Town Hall, some of the latter came into collision with the Parnellites. A fight took place on the Town Hall steps, and the scrim- mage was renewed upon the anti-Parnellites trying to force their way into their opponents' meeting. The occurrences of Sunday were even more exciting and' serious. The Parliamentary party's candidate, Alderman Collery, went with some of his most prominent sup- porters, including Mr. Michael Davitt, to Dromore West, in the Tiereragh district, from which Mr. Parnell drew his escort on Saturday. As soon as the visitors arrived in the place there were unmistakable signs of a disturb- ance, and as sopti as the anti-Parnellites began to carry out their arrangements for a meeting there was developed an unusually violent manifestation of hostility. The police endeavoured to keep the two forces apart, but never achieved more than a partial success. Ultimately the crowds came to pretty clo3e quarters' with the result that Alderman Collery and his friends had to beat hasty retreat. They were followed for a long distance and pelted with stones, one of which struck Mr. Pinkerton, M.P., on the head, inflicting a serious wound. Several other persons were injured. Tuesday was a quiet day in North Sligo. The whole whole of the day was devoted by both sides to canvass- ing. Mr. Parnell did not leave his hotel. In the even- ing the Anti-PArnelliees held a highly successful meeting In Sligo Town Hall, when Mr. Michael Davitt, replying to Mr. Parnell, denied that the Anti-Parnellites had com- menced the rowdyism, which, he said, had its beginning at Ballinakill, when the Parnellites broke up the opposi- tion meeting. Archbishop Walsh, in an interview with a correspon- dent, has expressed himself highly satisfied with the result of interviews vvirh the Pope, who, he says, entirely approves the course taken by the Irish bishops.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION Y. WIDNES PARISI( CHURCH. —This return fixture was played at Warrington,on Mon- day, and the home team was again censiderably weakened. The visitors kicked off, and at once made for the Warrington end, but were returned by Davies with a heavy kick down the field. This en- abled the home forwards to get close in but they could not make anything of it. The visitors gettingpossession raced away down the right wing, and crossing to the left, notched the first goal 15 minutes from start. Some give-and-take play ensued, but ultimately Widnes scored another goal, thus bringing half time, Widnes leading by two goals to none. In the second half the visitors managed to score three more,while the home team scored two, thus Widnes won a good game by five goals to two. Warburton, for Warrington, put one through his own goal. Warrington team :—Smith, Davies, Mather, Mar- tin, Onions,Warburton, Clayt,on,Ball ; substitutes, Powell and Mather. Referee, Mr. A. Carter. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION Y. EARLF.STOWN RESERVE.— These teams played their return fixture on Saturday last, on the ground of the former, and as in the first encoun- ter, proved disastrous to the Warringtonians. The home had a very poor team on, only about six of the first team appearing on the field. Onions kicked off for War- rington, and with a bit of neat passing by Powell, T. Mather, and Clayton, worked the ball well up, but were repulsed by the visitors' backs, who played a splendid defence: The Earlestown right getting possession,cvorked well down and notched the first goal ten minutes from start. The home team now fell off, and the visitors had it about their own way, putting on three more goals be- fore half time. After the re-start, the home team played up well for the first 15 minutes, but the combinaton of the visitors completely nonplussed them, and putting on four more goals, thus won an easy game by Earlestown 8 goals, Warrington none. Warrington team —Goal, Carter_ ; backs, Davies and J. Mather ; halfbacks, War- burton; T. Phillips,,and Avling ; forwards, Clayton, Adams, Onions, Powell, and T. Mather. 4eferee, Mr. J. Watson. _ _ ,

div.head: GOOD FRIDAY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: GOOD FRIDAY AT WARRINGTON.

The following reports were set up for our last issue, but were left over through an oversight : Good Friday was, of course, generally observed as a holiday in Warrington Services were held during the day at all, or most of, the churches in the town, and also at the Catholic, and some of the Nonconformist places of warship. Secular amuse- ments were indulged in to a considerable extent by the populace, and the ever-attractive football in the afternoon drew a crowd down to the Wilderspool enclosure, to witness a game between the local "A" team and.a similar, contingent of players from the ancient town .of Lancaster. Boating on the river was to Some extent indulged in, and many people left the town by rail and road. All outdoor plea- sures were, however, greatly marred by the.adverse weather. An icy cold wind blew throughout the day, and at times there were rather heavy falls of rain.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY MEETINGS.
div.p: SALVATION ARMY MEETINGS.

In the morning the band of the Warrington corps of the Salvation Army met at the barracks in Academy-st., and had a march 'out; and subse- quently there Was a meeting at the barracks, entitled "An hour and a half at the cross." In the afternoon the corps had outdoor demonstrations at Sankey Bridges, and in,Winwick-road, and these Ivere followed by a tea at the barracks in welcome to the new officers of the corps, Captain Nelms and Lieutenant Simms. After tea there was ,a musical demonstration.. Captain Wilson, of Canada, secre- tary to Major Baugh., of that country, and formerly of Warrington, preAiding. The " Stockport musical troupe ". was in attendance, and included "the converted actor "'and "the saved race-runner." ST. ALBANS CATFIOLIO‘ CHURCH.

On Thursday morning a solenan procession took place, to the Altar of Repose, Father Feeny officiating. On Good Friday Alms of the Fe-sanctified com- menced at ten o'clock in the morning. During the ser- vice; the unveiling of the Cress and procession of the Sacred Host from the Altar of Repose, and the kissing of the Cross took place. In the afternoon the service of the Way of the Cross commenced at three. o'clock. ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHLTR.CH, BUTI'ER- , -MARK ET-STREEt.

The Holy Week 'services commenced on Thursday morning, when the Sacred Host was carried in preces- sion to the Lady Chapel, in whieh was erected the Altar of Repose. Prayers were recited in the evening before the sepulchre or Altar of Repcse. The Lady Chapel was beautifully adorned with.flowers and plants, and lighted with many candles. On Good Friday morning Mass of the Pre-sanctifred commenced at ten o'clock, Father Flanigan officiating; during which the 'unveiling of the Cross, theprocession of the Host from the Chapel ef Re- pose, and the kissing of the Cross, took place. The ser- mon was preached be Father Sumner, Rector of St. Mary's. In the afternoon the service of the Way of the , Cross commenced at three o'clock. MEETING OF LATCHFORD BAPTISTS. The annual tea meeting in connection with Latchford Baptist Chapel was held on Good Friday. About 160 persons sat down to tea, the tables being attended to by the following ladies :—Mesdames Varley, Davidson, S. Albinson, A. Wilkinson,J. Albinson,Buckley,J. Fairhurst,' junr., Pearson, Dutton, Adams, Cliffe, and Jones; Misses Boardman, Davidson, Albinson; Nellie Fairhurst, Light- foot, Wells, Smith, Caldwell, Wilkinson, Carter, and Jones. After tea a well-attended meeting was held in the chapel. The Rev. J. W. Varley presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. C. J. Green, of Liverpool ; Rev. J. Yonge, and Rev. E. Moore. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening address, said he had just been reading an old report, that mentioned the do- ings of what was then known as the North-Western As- sociation of Baptist Churches, and on turning to the church of which he had the honour to be pastor,he found that 20 years ago that church numbered 45 members. He thought, if he was not mistaken, that it had ten teachers in the Sunday School and 70 scholars. A large number of things had hap- pened during the last twenty years, and one of the pleasantest was that that Church was not worse but a good deal better than it was then. During the last year they had received into the fellowship of that church four by baptism, and two by profession; one had been erased and another one had been dismissed to the church from which he came, so that they had a clear increase of four upon the year's working. They had a total number of members of 99 upon the books, so they would see that,during the last 20 years.the membership of the church had increased more than 100 per cent. If he were not mistaken the scholars in the Sunday School numbered close upon 100, so that the per centage of increase there had been something like 50 per cent. During the last year they had had a bazaar for the purpose of raising money for the re-seating of that place of worship and of making alterations -to other buildings. They had raised £215 clear money as a result of the bazaar, and the church accounts showed another sum of something like £l5O, so that they had raised in twelve months £365, a result not at all small, considering the size of the church and congregation. (Hear, hear.) They should have to worship in the Sunday school whilst that chapel was being re-pewed, but they trusted, if all went well to be able to open the premies as a whole Moak the third Sunday in May. Altogether their work as a church had been one of progress, and they might anticipate that in the near future they should have even greater blessings then they had had in the past, (Hear, hear and applause.) Addresses were subsequently given by the Rev. E. Moore, theßev. C. J. Green, and the Rev. J. Yonge. The programme of music that was rendered ineluded an- thems by the choir, songs by Mrs, Fairhurst, Miss Light- foot, and Mr. Isaac Wilkinson; and a performance on the violin by the Rev. E. Moore.

MURDER OF A SWEETHEART AT OLDHAM.

The neighbourhood of Townfield, Oldham, was thrown into a state of great excitement about midnight on Sun- day, by the rumour that a horrible crime had been com- mitted. The report turned out to be only too true. A girl named Moran had had her throat cut, as is alleged, by her sweetheart, a young man named Alfred William Turner. It seems that about nine o'clock on Sunday night Turner went to the Townfield Police Station in a state of excitement. He complained that himself and his sweetheart had been attacked by two tramps near the Woodstock Spinning Company's Mill at Higginshaw, and that thegirl's throat had been cut by the men. He added that she was now lying where she had been maltreated, and requested that a policeman might be sent along with him to assist in her removal. It was seen, however, by Inspector Warburton, who was in charge, that Turner's clothes were bespattered with blood, and suspicion was eacited in his mind by this fact. He sent Police-constable Conway along with the man and they proceeded to a Piece of waste ground near the Woodstock Mill. When they arrived the officer found the young woman lying full length on the ground in a pool of blood, and blood was yet issuing from a long and wide gash in her throat. Conway, it is stated, stooped down to her, and asked her who had caused the Wound in her throat. She was very weak from loss of blood, but she inclined her head towards the spot 'where Turner, her lover, was standing. Conway removed the injured woman to her home in Back Hope-st., and a doctor was sent for. Dr. Thomson arrived, and ordered her removal to the Infirmary. Conway then arrested Turner and took him to the Townfield Police Station, Where he was lodged in the cells after having been charged With the attempted murder of Moran. The poor girl was taken to the Infirmary, and it was found that she was in a very dangerous condition. Her conditienwas so serious at an early hour on Monday morning that at eight o'clock it was deemed advisable that her depositions Should be taken, and Dr. Platt, as the nearest magistrate, veas sent for to the Infirmary. The prisoner, in the cus- tody of Police Constables Burgess and Boardman, was brought to the bedside of his victim, and heard the state- ment made by her. Her examination was a very painful task. She spoke with the greatest difficulty, as • may be imagined when it is stated that the wound .in her throat was at least half an inch wide. The prisoner was ap- parently quite unconcerned at his position. The prisoner was charged later in the day before the magistrates, and the Chief Constable stated that the girl in her depositions, swore that he took her into a field and there accused her of keeping company with another yoßth. This the denied, and he thereupon seized her by the throat, drew a knifie from his pocket, and cut her throat. He was remanded for a week. Turner is 21 and Moran 18 years of age. Moran died on Monday night. INQUEST.

An inquest was held at Oldham, on Tuesday, on the body of the young woman Moran, whose sweetheart, Alfred William Turner, is in custody on a charge of mur- dering her by cutting her throat in a field on the out- skirts of Oldham. The jury found a verdict of wilful murder against Turner, who will be brought before the inagistrates.
CONFESSION OF TRH CRIME.

On Wednesday, Turner was brought before the magis- trates,-and the cas3 was fully gone into. The prisoner seems to have abused the girl whenever they met, to have kicked her with great violence, and to have threa- tened to murder her if she would not marry him. Wit- nesses stated that the girl was not willing to keep nom. pany with him, but he appeared to have terrorised ner to such an extent that she went for a walk with him on several occasions. At the completion of the evidence, the prisoner, following the example of the Bolton mur- derer. made a full confession,of his guilt. He was corn- Milted for trial at the Manchester Assizes.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
Tatitsnlr.—Before His Honour, Judge_ Ffoulkes
A GOLD WATCH TRANSACTION.

Messrs. -Finklestone and Co., of 21,-Heywood-street, _Cheethain, Manchester, claimed £2O 15s. froni James Yates, a collier, living at Collins Green, this sum being the balance of £24, the price of a gold watch defendant had received from the plaintiffs. Mr. Cottingham, bar- rister, (instructed by Mr. A. Brown, of Warrington), aPPeared for the piaintiff's, and Mr. Mulholland (in- structed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw, of War- rington), represented the defendant. It appeared that, about the middle of last year, a traveller of the plaintiffs, named Levy, made a bargain with the defendant for the latter to take a gold watch ,valued at £24, the price to be Paid in instalments. After the defendant had received the watch he paid several instalments, and the claim was for the balance owing. For the defence, it was stated that the defendant soon found that the watch went very badly, and after it had been sent back once or twice for repairs, it was given back to Levy by Yates in a public- house at Collins Green. It was then sold by Levy to another man named Doran, who had it in his possession for five or six weeks, though it was afterwards got from Doran and left at Yates's house by Levy, in spite of the Protestations of Mr. Yates that they did not want it. This last transactidn, it was held, amounted to a recis- alon of the contract with Yates, and his Honour, agreeing with this argument, gave a verdint for the defendant xitthc?sts. On a ceunter-clairn for £3 55., the amount of with costs. h instalments paid by Yates,a verdict as also given against Messrs. Finklestene and Cimpany Mr. Mulhol- land produced the watch in court, and said that Mr. Davies was quite prepared to hand it over to Ilifeserl• Finklestone as soon as the costs of the action were paw. —Mr. Cottingham inquired if he was to understand that his Honour was of opinion that the contract, which had been entered into by the plaintiffs and the defendant, eould be rescinded by Levi, who was only .the traveller id the plaintiffs.—His Honour declined to pass an opinion on that point, because it had never been raised.—Mr. Cottinghatn : Your judgment Ithink,vras bped on that. Honour: I say nothing more. A BUILDER'S CLAIM: MATTHEWS V. WILLIAMS.—In this ease !dr. P. Davies represented the plaintiff and Mr. A. Browne the defendant. In his opening statement Mr. Davies said the plaintiff was a builder carrying on busi- ness in Ellesmere-st., Warrington, and the defendant was a broker. When some old buildings were being pulled down in Bridge-st., to make room for new property the Plaintiff entered into an arrangement with the defendant to., buy some bricks which comprised part of an old build- elg• Plaintiff was to have all the bricks in parts of the building pointed out to him by defendant, less 23,500 which had been previously purchased by a Mr. Allen,and for these he was to pay the defendant £l3. He found, however, when he went to get the bricks away that he Would only be allowed to take a small portion of the bricks that he understood he was to have. He, there- fore, now sought to recover the £l3 and £7 for loss of time. In defence it was contended that the bargain agree upon was that plaintiff was to take what bricks Were left after Mr. Allen had got his stipulated number, and that if plaintiff had made a mistake as to the number that would be left it was his own look out. His Honour gave a verdict for the defendant.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE THELWALL MISSIONARY.

Mr. Moore, who has for some time discharged the tinties of misionary on the Thelwall section of the Ship Canal, left Thelwall on Tuesday morning for his new sPhere of labour at Pool, Dorsetshire, where he will at- tend to the spiritual wants of the sailors. On Sunday he preached his farewell sermons at the Mission Halt. „ There was a large congregation at each service. Mr. 'Moore made feeling allusion to his connection With the nlission. He will,be succeeded by Mr. Joseph Holliday, of Stockton-on-Tees. 6. THE ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER. John Sheen, the young man against whom the Coro- ner's jury last week returned a verdict of manslaughter ja the fatal burning case at the Ship Canal Works near Ellesmere Port, was brought before the magistrates at Chester Castle on Saturday,chargedovith the manslaugh- ter of James Birnie, a fellow-workman, hy setting him on fire. In addition to the evidence giiren at the inquest, Lnlel Allsop,alimpman, said he had seiteral times seen ,13irnie loading waggons ne-ar the fire, and'the prisoner nad no authority to order him away. Before lying down by the fire Birnie mentioned that he was waiting to go on nuty at nine o'clock. In cross-examination the witness 'said there was at the time of the occurrence a sharp wind blowing over the fire towards Birnie. The effect of pri- soner throsWrifthe Incigeri bil on the fire was to create a ,niorneutary flash, and when Birnie called out witness Ba, W that prisoner had got him on his legs and moved uin‘ a tew yards from the fire, where he was trying to extinguish the flames with his hands.—Prisoner was re- 4:landed.

div.head: NEW ORLEANS MASSACRE.
div.p: THE NEW ORLEANS MASSACRE.

M'Cauley's body was shockingly mutilated. ' 'Baron de Fava, the Italian Minister at Washington, on , l'uesday,.presented to the State Department his 'letters 1)! recall. WARRINOtON EXAMINEE SAYS : " TUE MARMALADE TRADE.—The severe' "weather we have recently experienced in" "this quarter has extended as tar south as " Seville. It is in the neighbourhood of" "Seville. that the oranges beat suited for " "marmalade making are grown. A recent" "frost (the like of which has not been ex'" •• perienced for ten years), has played havoc" "with the fruit, and, although though the" " full extent of the damage is not yet" " known, it is believed that fully one half " " the orange crop has been destroyed." " Lackily one shipment has been made to" " Liverpool before the disaster occurred, by" "SS " Zurburan," which has just arrived." "The Liverpool firm of W. H. Flett," " Limited, have been fortunate enough to" " have a large consignment on Board this " "vessel, but they do not anticipate getting" "nearly sufficient to meet the demand for" " their well known marmalade, the sale of " "which is fast increasing."

COMMON-SENSE VERSUS "PLUTO." Sir,—Your coriespondent " Pluto " in his last letter says" I cannot drag my language any lower to suit them" (myself and others.) He ia right ; he cannot. We have it on the best authority that it is not what goes in- to but what comes out of the mouth of a man that defiles him ; and your correspondent had a thousand times bet- ter be tarred and feathered to-morrow than suffer that inner defilement of which he seems in such immediate danger. With this word of solemn warning, I leave him. Yours, Sm.
MASTER OF ARTS.

THE ST. BA.RNABAS SCHOOL DISPUTE. Sir,—l was pleased to read the article in your paper of the 21st March, having reference to the St. Barnabas school dispute ; also your suggestiot that a subscription be opened on behalf of those gentlemen who have to bear the expense of the late trial. I wish you would take the matter up, and give a report now and again of the sympathisers with the men who have so unwittingly been drawn into this quagmire. I assure you they will have my assistance both by word and deed as soon as the worst is known. On behalf of those concersed I thank you very sincerely for your timely article.—Yours
THOS. MORRIS.

March 31st, 1891. [We shall be glad to assist in this matter. A good way of getting to work would be for sympathisers to com- municate with us, or Mr. Morris, who would probably be willing to act as treasurer of such fund as might and ought to be raised.—En. Ez.

THE ASSESSMENTS OF' LATCHFORD. Sir,—I note in your last issue a report of a meeting of ratepayers of Latchford. At the meeting I see Mr. J. Shaw Green was anxious to be informed whether the whole of Watrington was to be served the same in matter of assessment. Asa ratepayer on this side the bridge, I think it only fair that all parts of the borough should pay equal shares, but in spite of Messrs. Hawkins and Lunt's reply that the overseers kept raising assessments whenever they knew the rents had gone up, I wish to say that I know several cases where this has not been done. A friend of mine living in Wi!derspool-road pays the same rent that I do, but lam assessed at £4 more. Another friend in Latchford is rated £2 108. less than what he would be on the Lancashire side. I know it is possible the gentlemen questioned will reply that they did not know the rent. In these times this is no excuse. Mr. Tunstall finds out the rent, and so anomalies very rarely exist, whilst in Latchford, I believe if the truth were known anomalies are the rule and not the excep- tion. I trust in the interest of ratepayers on this side of the river that Messrs. Sliaw Green and Pierpoint will not rest satisfied with the mild protest of the Latchford overseers, but will investigate the matter to see where the truth lies.—Yours,
A RATEPA.YER.
SUNDAY TRAINS FOR RUNCORN..

Sir,—ln connection with this matter, which has formed the subject of correspondence in your columns for some little time past, perhaps you will permit me to give my experience. Some three winters ago. I left Runcorn for Chestet on Saturday afternoon to spend the week end with my friends. Circumstances compelled me to return on Sun- day evening. On alighting at Halton-road Station, I found sleet and rain were falling heavily, and at the end if the unpleasant journey of over three miles my boots and clothing were saturated, and I contracted a severe eold, from the effects of which I suffered for many weeks. I have had similar experiences since then. Complaint is made that most of the wealthy gentry have left the neighbourhood, and that consequently the town is deprived of their influence and support. Can it be wondered at that such should be the case when there is so much difficulty in getting into and out of the town,and when a residence in Runcorn practically means isolation ? Those who have the interests of the town really at heart should use their influence in endeavouring to re- move the disadvantages which it labours under in this respect.-1 am sir, yours truly, H. Runcorn, March 31st, 1891.

div.head: RIGHT REVEREND FATHER JAYNE AND
div.p: THE RIGHT REVEREND FATHER JAYNE AND

MS GIFT. Sir,—We, poor inhabitants of this ancient city of Ches- ter, have many things to be thankful for. If our bread is sometimes precarious and scanty, our water is sure, for have we not the noble Dee making its, graceful wind- ings almost at our doors? But the blessing which,above all others, fills us with gratitude, and makes our cup run over, is embodied in the near presence of a great man in Israel. His name is Jayne, and by way of honouring the Divine Teacher who-commanded His disciples to call no man their father, he is called the Right Reverend Father in God, Lord Bishop of Chester. And according to his own testimony—and who will dare to dispute it ? he is an accredited messenger of the King of Kings and Lord of Lords. With all this honour and glory upon him, he is so humble that we sometimes get a sight of him, and by a great effort may almost touch the hem of his garment when lie is not in his carriage. Yea, lie ac. wally c,oadcends to reside in a palace not far from our

squalid abodes, and to superintend the cure of our souls (our poor bodies are of no value in theology) for the paltry wage of £4,300 a year and a seat in the House of Lords, not the Lord's House. How very wonderful is all this, and what a crushing rebuke it administers to the pomp and magnificence of the poor fishermen of Galilee, who were sent out to preach the Gospel without purse oree.rip But this is not all. The good father's sheep are not all embraced in the fold at Chester, and, good shepherd that he is, he makes periodical journeys to the more remote parts of his diocese in order to confer his episcopal blessing upon the disciples there. A few months ago the newspapers informed us that he jour- neyed all the way from Chester to Stockton Heath, near Warrington, to perform the ceremony known in the Prayer Book as the order of confirmation. The Pressman did not tell us whether the reverend father travelled on foot after the manner of the Master whom he professes to follow, or on the comfortable cushions of a first class carriage. Most likely the latter was his mode of tran- sit, aysbeing more in harmony with his dignity and the spirft of the times. When he arrived at Stockton Heath, he found a large congregation composed of ecclesiastics and people called laymen, and the candidates for the holy office lie had come to administer. These were young people who had been gathered out of surrounding districts, and having been duly sprinkled and crossed in their infancy were regarded as" members of Christ, children of God, and inheritors of the kingdom of Heaven." If the blessings thus described were real and not shams the ordinary mind fails to see what more they required. But the keen insight of Father .Jayne saw that there was still something lacking to crown the spiritual edifice in these young disciples. And so, ad- dressing them, he said, "lie was there to bring them a gift—not to give it them—as one of the appointed and accredited messengers of the King of kings and Lord of lords. The gift was the King's, and the messenger was nothing in himself, except as the appointed and author- ised bearer of the gift. That gift was the greatest and best of all possible gifts—The gift of God's holy spirit." How the hearts the of young people must have waited in hushed expectation for the coming of their ghostly father! Rut oh, how tantalising to be told that he had brought them the gift of God's spirit,but was not going to give it to them. Had he travelled all the way from Chester merely to mock them and then send them empty away? They must have returned to their homes with strange thoughts, if they thought on the subject at all. How the reverend father enjoyed his lunch and champagne after the performance, it not my business to enquire, although it cost the poor agricultural labourers of England some £l2. But I may be permitted to express my astonishment and regret that such performances are still accepted as Christian teaching even i a the nineteenth century.—Yours truly,
RUABON.
Chester.
BIBLE HISTORY.
Sir,-1 hope you •will oblige by putting the enclosed extracts from the history of the Bible in your paper.— Yours truly,

div.head: IL C. BARNARD.
div.p: IL C. BARNARD.

7, Laira-st., Warrington. [rournacrs.] Of the many traditions which accord with the Mosaic history and which prevailed among the ancient nations, and still exist in several parts of the world, the follow- ing must be considered as singularly striking: That the woild was formed from some rude and shapeless matter by the spirit of God ; that the seventh day was a holy day ; that man was created perfect, and had the dominion given him over all the inferior animals ; that there had been a golden age, when in a state of inno- cence man had open intercourse with heaven ; that when his nature became corrupt, the earth underwent a change, thzt sacrifice was necessary to appease the offended Gods; that there was an evil spirit continually endeavouring to injure man and thwart the designs of the good spirit, but that he should at last be finally sub- dued, and universal happiness restored through the intercession of a Mediator ; that the life of man, during the first ages was of great length ; that there were ten generations previous to the deluge ; that only eight per- sons were saved out of the flood, in an ark, by the interposition of Deity. These and many other similar traditions are related to have been prevalent in the ancient world, by Egyptian, Plicenician. Greek, and Roman authors.--ifeurice's History of India. It is no small satisfaction to the friends of revealed religion that this argument has of late years received additional strength, from the discovery of an almost corresponding traditien, traced up among the nations whose records have been the best preserved to times even before the ago of Moses. The treasure of oriental learn- ing which Maurice collected with so much industry, and explained with so much judgment, in his" History and antiquities of India," supply abundance of incontrover- , tible evidence for the existence of opinions in the early ages of the world, which perfectly agree with the leading articles of our faith, as well as with the principal events related in the Pentateuch. In one passage he says. "whether tho reader will allow or not the inspiration of the sacred writer, his mind, on the perusal, must be struck with one very remarkable fact, namely, that the I names which are assigned by Moses to eastern countries and cities, derived to them immediately frcan the patriarchs, their original founders, are for the most part the very names by which they were anciently known over all the east. Many of them afterwards were trans- lated, with little variation by the Greeks, in their sys- tems of geography. Moses has traced, in one short chapter (Gen. 10) all the inhabitants af the earth, from Caspian and Persian seas to the extreme Gades, to their original, and recorded at once the period and occasion of their dispersion."—Histery of Hindostan, vol. 1. Whoever is acquainted with the writings of Bryant , and Maurice, and with the Asiatic researches, cannot but have observed that the accounts of the Creation, the fall, the deluge, and the dispersion of mankind, re- corded by the nations upon the vast continent of Asia, bear a strong resemblance to each other and to the nar- rative in the sacred history, and evidently contain the fragments of one original truth, which was broken by the dispersion of the patriarchal families, and corrupted by length of time, by allegory, and idolatry. From this universal concurrence on this head, one of these things is necessarily true: either that all the traditions must have been taken from the author of the Book of Genesis, or that the author of the Book of Genesis made up his history from some or all of such traditions as were already extant ; or, lastly, that he received his knowledge of past events by revelation. Were, then, all these traditions taken from the Mosiac history? It has been shown by Sir W. Jones and Maurice, that they were received too generally and too early to make this supposition even possible, for they existed in different parts of the world in the very age when Moses lived. Was the Mosaic history composed from the traditions then existing ? It is certain that the Chaldeans the pessians, the most ancient inhabitants of India, and the Egyptians, all possessed the same story; but they had, by the time of Moses, wrapped it up in their own myste- ries, and disguised it byytheir own fanciful conceits: and surely no rational mind can believe that if ?Awe had been acquainted with all the mystic fables of the East as well as of Egypt, he coOd, out of such endless variety of such obscure allego ,by the power of human sagacity aloae, have disco the real origin; much he's that from a partial . ge of some of them, he could have been .able tos discover facts which suit and explain them all. This plain recital, however, of the Creation, the fall, the deluge, and the dispersion of man- kind, does unquestionably develop that origin, and bling to light those facts; and it therefore follows, not only that the account is the true one, but there being no human means of his acquiring the knowledge of it, that it was, as he asserts it to have been, revealed to him by God Himself.

A HALTON FARMER AND HIS RATES. INTERESTING DECISION. John Rutter, farmer, Halton, was summoned be- fore the Runcorn magistrates on 'Tuesday for £4 4s. 144. poor rate.— Mr. A. Lismkeruppeared for the overseers and Mr. Maddock represented the defend- ant.—Mr. Linaker said the amount was tke ,defend- ant's proportion of the rate in respect of his occupation of Halton Lodge Farm, from the begin- ning ot October last to 24th November, which was the date the incoming tenant, Mr. Once, took possession. The defendant contended that he had no beneficial occupation between those dater, , because the landlord took possession in May last, re- leased all his effects,and discharged what liabilities there were against the farm in the way of rates, &c. The defendant remained in occupation of the house up to the Lth January, but he was not asked for any proportion in respect to that. If the objection that he had no .beneficial occupation was pressed he must ask the Bench to .follow the ruling in the case Regina v. the Justices of Warwickshire, where it was ruled that if a party con- tends that his occupation was not beneficial he must proceed by appeal at Quarter Sessions.—Mr. Woodier, the assistant overseer, said the total of the rate for the half year was £l6 ss. 54., and the defendant's proportion as stated. Mr. Grice, the present ten- ant, had appealed to the Assessment Committee against his assessment, which had in consequence been reduced by about £79. His proportion of the rate was therefore reduced from £l2 0(1. 51d. to £9 us. sp. Messrs. Pickering and Nightingale, of Chester, paid tho previous rate, he presumed out of the estate.— Mr. Maddock called the defendant who said his tenancy of the farm ceased on the 28th May, 1890, when his landlord, Lord Cholmondelev took possession because his rent was in arrear.—Mr. Brundrit : How did he come in possession ?—Mr. Maddock Ho came in under a clause in the agreement by which if the rent was in arrear he should take possession of the farm.—Defendant said from 28th May he managed the farm for Lord Choi- mondeley but there was a man in possession all the time ' until the sale on the 21st November. lie simply remained

in the house ; be was not the occupier; the other man was practically master, and Lord Cholmondeley's agent paid the tithe, poor rates,and everything that was due.— By Mr. Brundrit : He was acting on behalf of Messrs. Pickering and Nightingale, Lord Cholinondet-ay's agent. ] Mr. Nightingale visited the farm every Friday afternoon. —By Mr. Linaker : He never gave any notice to the assistant overseer.—By Mr. Maddock ,: He had reason to believe Mr. Woodier know because "ht. had been paid one rate by Mr. Nightingale, and had arplied to that gentleman for the present ttY,e.—Mr. Maddock said these proceedings were taken -became the assistant overseer had been unable to obtain -the rate from the persons to whom he had applied. *The defendant's occu- pation ceased when the landlord te.ok possession.—Mr. Rutter recalled, at Mr. :Linakeea request, said after the realisation of his effectsiin Novernb4r a balance was paid over to him by Lore Gholmondeley.—Mr. Linaker : There is beneficial occurration.—The Bench were of opinion that Mr. Buttes occupation had not been proved, and dismissed the summons.—Arthur Grice and George Gric• were then summoned for the other propor- tion of the rate—viz., £9 us. Bd.—Mr. Grice, the father of the two persons summoned, appeared and said he was the tenant.—Mr. Woodier said the sons lived at the farm and worked the place,and they told him to make to rates out to them.—Mr. Grice said he did not commence to pay rent until the 3rd April.—Mr. Brundrit said the rate was not apportioned to all in the rate book; how could he summon these people ?—Mr. Linaker : The sumer:one was issued before I saw it, and the assistant overseer must take the consequence.—The summons was dis- missed.
MR. IRVING.

ing," is the "stage name" of John be famous actor was born on , February 6, 1838, at Kemton, near Glastonbury, and was lucated at Dr. Pinches' !hool, in George-yard, Lom- .rd-st., London. Ile made first appearence on the Irds of the Sunderland ,eatre, September 29, 1856, Id came out next at Edin- ,urgh, February 9, 1837, re, er more than two years and a

)er of 1859, he appeared at the Princess's Theatre, where he remained about two months. le afterwards held engagements in Glasgow and Manchester. In 1865, in conjunction with Mr. McCabe, he appeared in a performance which was undertaken to expose the so-called. "spiritual seances" of the Davenport Brothers. On leaving Manchester he took a farewell benefit at the Free Trade Hall. From January, 1866, to July in that year he was engaged at the Prince of Wales's Theatre, Liverpool, and on July 30th was engaged to play with Miss Kate Terry, at Manchester, by Mr. Dion Boucicault in an original play of his, entitled "Hunted Down." This led to a London engagement, when he came out at the St. James's Theatre, as Doricourt in the "Belle's Stratagem." Ile next played the gambler, Itawdon Scudamore, in " Hunted Down," and from this time he became identified with the portraiture of villainy in all its forms. Mr. Irving also achieved successes in other roles. His representation of Hamlet at the Lyceum Theatre, in October 1874, produced a great sensation among the play-going public, and opinion was at first much divided as to the merits of the perform- ance, but it is now generally admitted that by his rendering of this and other Shakespearian parts, Mr. Irving has placed himself at the head of Eng- lish tragedians. In 1885 Mr. Irving won an unpre- cedented success with his new dramatic version of "Faust." Mr. Irving, in company with Miss Ellen Terry, has made two theatrical tours in the United States.
Mit. TOOLE.

John Laurence Toole, the comedian, was born, in London, on March 12, 1830, and was educated at the City of London School. He became a clerk to a wine merchant, but quitted this occupation, his taste lying in another direction. Having been smitten with the "bias lramatic," he V 7815 induced to lin the City Histrionic Club, 'here his qualifications for ;e dramatic profession were 400 n recognised, and he found

_unity for appearing before a r• lie audience at a benefit to Mr. F. Webster, at the Haymarket Theatre, July 22, 1852. Having successfully passed this ordeal, he resolved to become an actor, and commenced his professional career under Mr. Charles Dillon, at the Queen's Theatre, Dublin, where he achieved great success. After further testing his powers at Belfast, Edinburgh and Glasgow, he accepted, in 1854, an engagement at the St. James' Theatre, London, and sustained a variety of characters in low comedy with consider- able success. His style of acting is marked by a close fidelity to nature in every character he under- takes, whether it be in the broad region of farce, or in the more important parts in which tears and laughter equally predominate; such as " Caleb Plummer," in the version of Mr. Dickens's "Cricket on the Hearth," or the honest fireman," Joe Bright," in the drama "Through Fire and Water." For several years, Mr. Toole was in the habit of making a professional tour in the provinces, where he is as great a favourite as in the metropolis. In July, 1874, he went on a " starring " tour in the United States, and made his American debut at Wallack's Theatre, New York. In 1880, he commenced the management at the Folly Theatre, which he re- christened, and called after his own name—Toole's Theatre. In 1888, Mr. Toole published his reminis- cences, and last year he was accorded numerous farewell banquets on his departure for a tour in Australia.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
MAGIC LANTERN EXHIBITION.
Last evening, in connection with the Wesleyan Band of Hope, a public meeting was held in the schoolroom, when a magic lantern exhibition was given. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Gaudy.

div.head: MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.
div.p: MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.

On iiedii-e7day-eveuing,the concluding concert in connection with the Mutual Improvement Associa- tion was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom. There was a large attendance, and the meeting was pre- sided over by Mr. D. Garnett. An excellent pro- gramme, consisting of songs, pianoforte, cornet, ' clarionet, and violin solos, was gone through in a manner which elicited frequent applause from the audience. The following ladies and gentlemen took part in the programme :—The Misses Birtles, Fan- shaw. Garnett, and Langdon, and Messrs. Guest, Wigfield, Fanshaw, and Jones. During the evening refreshments, generously provided by Mr. Garnett, were handed round. A most enjoyable evening was brought to a conclusion by singing the National Anthem.

SUNDAY SCHOOL TEA PAILTY. Last evening week the annual tea party and en- tertainment of the Wesleyan Sunday School was held in the schoolroom. Tea was on the tables at five o'clock, and about 150 persons were present, who did every justice to the good things provided. The tea was prepared and the tables presided over by the lady teachers of the school. The first item on the programme was the general secretary's (Mr. B. Hobson's) report, which showed that the number
of scholars in the school was 222, with an average

attendance of 114 in the morning and 154 in the afternoon. The number of officers and teachers is 30. The Juvenile Missionary collection was largely in excess of the previous year. The secretary's re- port was followed by reports from the school trea- surer (Mr. John Jackson), the band secretary (Mr. T. Dunabin), and the Sick Club report was read by Mr. W. J. Wigfield. An interesting address was also given by Mr. Watson. During the evening , several double quartets were sung by the elder scholars with great taste and effect. Several reci- tations were also given by some of the scholars and friends. The prizes,which are given to the scholars for regular attendance, were kindly presented by Miss Parker. The first part of the programme was brought to a conclusion by a vote of thanks to all who had contributed to make the day's proceed- ings a success. The second part of the programme consisted of a magic lantern exhibition by Mr. R. E. Garnett, which was highly appreciated by the scho- lars.
THU RECREATION GROUND AND THE LORD OF
TUN MINOR.

As the result of a communication from the Assis- tant Overseer (Mr. T. IL Wilson), the Hon. Michael Hughes and his agent (Mr. Campbell) met a depu- tation consisting of Messrs. B. Hobson, J. T.Gumer- sail, J. B. Aitken, C. E. Parker, J. Foster (senior overseer), and the Rev. E. S. Jackson, on Monday, at the residence of Mr. M. Pownall, Great Sankey. Mr. Foster briefly mentioned ,the matter of the re- creation ground, and referred to the difficluty the ratepayers had experienced with regard to it, as it was not in a fit state for recreative purposes.—Mr. Hobson said the inhabitants of the township, who had hitherto had the free and uninterrupted rights of the heath, felt it would be a great hardship if the whole of the heath was enclosed without leav- ing some part for recreative purposes. A public meeting had adopted a memorial which was sent to the gentleman appointed by the Enclosure Commis- sioners,requesting him to make an enquiry into the matter. He approved the request, and promised to recommend it to the Commissioners. Subsequently it was decided that the non. Michael Hughes,Sherdley Hall, near St. Helens, was the rightful lord of the manor. Eventually a provisional order was received from the Commissioners, acceding to the request of the inhabitants, provided the right of herbage was made over to the lord of the manor, but with full rights to the people to enjoy the free use of the ground. He asked Mr. Hughes to give the right of herbage to the overseers for the time being.—The Hon. Michael Hughes said he would have been pleased to have fallen in with the wishes of the de- putation and the inhabitants generally, but that was impossible. The matter had been talked over by Mrs. Hughes and himself, but they were tied down by the estate being entailed, therefore, he re- gretted that they could not do as they had been re- quested.—Mr. Hobson tken asked Mr. Hughes if he would lease the ground to the overseers for a long period at a peppercorn rent.—Mr. Hughes replied that for the same reasons Le did not see how he, could grant this request. He thought the best plan would be to let the ground to the overseers of the township, at a fair yearly rent, and afterwards re- duce the rent by a gift. That would bring it some- thing near what the deputation required, and he thought Mrs. liughes would be agreeable. He pro- mised to consult with her when he reache I home, and write them his decision.—The deputation ex- pressed themselves satisfied with the offer Mr. Hughes had made, and the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the lion. Michael Hughes for the kind and genial manner in which he had entered into the spirit of the matter.

div.head: FRIENDS' SCHOOL, PENKETH.
div.p: FRIENDS' SCHOOL, PENKETH.

On Good Friday, the annual gathering of the old scholars took place at the Friends' School, Penketh. In the morning, the school football team opposed a team of old boys, and gave them a thorough thrashing, the score at the close of the game reading—Present, 11 goals, Past, nil. Despite the unfavourable state of the weather, there was a large attendance of old scholars and sup- porters of the school. The school museum was thrown open for the inspection of the visitors, members of the eld club acting as guides. After dinner, at which a large company was present, the old scholars were photo- graphed in a group by Mr. Hall (Lymrn). At the after- noon meeting, the President of the Old Scholars' Associa- tion, Mr. C. Bradshaw (Manchester) occupied the chair. Araongst the andience were—the Headmaster, Mr. J. T. Gummersall ; Alderman Holmes, Warrington; Mr. S. Whalley Davies, Birkenhead, treasurer; Mr. F. W. Fol- lows, secretary, Manchester; Mr. C. J. Holmes, Warrington; Mr. J. E. Davies, Warrington ; Mr. John Holdswerth, Eccles ; Mr. B. Matthews, Newcastle -on - Tyne; Mr. J. Spence Hodson, Manchester. After an address by the Chairman, the Secretary stated that the balance in hand, after paying all expenses during the year,a mounted to £l3. He hoped that, with the subscriptions which would be paid that day, the sum le hand would be about £3O. It was not intended that that money should lie idle ; he therefore, invited suggestions as to the manner of its dispasal.—Mr. S. W. Davies, after a reference to his eariy connection with the school, which dated back to 1836, spoke of the , necessity which existed for helping the old scholars after they had begun life in the outside world.—The Secretary expressed a hope that that day's meeting aveuld result in something tangible. Since the days of which Mr. Davies had epoken, every effort had been made to make it a real , home for the boys and girls who were being educated ' there. There was an able man at the head of affairs, and he hoped that Mr. Gumersall would stay at Penketla for • many years to come. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman moved that the balance of subscriptions and donations ; in the hands of the treasurer be carried forward to next year's account as a reserve fund, and then be expended • in the erection of a gymnasium, or in some other manner to be decided upen.—Mr. B. Matthews seconded the pro- - position, and it was agreed to.—On the motion of Mr. ' F. Haselden, seconded by Mr. A. Ratcliffe, and supported ; by Mr. W. Timeerley, the Chairman, and the Secretary, Mr. J. Spence Hodson was elected an honorary member of the association.—The Chairman nominated Mr. F. W. L Monks (Warrington) as president for the ensuing year.— I The motion was seconded by Mr. C. J. Holmes, and carried, the understanding being that if Mr. Monks de- dined to accept the post, Mr. Bradshaw would act for another year.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought I the meeting to a close.

Mn. CUARLES LISTRR, J.P., of Agden Hall. Lymm, was one of the magistrates who voted against the granting of the license to the Manchester Palace of Varieties. SUDDEN DEATII OF A CIFILD.—The death of an infant named Alfred Holt, aged seven weeks, Fon of J. F. Holt, labourer, Statham, has been reported to the Lymm police. The child, which has been a healthy one from birth, experienced some difficulty ia breathing on Thursday Last week, and on Friday morning when the mother awoke at three a.m., she was horrified to find her child dead in her arms. The facts of th• case were reported to the Coroner, who deemed an inquest unnecessary. SATURDAY NIOUT CONCERTS.—ThW last but one of the series of popular penny concerts was given in the Ilridgewater Rooms on Saturday evening. There was a large attendance, and an enjoyable programme was sub- mitted. Mr. Allen occupied the chair, and in addition to the usual "ten minutes' address," gave a reading. Miss Tipping played a pianoforte solo in a pleasing manner, and Misses Dutton, Brown, and Thorpe were duly applauded for their songs and duets. Messrs. G. and Thomas Warburton were encored for an instru- mental duet, and Messrs. Collier, Hall, and Briggs were very successful in their trio " Jonny Schmoker." The two last-named each contributed a reading.

div.head: NUTGROVE WESSEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: NUTGROVE WESSEYAN CHAPEL.

The Nutgrove Wesleyan Chapel was crowded on Mon- day evening when the Rev. P. Mackenzie, lectured on "The tongue; its use and abuse." The lecture was in- teresting and instructive. The chapel was decorated with plants kindly lent by Mr. Nuttall. Dr. Hawkes,of Liverpool, occupied the chair, and among those present were the Rev. A. P. Watson, the Rev. G. Hammond, and Mr. Andatton (secretary).

div.head: ANNUAL SAILING MATCH.
div.p: ANNUAL SAILING MATCH.

The annual event was on Saturday witnessed by several thousand spectators. The course was from Widnes to a buoy moored at Six Acres, near Walton Bridge, and thence to the west end oi Thewlis's wall, near Bank Quay. There was a favourable wind at the start, which was made with an hour and a half flood. For some time the boats kept well together, but eventually Tom Bowling forged ahead and maintained a premier position throughout. The Thistle made a good second. There was an exciting struggle for third plaLte, Pink and Seagull being the competitors for the honour. The former, however, ultimately sailed in third winner. Seagull was 4th and Gipsy sth. The following is a list of the boats that took part in the race :—Tom Bowling, Captain A. W. Howard; Thistle, Captain E. Gleave ; Pink, Captain W. Warburton ; Seagull, Captain T. Skel- horn : Gipsy, Captain Joseph Lea; May Fly. Cap- tain J. Thomas ; Blue Bell, Captain J. E. Jefferson ; Deerfoot, Captain Monks; Florence, Captain 11. Warburton; and Saxon, Captain John Lea. The officials were Messrs. John Whitfield, treasurer; C. Naylor, secretary ; C. Gill, number taker; G. G. White, judge; and Mr. Rath bone, starter. The race was considered to have been a good one, and the knowing Ones amongst the crowd had many critic- isms to offer regarding the "seamanship " of the navigators. The pilot of the winning boat received every credit for his skilful management. A COURAGEOUS POLICEMAN RESCUES A CHILD. A child named William Welsby,son of Thomas Welsby, wiredrawer, 22, Railway-square, Bank Quay, Warring- ton,was one of the thousands of spectators gathered along the banks of the river to witness the local boat race. He was romping about on the bank between Mr. Crosfield's crossing and Mr. Litton's mill,when frmn some cause he fell into the water. Police-constable Turner was on duty near the spot, and hearing the screams of the people he hastened thither. Seeing the boy's perilous position, he throw off his helmet and jumped into the river, which at this point was rather deep, and succeeded in reaching the lad as he was sinking for the second time. Theofficer was up to the neck in water and weighed down by his heavy coat.and, being no swiminer,he had great difficulty in reaching the bank. He,however,preserved his presence of mind, and succeeded amidst the applause of the on- lookers, in bringing the lad to the bank,where there were many willing hands to assist the rescued and the rescuer. The boy was rubbed down, and then promptly con- veyed home. The rescue was witnessed by a large crowd of people, who complimented Constable Turner on his heroic conduct.

SHOCKING ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER AT ST. HELENS. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, before Alderman J. 11`Bride and Mr. W. J. Thompson, Geo. Warren, of 13, Elliott-street, was charged on re- mand with unlawfully wounding his wife Esther on the 20th ultimo.—Chief Constable Wood prosecuted and stated that the prisoner struck his wife many times on the head with a piece of iron, inflicting several wounds, some of which penetrated to the hone. The injured woman had since been confined to bed in the hospital, and he asked for the prisoner's committal to the assizes.—Eather War- ren, the prosecutrix, was then called. Her head was bandaged, and she appeared to be in a very weak condition. She was provided with a seat while giving her evidence. She stated that the prisoner was her husband and was a bottle maker. She was married to him about three years and three months ago. During the greater portion of that time they lived very unhappily together. He was ad- dicted to drink and neglected his work, and very often assaulted her. She had to leave him several times on account of his violent conduct. About twelve months since he was sent to Rainhill Asylum. He was liberated about last Christmas, and they afterwards lived toge- ther for atYout three weeks. She then left him because Ihe would not go to his work. He threatened her on one occasion wheu she spoke to him about it. He then went to live with his parents in Elliott-st., and she went to live with her mother in Campbell-St. Whilst they were living apart he asked her to go and live with him, but ehe told him she would not do so until he got back to his work. On the night of Friday, the 20th ultimo. she was going along Peter-st.when the prisoner came behind her and said, "Hello, is that you ?" She replied, "Yes, it's me," and turned round to look at him. Re then drew some weapon from his coat sleeve or from his pocket and struck her a violent blow on the forehead. She screamed and ran into a house, No. 75, Peter-st. The prisoner followed her and struck her on the head in the lobby. In the kitchen he again struck her and knocked her down. He seized her by the arm, and with his other hand he beat her awfully aboutthehead with the weapon. She lost a great deal of blood, and he went out by the front door, leaving her Icing on the floor. She was shortly afterwards assisted to Dr. Cotton's surgery, in Liverpool- road, where the doctor dressed her wounds and ordered her removal to the Providence Hospital. The prisoner knew what he was doing when he assaulted her with the weapon. —The prisoner said he had no questions to ask.—Mary Elizabeth James, wife of William James, 75, Peter-st., gave corroborative evidence that she saw the parties Tun into her house. She was in the back kitchen, and saw the prisoner attack the wife as described by the prosecti- trix in her evidence. The prosecutrix was coverethwith blood, and witness ran out by the :back door.—Tho pri- soner was asked if he had any question to ask the wit- ness, and he replied" ; I've nothing to ask nobody. You can do what you like to me—you can hang me."— Ann Jane-Hopkins, wife of John Hopkins, 11, Elliott-st., said she had known the prisoner for several years. On the night in question she was in his parents' house when the prisoner entered. He would not sit on the chair as, he said, lie was waiting to be locked up. He added, "I have killed her." There was blood on his face and hands, and he wanted to wash his hands.-Dr. Cotton gave evidence that the prosecutrix was brought to his surgery He found her suffering from eleven severe contused wounds on the scalp, two of them being from three or four inches long, and the others about one or two inches in length. Three or four of the wounds had penetrated the bone. The poker produced would be likely to cause the wounds. He considered the woman's life was in danger for several days, and she was not yet quite out of danger.—Police Constable James Harrison proved the prisoner's apprehension.—This concluded the evidence, and the prisoner, after being cautioned, was asked if he had anything to say. He replied—" Yes. Well, I feel that bad I don't care whether I die or not. You can put me down now if you like. I would be better off if I was dead, because I am in so much pain and misery. As for the doctors in St. Helens—l was never fit for work, and I was never examined properly as I should have been. That is all I have to say. You can de what you like—a fellow is better dead than al- ways he in pain and misery. Hang me to-morrow if you like ; that dosen't fear me in the way I am now. Mv head is knocking about with pain, and has been like that for a good while."—The prisoner, who had manifested a callous disposition and seemed totally indifferent to the proceedings, was then committed for trial at the next assizes. On being removed from the dock, he exclaimed "There'll boa b-- coffin for me beforethree months.'

WIFE MURDER AT BIRMINGHAM Yesterday morning a man named John Patchett, aged 30,a brushmaker, gave himself up to a police- man at Birmingham, stating that he had stabbed his wife. The officer went with him to his home in Cheapside, and found the woman lying at the bottom of the stairs. The constable took from her arms a six months' old baby, which was crying, and found that tha woman was dead, having received a deep wound in the throat. It seems that the par- ties had quarrelled upstairs, and that the woman on being wounded rushed to the staircase, and fell down. Patchett used to be a steady man, and it is , alleged that he was driven to drink by the de- ceased's intemperate habits. TERRIBLE COLLIERY ACCIDENT IN STAF-

div.head: FORDSIIIRE.
div.p: FORDSIIIRE.
TEN LIVES LOST.

On Thursday night a dreadful explosion hap- pened at Gladderdale Pit, Apedale, near Newcastle- under-Lyne, by which ten men and boys are re- ported to have lost their lives. The bodies have not been recovered. The colliery belongs to the Mid- land Coal, Coke, and Iron Co., and the pit adjoins the Burley Pit, in which 19 lives were lost a few years ago. The explosion occurred in the Bullhurst seam. A party of explorers, who descended as soon as pos- sible, found that it had taken place where a work- man, named Knight, had been making a cutting, and it is thought his shot caused the accident. The names of the killed are :—John Warburton, fire- man, married, Audley ; A. Knight, married, Ches- terton ; Fred Webb, married, Wood-lane ; George Hall, married, Chesterton; James Holland, mar- ried, Dunkirk ; Joseph Birch, single, Dunkirk. It appears now that the explosion occurred at eight o'clock on Thursday night. This fact will partially account for the small number of men in the mine at the time of the catastrophe, as in busy seasons about 250 men are employed there. The explosion was heard for a mile or so around, but it was not until yesterday morning that the news reached Chesterton, where six of the victims lived. The inquest will be opened to-day (Saturday.)
DISORDER AT THE MINERS' CONFERENCE IN
FRANCE.

PARIS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The Miners' Conference this afternoon was marked by scenes of wild dis- order. Business being rendered impossible, the con- ference, which was to have closed to-day,decided to have an extra sitting to-morrow and then abruptly adjourned.
THE ELECTION AT SLIGO.

div.head: VICTORY OF THE NATIONALIST-
div.p: VICTORY OF THE NATIONALIST-

The polling for the election of a member for the par- liamentary division of North Sligo, vacant by the death of Mr. Peter M' Donald, commenced on Thursday morning ,at eight o'clock. There are fifteen polling stations in the nine electoral districts of the division. Mr. Parnell walked round the streets just after the opening of the booths, but was hardly noticed. About midday there was considerably increased excitement in Sligo town. consequent upon the arrival, in marching order, at the Court House polling booth, of three successive contin- gents, each of about 300 electors, from the outlying parishes in the Sligo district. The last batch of ballot boxes arrived at Sligo from the country districts at seven o'clock on Friday mivrning and the counting commenced at ten. The corrected result was declared as follows : Celery (Anti-Parnellite) 3,261 Dillon (PArnellite)
Majority against Parnellite
TABLEAUX AT THE MOUNT SCHOOLS.

On Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, in the pre- sence of large audiences, exhibitions of tableaux were given at the Mount School, in aid of the War- rington Parish Church improvements and the Crossley-St. new mission room. The tableaux were representative of the following subjects :—The Sleeping Beauty, Pygmalion and Galatea, Auld Robin Gray, The Interrupted Dance, The Village School in Days gone by, Forty Winks, Happy Days, Childhood's Tears, An Unwarrantable Intrusion, April Ist, William Tell. The tableaux were admir- ably exhibited, and showed both realistic conception and artistic training in the repre- sentatives of the characters depicted. Musical selections and songs were at intervals given by a quintette string band, and ladies and gentle- men :—Overture, " Marionette Overture," (Gurlitt); song," Galatea," Mr. R. Fairclough ; song, 4- Auld Robin Gray," Miss Maddock; entertainment, Quin- tette Minuet by Boccerini, McCarthy ; chorus, " Nineteen Birds," school children ; chorus, " Three Crows," school children ; song, " Old and New," Miss Slater; vo,;al waltz," See-saw," school children; chorus, " Georgie Porgie "; Quint,-;t1 e, Roundelay by Boggetti ; entettainment, IL McDougall, Esq., Song " When the heart, is young," Miss Slater; Quintette, Lain du Bul ; song," Saint Anthony" Mr. P. C. Price ;concluding with a Quintette "Kangaroo." The string quartette, was composed as follows :—ist violin, Mr. R. IL Pearson; 2nd violin, Mr. John Roberts; Viola, Mr. John Burrows; 'cello, Mr. H. Bond ; basso, Mr. Whitfield. Mr. Alfred Woods officiated as stage manager and he in conjunc- tion with Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Willcocks, Mrs. R. Fairclough, and Mrs. J. Fsirclough, the prin- cipal promoters of the entertainment, may be con- gratulated on the results of their exertions. It is worthy of mention that the programme was adorned with illustrations of the tableaux which were most artistically designed and executed by Mrs. Houghton of Warrington.

div.head: VIOLETING IN MARCH.
div.p: VIOLETING IN MARCH.

IV The lastest issue of the Camelot series published by Mr. Walter Scott is " Our Village by Mary Russell Mitford, edited, with an introduction, by Ernest IthyE." No genuine lover of nature can spend a shilling better than in the purchase of this charming volume. Miss Mitford's prose is worth studying; it has the elements of poetry in it. We give a seasonable extract from the chapter on " Vio- leting ": Now a few yards farther. and I reached the bank. Ah I I smell them already—their exquisite perfume steams and lingers in this moist, heavy air. Through this little gate, and along the green south bank of this green wheat-field, and they burst upon me, the lovely violets, in tenfold loveliness. The ground is covered with them, white and purple, enamelling the short, dewy grass, looking but the more vividly coloured under the dull, leaden sky There they lie by hundreds, by thousands. In former years I have been used to watch them from the tiny green bud, till one or two stole into bloom. They never came on me before in such a sudden and luxuriant glory of simple beauty—and I do really owe one pure and genuine pleasure to feverish London! how beauti- fully they ate placed, too, OD this sloping bank, with the palm branches waving over them, full of early bees, and mixing their honeyed scent with the more delicate violet odour! How transparent and smooth and lusty are the branches, full of sap and life: And there, just by the old mossy root, is a superb tuft of primroses, with a yellow butterfly hovering over them, like a flower floating on the air. What hap- piness to sit on this tufty knoll, and fill my basket with the blossoms ! What a renewal of heart and mind! To inhabit such a scene of peace and sweetness is again to be fearless, gay, and gentle as a child. Then it is that thought becomes poetry, and feeling religion. Then it is that we are happy and good. Oh, that my whole life could pass so, floating on blissful and innocent sensation, enjoying in peace and gratitude the common blessings of Nature, thankful above all for the simple habits, the healthful temperament, which rendered them so dear! Alas! who may dare expect a life of such happiness? But I can at least snatch and prolong the fleeting pleasure, can fill my basket with pure flowers, and my heart with pure thoughts; can gladden my little home with their sweetness; can , divide my treasures with one, a dear one, who can- not seek them; can see them when I shut my eyes; i and dream of them when 1 fall asleep.
