THE CLITHE ROE ABDUCTION. FURTHER DEMONSTRATIONS. Another unsuccessful attempt was made at Clitheroe on Mouday night to burn the effigy of Mrs. Jackson. Large crowds gathered in the streets hooting and groan- ing as on Saturday night, the hostile demonstration be- ing particularly marked in front of Mr. Baldwin's house. Extra police have been brought into the town from Blackburn, and to this is. probably owing the fact that there was no renewal of the rioting on Sunday. The police were at times severely hustled. An influential committee formed in the district has is- sued an appeal for funds to carry the Clitheroe abduction case to the House of Lords in the interests of religion and morality. TEACHERS' CONFERENCE. CONFERENCE. The twenty-second annual Conference of the National Union of teachers was opened at Cardiff on Monday- Mr. George Collins, member of the London School Board, • was installed president for the ensuinc, year, and de- livered the inaugural address, in which he dealt with the condition of national education. Now that it had been established for twenty-one years, he held it to be an en- couraging sign that while the expenditure on education had increased, that on pauperism and crime diminished. In the evening the delegates attended a con versaziono at University College. On Tuesday the question of the supply of school- teachers was one of the subjects discussed. It was de- cided that the next annual conference should be held at Leeds at Easter, 1892. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT RIXTON. -- Late on Saturday night, an outbreak of fire was discovered on a farm at Rixton, belonging to Mr. J. 'Stubbs, Rixton. Intelligence was sent to Warring' ton, and the fire brigade turned out promptly. :10 sacks of thrashed oats, 21 stacks of hay, and corer and a large quantity of potatoes and other produce, • together with the building in which it was stored, • were destroyed, the damage amounting to baween' £7OO and £BOO. The farm produce was insured. The origin of the tire is unknywn. Information of the oat' break was received by telegram from Glazahrook way station, and the Warrington Fire Brigade under the direction of Mr. Frank Turner, the supetintendent, soOn started for the scene of the conflagration. They sOOO got to work, and played on the building and stacksiurr tel half-past seven on Sunday morning, when they were requested by Mr. Stubbs to discontinue their efforts; Mr. Stubbs saw that it was impossible to save any ot the stock, and the brigade, therefore, returned home. singular circumstance is related by the superintendent. He states that on arriving at Rixton he sat,/ a nuniber, of labourers talking in a lane near the fire. He askeu them to render assistance during the fire, but they sul; lenly- refused to do so. Shortly afterwards it was fouou, that the hose had been_ wilfully damaged, and fresh had to be laid down.- No clue has yet been obtained as to the perpet!ators of the outrage. . .

• ROBBING A STEPFATBEIL—DanieI Massey. 13 years of age. was charged with stealing a waistcoat belonging to his step- father, Thomas Johnson, of SO, Cooper-st. The boy had pawned the waistcoat at Mr. Lightfoot's pawnshop,! or Is. 6d. and then gone to Overton Hills where he spent the money.— Mr. Brundrit said the boy had been in trouble a short time since when he received six strokes ;they would now try twelve strokes and if he did not Improve he would be sent to a Re- formatory School.—The prisoner (who was weeping) :I want to go there now. WON THE MATCH AND LOST MIS MONEY.—Jabez Peck- stock, a young man was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly on Saturday night. A Constable said the prisoner was fighting opposite the Royal. The Prisoner said he had bet a man ss. to 4s. that Runcorn beat St. Helens Recreation and like an honest man handed over the ss. When the match was over the man refused to pay him the 9s. or return him his stake and that caused the dispute. He had not got the money yet. (Laughter.) A fine of ss. and costs 10s. 10d. was inflicted. --- WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. A. Fletcher. and Mr. J. Bingham. MISCELLANEOUS.—For being drunk John Spencer, James Killalea, Thomas Killalea, and Patrick Leonard, were each fined ss. and costs. William Whitley Coates (Gateacre), was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk while in charge of a horse and trap.—Joseph Killalea was bound over to be of gwd behaviour for three months for creating a breach of the pea. Thomas Clare, Church-street, was malcted in the sum of 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing his dog to be at large unmuz- zled. ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF PlGS.—Samuel Ryes, lodginghouse keeper, Lugsclale road, was summoned for having on the 23rd , March removed eight pigs from Northwich in Cheshire, to Widnes in Lancashire, contrary to an order issued under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act.—The defendant, who , said he did not knew he required a license to remOve the pigs, was fined 10s. and costs.

BArLIE OF FLOWERS AT GRASSE. GRASSE, MONDAY.—The battle of flowers and vreoeso, aion, organised in honour of Queen Victoria, passed eff most successfully, being favoured by splendid weather. Thousands of visitors flocked into the town to witness the festivities. THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC. 300 DEATHS IN ONE DAY. CHICAGO, TIIESDAY.—Mr. Tomlinson,registrar of deatha reports that nearly 300 deaths have taken place during the last 24 hours. This is the highest record since the commencement of the influenza epidemic. Yesterday the streets leading to the graveyards were completely blocked with funerals. Three processions became en- tangled in Warren-avenue' and the greatest confusion ensued. It is estimated that no fewer than 600 tyKlies are awaiting burial to-day. The weather is rainy though warm. EXTRAORDINARY SCALDING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. The adjourned inquest on the body of James Crow, aged 47, of Prescot-st., who died at the Acci- dent Hospital, on the 25th Mt., was resumed at the Police Court, on Wednesday afternoon. Mn C. B. Richmond, the inspector of factories, was present. Mr. Knowles represented the Widnes Alkali Com- pany. The evidence adduced showed that at mid- night on the Ist March the deceased, who was s boilerman at the Widnes Alkali company's Works; went to inspect a tank in the yard. A few Minutes later Thomas Risley, an engine driver, met him cow- ing from the place, and he said he had slipped off the ladder and fallen into the tank. He did not complain of being scalded, but said he would go home and his clothes were wet through. On his arrival home he was found to be badly scalded about the lower portion of the body and after being at home for ten days, Dr. Allen his medical attendant ordered his removal to the Accident Hospital, ill order that he might have better accommodation and 'he died there as stated. The deceased informed his " wife and son that the ladder " canted" over and eo caused him to fall into the tank which is 4 feet above the ground. Risley said the water in the tank was heated by the steam from the exhaust pipes but he could easily bear his hand in the water, but Mr. Richmond said he was informed the average heat of the water was 170 degrees.—The jury returned verdict of '• accidental death," and expressed tile opinion that no blame attached to the firm or anY other person.
